Welcome — here's the plan

You're starting from zero, you've got a few hours a week, and the goal at the end of all this is a simple game and a simple app — with mobile versions of both somewhere down the road. Here's the path this guide follows, and why it's shaped this way.

Why JavaScript, not Python? Python is usually the "easiest first language" advice — and it's not wrong in general. But it hits a wall right at your mobile step: there's no strong, well-maintained bridge from Python to a real mobile app or game. JavaScript carries through every stage above with the same language — web app → browser game → installable mobile app (React Native) and mobile game (Phaser wrapped with Capacitor). One language, no relearning later.

What you actually need to start

✅ A web browser

Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari — whatever you already have. This is where all your code will run, for a long while.

✅ A free text editor

VS Code (Visual Studio Code) is the standard choice — free, works on any OS, huge community. Download it from Microsoft's official site and install it like any normal app.

🚫 No Python needed

We're going the JavaScript route (see above) — no separate language to install.

🚫 No Xcode / Android Studio yet

Those are for real native mobile builds — that's section 12+ territory, months from now. Don't install anything mobile-related yet.

What name should go on your certificate?

You will earn two of them by the end of this. This is the only place you type your name — the badges, the certificates and everything else read it from here. It stays in this browser and is sent nowhere.

How progress + check-ins work

The sidebar on the left shows the whole path — locked sections have a 🔒. Sections unlock for real: there is no "click next to continue" button anywhere in this guide. A section opens the next one only once you have passed every gradable exercise in it and solved the puzzle hidden inside it. Your progress is remembered on this device, so you can close the page and come back to exactly where you were.

Two things to know about those puzzles, because they are not signposted. Most sections contain a small number of exercises marked Clue found when you get them right — the row of slots under each section title shows how many are still hidden. Collect all of a section's clues and a hidden panel becomes reachable somewhere in that section's text. Nothing marks it. Somewhere in that section, one word is carrying a claim that is wrong — and the clues are what tell you enough to spot it. When you find it, double-click it, or press and hold it on a phone, and the panel opens. This is the only place in the guide that tells you the gesture; no section will remind you. Everything you find is kept in the Badges & Clues panel in the sidebar, where you can read any of it again. That panel also holds a badge for every section you finish outright — each one named for what you can do afterwards rather than for the section it came from; the clues themselves tell you roughly what you are looking for.

There is also a quick-note box at the bottom of every section for jotting a thought in the moment, and a standing My Progress Notes page (left sidebar, always open) if you want to log notes or screenshots as you go and compile them later. Everything you write stays only on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Prove it all works

The code boxes in this guide are convenient, but they are not the real thing. Every browser has a proper JavaScript console built into it, and you should meet it now — it is where you will check things, test one-liners, and read your error messages for as long as you write JavaScript.

Open it:

  • Chrome or Edge on Mac: Cmd + Option + J
  • Chrome or Edge on Windows: Ctrl + Shift + J
  • Safari: first turn on Settings → Advanced → "Show features for web developers", then Cmd + Option + C
  • Any browser, the slow way: right-click anywhere on a page → Inspect → the Console tab

You should get a panel with a blinking cursor next to a > prompt. Type this into it exactly, then press Enter:

[1, 2, 3].join("-")

What did the console give back? (Type it here exactly as it appeared, without the surrounding quote marks. On Safari: if you also see something like = $1 tacked on the end, that is just Safari numbering the result so you can reuse it later — it is not part of the answer, and you do not need to type it.)

The console is also where errors go. When a page's JavaScript breaks, nothing visible happens on the page itself — the message goes here instead, in red, with the file and line number. A very large share of "my code does nothing and I do not know why" is solved by simply having this panel open.
WatchFuture Fullstack · 7:39

The JavaScript Console Explained for Absolute Beginners

If you want to see someone else do what you just did: it explains the console as a window into the JavaScript engine, opens DevTools, separates ordinary log messages from the red error box, then types 6 + 6 and gets 12. Pitched at genuinely zero.

Setup checklist

Five things. This one is on your honour — the guide has no way of seeing your machine, so ticking the box without doing them only cheats you.

  1. Install VS Code from the official Microsoft site, and open it at least once.
  2. Make a folder somewhere sensible for your code — Documents/code is fine — and open that folder in VS Code (File → Open Folder).
  3. Create a file inside it called index.html. Leave it empty for now; you just need to have made a file.
  4. Open your browser's developer console using the shortcut above, and find the Console tab.
  5. Run [1, 2, 3].join("-") in it and read the answer, as above.

Honest pacing note. At a few hours a week, expect a first simple app to take roughly 2–4+ months, and a first simple game another 2–6 months on top of that — realistically one after the other, not side by side. Mobile versions come after both, and add real additional months. This isn't a "learn to code in a weekend" plan. It's a real one.

Variables & data

What this section lets you do

Section 1 got your tools ready. This is where you start writing code that does something.

By the end of this section you’ll be able to:

  • show words and numbers in the console
  • do sums with code
  • give things names, so your code can keep track of a score, a name or a price
  • tell different kinds of information apart, and turn one kind into another
  • tidy up messy text and numbers that a person has typed in

How these pages work. Each page teaches one new thing. You’ll usually guess first, then see what really happens. Guessing wrong is fine — a guess is never marked. It’s how you find out what you actually thought.

Showing something: console.log

The idea: console.log shows something in the console.

At the end of this page you’ll explain console.log in your own words, as if to someone who has never seen code. Keep that in mind as you go.

You copied a line like this in Section 1. Now you’ll find out what each part of it does.

Breaking it down

Read it from left to right. Each part has one job:

So console.log means the log tool that belongs to the console. A logbook is a written record of what happened, one line after another. Each console.log adds a line to the console’s logbook.

Words go inside quote marks. Numbers don’t need them: console.log(7) shows 7.

Who sees the console? You do — the person writing the code. It’s tucked away in the browser’s developer tools, the panel you opened in Section 1. People playing your game or using your app don’t see it unless they go digging in there. So console.log is your behind-the-scenes notebook for checking what your code is doing. It isn’t a way of showing things to the people using your app; that’s a different job, done with different code.

Another way to see it

The console is like a logbook that only ever gets new lines at the bottom. Step through this one line at a time and watch the console fill up. Each new line goes underneath the last; the old ones stay put.

Here’s console.log inside a finished program: the start of the scoreboard game. The console.log lines are bright. The rest is grey because you don’t need it yet.

  2. Take the quote marks away, so it reads console.log(Hello). You’ll get a red error: without quote marks, the computer looks for something called Hello, and finds nothing.
  3. Put the quote marks back and take away the closing bracket ). Now the computer can’t read the line at all.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

One instruction at a time

The idea: a program is a list of instructions called statements. The computer does them one at a time, from the top down.

Breaking it down

Each of those lines is one instruction. The real name for one instruction is a statement.

The computer runs statements in order, top to bottom, one at a time. It doesn’t skip ahead or jump back on its own.

The ; at the end of each line is a semicolon. It marks where a statement ends, a bit like a full stop at the end of a sentence. JavaScript can usually work out where a statement ends without one, but writing it makes it certain. This guide always writes it, and from here on, so will you.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till again. The order of the statements is the order things appear on the receipt.

Your turn
Statements run one at a time, top to bottom. ; marks where each one ends.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

StepThe line it runsThe console now shows

One line per step. Nothing happens until the step before it has finished.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Notes the computer skips

The idea: anything after // on a line is a comment: a note for people. The computer skips it.

Breaking it down

// is two forward slashes. Everything from them to the end of that line is a comment. The computer skips comments completely. They’re there for people.

A comment can have a line to itself, or sit after a statement on the same line:

Why bother? A comment is a note for whoever reads the code later, which is often you, weeks from now. Programmers also put // in front of a line to switch it off for a while, without deleting it.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till, with notes left by whoever wrote it.

Your turn
// note: everything after // on a line is a comment. The computer skips it.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Switch a line off and on. Press Edit the code. Put // at the very start of the middle line and run it: that line stops showing. Then take the // away and run it again: it’s back. The line itself never went anywhere. The // just tells the computer to skip it.

Who sees it: alert or console.log

The idea: alert("Hi") opens a pop-up that the person using the page sees. console.log("Hi") writes to the console, which only you see.

Here’s the mini browser again, with an alert in the JS tab. Press ▶ Run:

When you press Run, the pop-up appears on the page, in front of the user. The message "Only I can see this" goes to the console, which the user never looks at.

Breaking it down

alert is written just like console.log: what to show goes in the brackets. The difference is where it shows up, and so who sees it. This guide uses console.log almost all the time, because it’s for checking your own code. alert is for when you really want to stop the user and tell them something.

Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Ask one question: who is it for? A message for the person playing your game goes on the page, and alert is the simplest way to put it there. A message for you, while you check your code, goes in the console with console.log. Both are written the same way; only the first word changes.

Part A, in your own words

You’ve now met everything in a single line of code, and two places its messages can go. Before moving on, pull it together. First, check you can say what each word is:

Doing sums

The idea: the computer can do sums. + adds, - takes away, * multiplies and / divides.

Breaking it down

The keyboard has no × or ÷ key, so code uses * to multiply (Shift + 8) and / to divide (the key next to the right-hand Shift).

Notice there are no quote marks: these are real numbers, so the computer works out the answer.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till again: adding up three items, then sharing a £12 bill between 4 people.

Your turn
+ add · - take away · * times · / divide. These are operators.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Quote marks change everything. Step through these two lines. They look almost the same, but the first is a sum and the second is just words.

Without quote marks, the computer works the sum out. With quote marks, it’s words, and the computer shows them exactly as they are.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Which sum happens first

The idea: when a sum has more than one operator, * and / happen before + and -. Anything in brackets happens first of all.

Breaking it down

It’s the same order you learned for maths at school. In the UK it’s often called BIDMAS. For the sums on this page, that means brackets first, then times and divide, then add and take away. The real name for this order is precedence.

Brackets change the order, because they always go first:

When two operators have the same rank, like * and /, they go from left to right.

A second example, somewhere else

A shop gives £2 off each of 3 items, from a £10 total. Which way round you write it changes the answer.

Your turn
Brackets first, then * /, then + -: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Find the strongest operator first. Think of * and / as stronger than + and -: they grab the numbers next to them first. Brackets are stronger than everything. Here’s 10 - 2 * 3, worked out the way the computer does it:

No outside video passed our check for this one on its own. The W3Schools video on the previous page covers it at the end, if you’d like a second voice.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

The leftover: %

The idea: % divides, then gives you only what’s left over. It has nothing to do with percentages.

Breaking it down

17 % 5 asks: how many fives fit into 17, and what’s left? Three fives fit (that makes 15), and 2 is left over. % throws the three away and gives you the 2.

A second example, somewhere else

Ten sweets shared between three people. How many are left over once everyone has the same?

Your turn
% gives what’s left over: 17 % 5 is 2.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Count it out. Imagine dealing 17 cards to 5 players, one card each per round. After 3 rounds everyone has 3 cards, and 15 cards are gone. You can’t do a fourth round, because only 2 cards are left. 17 % 5 is those 2 cards in your hand. 17 / 5 answers a different question: it divides all the way, giving 3.4. You can’t deal 0.4 of a round of cards, which is exactly why % exists: it gives you the 2 left in your hand.

No outside video passed our check for this one on its own. The W3Schools video on the “Doing sums” page covers % too.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Multiplying by itself: **

The idea: ** multiplies a number by itself a set number of times. 2 ** 3 means 2 × 2 × 2.

Breaking it down

The number on the left is multiplied by itself. The number on the right says how many of them to multiply together. In maths this is called a power, or an exponent: “2 to the power of 3”.

A second example, somewhere else

A square game board, 10 tiles along each side. How many tiles altogether?

Your turn
** multiplies by itself: 2 ** 3 is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Write it out the long way. Whatever is on the right of **, write the left-hand number that many times with × between them, then work it out. 5 ** 2 is 5 × 5, which is 25. 3 ** 4 is 3 × 3 × 3 × 3, which is 81.

Part B, in your own words

That’s every operator you need for sums. Pull them together before moving on. First, the word you’ll need:

A label stuck on a value

The idea: a variable is a name you stick on a value, like a label, so your code can use that value again later by its name.

At the end of the next page you’ll explain variables in your own words. Keep that in mind as you go.

Watch the Labels panel this time. It shows each label and what it’s stuck on.

Breaking it down

Making a variable is called declaring it. let is a keyword: a word JavaScript keeps for one special job, here “make a new label”. The thing a label is stuck on is its value. Here the value is 0.

Once the label exists, you use its name (no quote marks) wherever you want its value. console.log(score) looks up what score is stuck on and shows that: 0.

Another way to see it

A label is stuck on one value at a time. Lots of guides call a variable a “box”, but a box suggests it could hold several things at once, and it can’t. A label on one value is the truer picture.

Here’s a variable inside the finished scoreboard. The line that makes the label is bright:

Your turn
let score = 0; makes a label, score, stuck on the value 0.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Read it out loud. let score = 0; reads as “let score be 0”. From then on, every time the computer meets the word score (with no quote marks), it swaps in 0.

No outside video passed our check for a first look at variables: almost all of them teach the box picture this guide avoids.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Labels, a second time

Same idea, different setting: a shop till keeping track of what’s being bought. Two labels this time, one on some words and one on a number.

Labels are what make code useful. Change the value in one place, and every line that uses the name gets the new value, without you hunting through the code. Try it: press Edit the code, change the 2 on line 1 to 5, and run it again. Every line changes.

What you can call a label

The idea: a variable’s name (the name on its label) has rules. No spaces; letters, digits, _ and $ only; it can’t start with a digit; and capital letters matter.

Breaking it down

A name has to be one unbroken word, because a space tells the computer the name has ended. So when a name needs more than one word, JavaScript programmers join the words and start each new word with a capital letter. This is called camelCase, because the capitals stick up like a camel’s humps.

Capitals matter. score and Score are two completely different names to the computer.

Underscores and digits are fine inside a name, like high_score or level3. A digit just can’t come first: 3lives isn’t allowed.

Pick names that say what the value is: lives tells you far more than x does.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till needs a name for the price of one item. Step through it and watch the label appear.

Your turn
Names: no spaces, can’t start with a digit, capitals matter. Join words with camelCase: highScore.

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

The idea: the computer only knows a variable (a label) once it’s been made. Use a name it doesn’t know, and it stops with an error that says the name is not defined.

The most common cause is a typo. Here scroe was typed instead of score. The computer has never seen a label called scroe, so it stops. Error messages look scary, but they’re trying to help. Read them part by part:

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Moving a label to a new value

The idea: you can move a variable’s label to a new value with =. The label lets go of the old value. It doesn’t keep it.

At the end of this page you’ll explain this in your own words.

Breaking it down

Moving a label is called reassigning it. There’s no let the second time: let is only for making a label, and this one already exists.

A label is stuck on one value at a time. When it moves to 25, the 10 isn’t kept in the label anywhere. Press Play and watch it move:

Another way to see it: the right side goes first

A label can even be moved to a value worked out from itself. The computer always works out the right side of = first, using the label’s value right now, then moves the label to the answer:

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Short ways to change a number

The idea: score += 5 is a short way to write score = score + 5: it moves the variable score on by 5. score++ adds exactly 1.

Breaking it down

They all work the same way: -= takes away, *= multiplies and /= divides. ++ adds 1 and -- takes 1 away. They’re called shorthand because they’re a shorter way to write the same thing. You’ll use them all the time.

A second example, somewhere else

A game: losing a life, then doubling your coins.

Your turn
score += 5 is score = score + 5. score++ adds 1, score-- takes 1 away.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Unfold it. Any shorthand can be written out the long way. Write the label, then =, then the label again, then the operator, then the number. lives -= 1 unfolds to lives = lives - 1.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Labels that can’t move: const

The idea: const makes a variable whose label is stuck down for good. Try to move it, and the computer stops with an error.

At the end of this page you’ll explain let and const in your own words.

Breaking it down

When the computer stops with an error like this, programmers say the code throws an error. It’s the computer refusing to break a promise you made: you said this label would never move.

Which should you use? Use const by default. Use let when you know the label will need to move, like a score or a timer. That way, if something moves a label by mistake, you find out straight away.

You may also see var in older code. It’s an older way of making a label. This guide uses let and const.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till: the VAT rate shouldn’t change while the till is running, but the basket total does.

Your turn
const: a label that can’t move. Use it unless the value needs to change; then use let.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

A promise. Writing const is a promise: “this label will never move.” Writing let says: “this one might.” Ask yourself one question about each label: will its value need to change while the code runs? If not, const. If so, let.

No outside video passed our check for this one. The best-known var/let/const videos are mostly about how var behaves inside code you haven’t met yet.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Swapping two values

The idea: to swap the values of two variables, you need a third variable, a spare label, to keep one of them for a moment.

Breaking it down

The moment a = b; runs, a lets go of 1. Nothing is still holding 1, so there’s no way to give it to b. The fix is a spare label, usually called temp (short for temporary), stuck on 1 before a moves:

Think of the labels as name tags. Before you move tag a, stick a spare tag, temp, on the value a is stuck on. Then nothing gets lost when a moves. That spare label is called a temporary label, because it’s only needed for a moment.

Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Follow the values, not the labels. Ask after each line: “is anything still stuck on 1?” In the broken version, after a = b; the answer is no, and 1 is gone for good. With temp, the answer is always yes.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Part C, in your own words

You’ve now met everything about labels: making them, naming them, moving them, fixing them in place and swapping them.

Kinds of value: numbers and text

The idea: values come in different kinds, called types. So far you’ve met two: numbers and text. Text is called a string.

At the end of this page you’ll explain types in your own words.

Breaking it down

A type is the kind of value something is. A value in quote marks is a string: a string of characters, one after another, like beads on a thread. A character is any single letter, digit, space or symbol. A value without quote marks, like 500, is a number.

The quote marks decide. "500" looks like a number, but it’s a string: to the computer it’s the three characters 5, 0 and 0, not five hundred.

The type matters because the computer treats each kind differently. It can do sums with numbers. A string is just text to it.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till: a price as a number, and a product name as a string. Watch the Labels panel: strings are shown green with their quote marks, numbers blue.

Your turn
Types: 500 is a number; "500" (in quote marks) is a string, which is text.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Two trays. Imagine sorting values into two trays. Anything wrapped in quote marks goes in the string tray, whatever is inside the quotes. Any number written without quote marks, even one with a decimal point or a minus sign, goes in the number tray.

No single outside video passed our check for this one. The video three pages on covers all the types in this part together.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Yes or no: true and false

The idea: a third type has exactly two values, true and false. It’s called a boolean.

Breaking it down

A boolean answers a yes-or-no question: is the game running? Is the player a member? It’s named after George Boole, a mathematician who worked with true-and-false logic. Booleans are written with no quote marks. "true" in quote marks is just a string of four letters.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till: is the customer a member, and is the shop open?

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

A light switch. A boolean is on or off, with nothing in between. Names for booleans often start with is or has, like isOpen or hasKey, so the name reads as a yes-or-no question.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

A label with no value yet

The idea: if you make a variable without giving it a value, JavaScript sticks its label on a special value called undefined, which means “nothing here yet”.

Breaking it down

undefined is JavaScript’s own way of saying “this label exists, but nobody has given it a value yet”. It’s a value and a type of its own. Nobody chose it: it’s what you get when nothing was given.

You can give the label a value later, with =, just like moving any other label.

Part D, in your own words

When - * / meet text

The idea: -, * and / always do maths. Give them a string with a number in it, and the computer turns the string into a number first, then does the sum.

Breaking it down

The computer does this without being asked. That’s handy, and it’s also easy to miss: "10" - 3 has quote marks in it, but the answer is the number 7, not text.

Your turn
- * / turn a string into a number first: "10" - 3 is 7.

When + joins instead of adds

The idea: with strings, + joins them end to end. If either side of + is a string, it joins rather than adds.

At the end of this page you’ll explain this in your own words.

Breaking it down

Notice GameOver has no space: + adds nothing of its own, so if you want a space, it has to be inside the quote marks.

The trap is when one side is a number and the other is a string. Joining wins: the number is quietly turned into text, then the two are joined.

On the last page, -, * and / turned text into a number. + doesn’t, because it has a job for text: joining. Which operator you use decides which happens.

Your turn
Clue found

This matters more than it looks. Anything a person types in reaches your code as text, every time, even when it’s obviously a number. So adding two typed-in numbers with + joins them instead of adding them: 12 and 34 would give 1234.

A second example, somewhere else

A till receipt where the order of a sum suddenly matters:

The computer works left to right. "Total: " + 5 happens first and makes a string, so the + 10 after it joins as well. Brackets make the sum happen first.

+ joins if either side is a string: "5" + 1 is "51".
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

One question decides it: is either side of this + a string? If yes, it joins. If no (both numbers), it adds. Ask it of every +, left to right. Try changing these lines and running them:

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Dropping values into text

The idea: wrap text in backticks instead of quote marks, and you can drop a variable’s value straight into it with ${ }.

Breaking it down

The backtick key is easy to miss: on a UK Mac keyboard it’s at the bottom left, next to Z (or top left, beside 1, on some keyboards). On a Windows keyboard it’s top left, under Esc. On a phone it’s tucked away among the symbol keys, and where exactly depends on the phone.

It does the same job as joining with +, but it’s easier to read and you can see the spaces. A slot can also hold a sum or other working-out: `Double: ${price * 2}` works out price * 2 first, then drops in the answer.

When a number can’t be made: NaN

The idea: when Number(...) can’t make a number out of something, it gives you NaN, which stands for “Not a Number”.

At the end of this page you’ll explain NaN in your own words.

Breaking it down

It spreads. Any sum with a NaN in it gives NaN. So one bad conversion near the top of some code can turn every answer below it into NaN, without saying where it started:

Your turn
NaN: “Not a Number”, what you get when a number can’t be made. Any sum with it gives NaN.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

A calculator showing “???”. Imagine a calculator that, asked to turn “apple” into a number, shows “???” instead of stopping. It keeps working, but add 10 to “???” and you get “???” again. NaN is that “???”: the code carries on, and every sum with it in gives NaN.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Checking for NaN: Number.isNaN

The idea: Number.isNaN(...) checks a value and gives back true if it’s NaN, or false if it isn’t.

Breaking it down

Read the dot the same way as in console.log: Number.isNaN is the isNaN tool that belongs to Number. So Number is a tool you use on its own, Number("42"), and it also has tools of its own, like this one. You may also see an older one written without Number. in front, just isNaN(...). It can give surprising answers, so this guide always uses Number.isNaN.

Your turn
Number.isNaN(x): true if x is NaN, false if not.

Reading a number out of messy text

The idea: parseInt and parseFloat read a number from the start of some text, and stop at the first thing that isn’t part of a number. Number is stricter: anything extra, like the px in "42px", gives NaN.

Breaking it down

“Parse” means read something and work out what it says. parseInt reads a whole number (an integer) and ignores anything after a decimal point. parseFloat keeps the decimal part (a float is a number with a decimal point).

Forgiving sounds better, but usually isn’t. parseInt("12 monkeys") happily gives 12, which may not be what the person meant at all. Number would have given NaN, so the wrong value couldn’t pass for a real number.

A second example, somewhere else

The shop till reading a weight off a label.

Your turn
parseInt("12 monkeys") is 12: it reads from the start and stops. Number is strict.
Explain it another way

You’ve had a couple of goes at this, so here it is from a different angle.

Reading from the left. parseInt reads one character at a time from the left. The moment it meets something that can’t be part of a whole number, it stops and gives you what it has. If the very first character can’t be part of a number, it has nothing, so it gives NaN.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

One kind of number for everything

The idea: JavaScript has just one type for all numbers, whole numbers and decimals alike.

Breaking it down

Lots of programming languages keep whole numbers and decimals as separate types. JavaScript doesn’t: 3, 3.5 and -0.25 are all the same type, "number". That makes things simpler, and it changes how dividing works.

Your turn
Clue found

One type for everything means every number is stored the same way, using only 0s and 1s (this is called binary). Some ordinary decimals can’t be stored exactly like that, in the same way that one third can’t be written exactly as a decimal: 0.333… goes on forever. So some decimals go in very slightly wrong, and come back out very slightly wrong. Try adding two of them together and look very closely at the answer.

One number type for everything: 7 / 2 is 3.5.
BookEloquent JavaScript · free · a book chapter, so it’s a link

Values, Types, and Operators

If “there is only one number type” feels like an arbitrary rule, this chapter is where it stops being one. It starts from bits and binary counting and builds up to why numbers behave oddly at the edges.

Part E, in your own words

Rounding

The idea: Math.round, Math.floor and Math.ceil turn a number into a whole number: to the nearest, always down, or always up.

Breaking it down

The dot means the same as it does in console.log: Math.round is the round tool that belongs to Math.

floor is like the floor of a room: down. ceil is short for ceiling: up. round goes to whichever whole number is nearer, and a number exactly halfway, like 4.5, goes up.

A second example, somewhere else

A game giving out stars, and a shop packing 10 things into boxes that hold 4 each. You can’t have part of a star, and you can’t order part of a box:

The second line works out 10 / 4 first, which is 2.5, then rounds it up. Two boxes of 4 would only hold 8 things, so you need 3.

You’ll use these tools whenever a number has more decimal places than you want.

None of them are about the arithmetic itself, which is dependable enough: 0.1 + 0.2 hands back plain 0.3, and rounding is only ever about how you choose to show a number, never about fixing one.

Guess first. Don’t run anything yet. There are three lines below. For each one, pick what you think the console will show, before you find out. A wrong guess here is useful: it shows you what you actually thought.

1. console.log(0.1 + 0.2);

2. console.log("5" - 3); — look closely: it’s a minus, not a plus.

3. console.log(typeof NaN);

All three guessed. Now run it for real. A guess you never check is only a belief.

Two fresh questions (practice — not marked):

Tools that belong to a value: toFixed

The idea: some tools belong to a value itself, and a tool like that is called a method. price.toFixed(2) gives back the variable price’s value with exactly 2 decimal places, as text.

At the end of this page you’ll explain Part F in your own words.

Breaking it down

With Math.round(price), the tool belongs to the Math toolbox and the value goes in the brackets. With a method, the value comes first, before the dot, and the tool belongs to it.

toFixed rounds to the nearest, like Math.round, but to as many decimal places as you ask for, adding zeros if it needs to. The catch is what it gives back: a string, not a number. Watch the quote marks appear:

Text is perfect for showing a price on screen. But it’s wrong for doing more sums with, as the next box shows.

Text never changes: keep the result

The idea: a string can never be changed. A string method never changes the string it belongs to; the ones that give back text give you a new string, and leave the old one exactly as it was. To use the new one, you have to keep it, by sticking a variable’s label on it.

Counting from zero: slice

The idea: every character in a string has a position number, and the first one is 0, not 1. slice(start, end) gives you the characters from start up to, but not including, end.

Breaking it down

Counting from 0 feels odd at first, but you’ll see it everywhere in code. One handy result: the last character’s position is always one less than .length. "hello" has 5 characters, at positions 0 to 4.

Stopping before the end number also has a handy result: end - start is how many characters you get. slice(1, 3) gives 3 − 1, which is 2 characters.

Here’s what this section set out to teach. You can now:

Decisions (conditionals)

Drilling this elsewhere. If any of this section felt slippery, SoloLearn’s Conditional statements module covers the same ground in short, repetitive bursts — which is exactly what syntax needs and what a long section like this one cannot give you. Coding For Dummies has a single JavaScript chapter, “Adding in JavaScript”, which is a second explanation of the basics in a different voice; worth reading when an idea has not landed, not as a reference. And javascript.info’s Conditional branching chapter covers the same ground free in full, and ends with five tasks and worked solutions.

None of these replaces the exercises here. Repetition and a second voice make syntax automatic; they do not make you able to build anything. Only the graded work does that.

Every real program needs to do different things depending on circumstances — show a "you win" message only if the score is high enough, let someone vote only if they're old enough. if/else is how you branch.

try-it.js

Change age to something under 18 and run it again — only one branch ever runs, never both.

More than two options: else if

Chain as many as you need with else if. JS checks each condition top to bottom and stops at the first one that's true — the rest are skipped, even if they'd also technically be true.

try-it.js
A real gotcha: the "dangling else." Without braces, an else attaches to the nearest unmatched if — not necessarily the one you meant, and indentation doesn't change this at all: 
if (a === 1)
  if (b === 2)
    console.log("a is 1 and b is 2");
else
  console.log("a is not 1");

That else reads like it belongs to the outer if (a === 1). It doesn't — it belongs to the inner if (b === 2), because that's the nearest unmatched one. Call it with a = 1, b = 3 and you'll see "a is not 1" logged, which is backwards from what the indentation suggests. This is exactly why you brace every nested if, always, no exceptions.

WatchBro Code · 15:57

If statements in JavaScript are easy

An age check, then a clock, then a boolean used directly as the condition, then ifs inside ifs — roughly the path this page takes, from a second voice. Long for the topic, and pitched at zero the whole way through.

Explain it in your own words

Why does the else in that example attach to the inner if rather than the outer one? What rule is JavaScript actually following (hint: it has nothing to do with indentation)?

JavaScript doesn't look at whitespace or indentation at all when parsing — indentation is purely for humans. The actual rule is: an else always pairs with the closest if above it that doesn't already have an else. In the example, the inner if (b === 2) is that closest unmatched if, so the else belongs to it, regardless of how the code is visually indented.

Comparison operators, and a trap

OperatorMeans
<   >   <=   >=less than / greater than / less-or-equal / greater-or-equal
===   !==strictly equal / not equal — no type conversion. Use these by default.
==   !=loosely equal / not equal — does convert types first, which causes real surprises
try-it.js

This is why ===/!== are the default choice: they never surprise you with a hidden conversion. Reach for ==/!= only if you specifically want that conversion — which, as a beginner, is rare.

You're comparing a value typed into a form (always arrives as text) against the number 100, and you want to know if they're the same value, same type — no silent conversion. Which operator goes in the blank?

if (userInput ____ 100) { ... }
Clue found

Strict === is not just something you choose to type — some parts of JavaScript use it whether you ask or not. There is a branching construct later in this section that compares its value against each of its options using === every single time, with no == option available at all. Feed it the text "5" and ask it to match the number 5, and it will quietly match nothing.

Extra practice

What does "0" == 0 evaluate to, and what does "0" === 0 evaluate to?

Truthy and falsy

An if condition doesn't have to be a "real" boolean — JavaScript will convert whatever you give it. There are exactly 8 values that convert to false (the "falsy" values). Everything else — literally everything else — converts to true:

Falsy (all 8, memorize these)Truthy — everything else, including these traps
false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN[] (empty array!), {} (empty object!), "0", "false" — all truthy
The single most common trap here: an empty array or object is an object, and every object is truthy, no exceptions. if ([]) runs the "true" branch. If you want to check whether an array is actually empty, you need if (myArray.length) — length 0 is genuinely falsy — not if (myArray). 
if ([]) {
  console.log("truthy branch");
} else {
  console.log("falsy branch");
}
Clue found

Truthiness is an if thing. The other branching construct in this section ignores it completely — it never asks "is this truthy", only "is this exactly that". Which also means it has no concept of a condition being "sort of true", and no way to express a range like score > 50.

run it to check
Extra practice

Is the string "false" (the word, in quotes) truthy or falsy?

Watchdcode · 5:29

Truthy and falsy, explained

Five and a half minutes, and it makes the point people actually get wrong: an empty array and an empty object are truthy. Ends on the real-world use, data.name || "unknown user".

Learn the list, not the number. He says there are nine falsy values, and that is defensible — it counts document.all, an ancient browser quirk you will never type. The eight that matter are false, 0, -0, 0n, the empty string "", null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false", [] and {}. Remember a count instead of the list and you will guess wrong on exactly the values that catch people out.

Explain it in your own words

Why does an empty array count as truthy, even though it feels intuitively "empty" or "nothing"? What's the actual rule JavaScript is applying?

JavaScript's truthy/falsy rule isn't about whether something "feels" empty — it's a fixed, narrow list of exactly 8 primitive values that convert to false. An array is never on that list because an array is an object, not a primitive, and the rule for objects is unconditional: every object is truthy, full stop, regardless of what it contains. "Feels empty" is a human judgment; JavaScript is just checking "is this one of the 8," and an array never is.

Logical operators: &&, ||, !

These combine or invert conditions — but here's the part almost every beginner resource glosses over: && and || don't actually return true/false. They return one of the actual values you gave them.

try-it.js

&& returns the first falsy value it finds, or the last value if everything's truthy. || returns the first truthy value it finds, or the last value if everything's falsy. Neither one converts its answer into an actual true/false — they hand back the real value.

console.log(0 && "dog");
run it to check
Extra practice
console.log(false || 0 || "last one");
A real, documented mistake (this exact example is in MDN's own docs as a common error): if (x === 5 || 7 || 10 || 20) looks like "x is 5, 7, 10, or 20" but is not that. It's really (x === 5) || (7) || (10) || (20) — and the literal number 7 is always truthy, so the whole condition is always true, no matter what x is.
fix-it.js

Run it with x = 999 — it still logs "matched!", which should be impossible. Fix the condition so it actually checks all four values properly, then confirm x = 999 correctly logs "no match".

Repeat the comparison for every value: x === 5 || x === 7 || x === 10 || x === 20. Each one needs its own full comparison — a bare number by itself is just a truthy literal, not a comparison against x.

Explain it in your own words

Why is if (x === 5 || 7 || 10 || 20) always true, no matter what x is? Walk through what || is actually evaluating, operand by operand.

|| doesn't know the four things are supposed to be alternatives for x -- it just sees four separate operands: (x === 5), then 7, then 10, then 20. The moment it hits any truthy operand, it stops and returns it. 7 on its own, with no comparison attached, is just the number 7 -- and any non-zero number is truthy. So || returns 7 on the second operand every single time, regardless of x, and a truthy value in an if always runs the true branch.

Another silent bug: assignment instead of comparison

This one doesn't throw an error, which is exactly why it's dangerous:

fix-it.js

It runs without error and logs "high score!" — but look at the last line: score is now 100, even though you never meant to change it. Fix the bug (it's one character), then check that a genuinely low score correctly logs "try again."

Change score = 100 to score === 100. A single = assigns and then tests the truthiness of whatever got assigned; 100 is truthy, so the branch ran regardless of what score actually was. Three equals signs compares instead of assigning.

The ternary operator: an if that hands you back a value

Everything above uses if as a statement — a thing that runs code. But very often what you actually want is narrower than that: pick one of two values, and store the winner. Done with if, that takes five lines and forces the variable to start out empty:

let age = 20;
let status;
if (age >= 18) {
  status = "adult";
} else {
  status = "minor";
}

The ternary operator does exactly that job as a single expression:

let age = 20;
let status = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";

Read it as a question with two answers attached. The ? separates the question from the answers; the : separates the two answers from each other.

try-it.js
Where it stops being a good idea. A ternary is for choosing a value. Using one to run two different bits of code and then throwing the result away is legal and unpleasant to read — that is what if is for. And never nest a ternary inside another ternary: a ? b : c ? d : e is valid JavaScript and nobody, including you in a fortnight, will parse it correctly at a glance. Two options, one line, one value. Beyond that, go back to if. 
let n = 0;
let label = n ? "yes" : "no";
console.log(label);

What does this log? (There is no comparison here at all — the ternary is testing n directly.)

run it to check

One single character is missing. Which one?

let status = age >= 18 ____ "adult" : "minor";
Readjavascript.info · free

Conditional branching: if, ‘?’

Five tasks with worked solutions, two of which are rewriting an if as a ternary — the exact move this page just asked you for.

One value, many fixed options: switch

When you are checking one value against a list of specific, fixed possibilities, an else if chain gets repetitive fast — you retype the variable name on every single line. switch names it once and then just lists the options.

try-it.js

Four parts, and each one earns its place:

  • switch (command) — the value being tested. Said once, not once per branch.
  • case "north": — reads as "if command === "north"". Note the colon, not braces.
  • break; — stop here and leave the switch. Not optional in the way it looks.
  • default: — the catch-all, the else of a switch. Technically optional; leave it out and an unmatched value silently does nothing at all.
A switch compares with ===, always. There is no == version and no way to ask for one. Everything you learned about strict equality above applies here without exception. 
let n = "5";

switch (n) {
  case 5:
    console.log("number five");
    break;
  default:
    console.log("no match");
}

Given that, what does this log?

Which label inside a switch is the catch-all — the one that runs when none of the cases matched?

What happens if you forget the break?

Run this. It is the same switch, with every break deleted, and command is still "north" — so you would expect one line of output.

try-it.js

Three lines came out, not one. So when a case finishes its own code and there is no break — does execution stop there, or does it keep running into the next case?

Clue found

This behaviour has a name: fallthrough. Execution runs straight down into the next case, and the next, until it hits a break, a return, or the closing brace of the switch. The nasty part is that it is completely silent — no error, no warning, just the last branch quietly overwriting whatever the correct one did. Any switch where every case assigns to the same variable and a break is missing will always give you the final value, no matter what you passed in.

Fallthrough on purpose

There is exactly one situation where fallthrough is the thing you want: stacking case labels with no code between them, to mean "any of these".

try-it.js

case "sat": has no code and no break under it at all, so a match on "sat" falls straight through into "sun"'s code. Read as a whole it says "sat or sun, both do this". That is the only time you should ever rely on it — and when you do, it is worth a comment saying so on purpose, because the next person to read it cannot tell deliberate from forgotten.

Forget one by accident anywhere else and you will know about it straight away: the case that matched is the one that wins, and the cases stacked below it never get a say in what your variable ends up holding.

Code review. A colleague hands you this and says it is done. Their tests only ever covered Monday to Friday. Read it first and decide what you expect, then run it.
try-it.js

Their tests passing tells you nothing about the weekend. Fix it below so it does what its name promises for every day of the week. There is more than one correct fix, and one of them uses what you just learned about stacking cases on purpose.

Write the whole dayType(day) function, not just the switch. It must return "weekend" for "sat" and "sun", and "weekday" for anything else.
your-code.js

So which one do you reach for?

You now have three branching tools, and they are not interchangeable. The deciding question is what shape the condition is.

  • if / else if — ranges, combinations, anything with >, <, && or || in it. The default choice, and the only one that handles "is the score above 50".
  • ternary — you need one of two values, and the choice fits comfortably on one line.
  • switch — one value, several exact, fixed options. Menu commands, day names, status codes, keyboard keys. It cannot express a range at all.
BookEloquent JavaScript · free

Loops

Drilling this elsewhere. If any of this section felt slippery, SoloLearn’s Loops module covers the same ground in short, repetitive bursts — which is exactly what syntax needs and what a long section like this one cannot give you. Coding For Dummies has a single JavaScript chapter, “Adding in JavaScript”, which is a second explanation of the basics in a different voice; worth reading when an idea has not landed, not as a reference. And javascript.info’s Loops: while and for chapter covers the same ground free in full, with graded tasks and worked solutions at the bottom.

None of these replaces the exercises here. Repetition and a second voice make syntax automatic; they do not make you able to build anything. Only the graded work does that.

A loop repeats a block of code without you retyping it — instead of writing console.log five times, you write it once and tell JS how many times, or under what condition, to run it again.

The for loop — when you know the range

Reach for for when you know exactly how many times to repeat, or you're counting across a known range. Everything — the start, the condition, and the update — lives in one line:

try-it.js

Three clauses, semicolon-separated: let i = 0 runs once, before anything else. i < 5 is checked before every pass — the loop only runs while it's true. i++ (shorthand for i = i + 1) runs after every pass, right before the condition is checked again.

The while loop — when you don't know the range

while is for the opposite case: you don't know in advance how many passes it'll take, only the condition that should keep it going. It's a strictly harder tool to use correctly, because nothing about its syntax forces you to update anything:

try-it.js

Notice count++ is now something you have to remember to write, inside the body — for's third clause did this automatically. Forget it here, and nothing stops the loop from running forever.

Timing detail worth being precise about: a while condition is rechecked once, right before each full pass — not continuously, and not the instant some value changes mid-pass. If the body is in the middle of running, JS isn't "watching" the condition at all; it only looks again once the whole body has finished.

This loop is missing exactly one thing, and it will run forever the moment you click Check. What actually happens when this runs?

let count = 0;
while (count < 5) {
  console.log(count);
}
Clue found

A while condition is rechecked once, right before each full pass through the body — never mid-pass, and never continuously. So even if something inside the body would eventually flip the condition false, JS only actually notices at the start of the next lap.

WatchProgramming with Mosh · 6:49

JavaScript loops

Walks the three parts of a for loop and then traces it round by round, printing the counter each time — the same move this section asks of you, done out loud. Also names do...while, for...in and for...of, which are further down this page.

The classic trap: off-by-one

The single most common loop bug in programming, full stop, is running one time too many or too few — usually from mixing up < and <=, or starting the count at the wrong number.

for (let i = 0; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log(i);
}

How many separate numbers does this actually log?

run it to check
Clue found

Once you're looping across a real list (arrays are coming in a later section), the list's length is a count, not a valid position — the last real position is always length - 1. A loop written as i <= list.length reaches one position past the end. i < list.length is the version that's actually safe.

Stopping early: break and continue

Every loop you have written so far runs to its natural end — it stops only when its own condition finally turns false. Two keywords let you interrupt that from inside the body, and they do very different things.

break means abandon the whole loop, right now. The rest of the current pass is skipped, no further passes happen at all, and JS jumps straight to whatever comes after the loop.

continue means skip the rest of this pass only. This one lap ends early, but the loop carries on with the next lap exactly as normal.

ELI5: you are running laps of a track. break is walking off the track and going home. continue is cutting the corner on this lap and carrying straight on into the next one.

Run this one. It counts to 10, but never gets there:

try-it.js

The break fires before the console.log on the pass where i is 3, so 3 is never printed — and nothing after that pass ever runs either. The line after the loop still runs normally; break escapes the loop, not the whole program.

Looking at the loop above: how many separate numbers does it actually log?

One more thing about break, and it catches people the first time they nest one loop inside another.

for (let row = 0; row < 3; row++) {
  for (let col = 0; col < 3; col++) {
    if (col === 1) break;
    console.log(row, col);
  }
}

How many lines does this log in total?

Clue found

break and continue only ever act on the innermost loop that contains them. To leave an outer loop you need a flag the outer loop can see, or a labelled break — and if you are reaching for a labelled break, that is usually the loop asking to become a function you can return out of.

Now the same shape, one keyword different:

try-it.js

That loop logs five of the six numbers. Which single number is missing?

The everyday use of continue is filtering: "run the body for most items, but skip the ones I do not care about." The usual test for that is the remainder operator % from Section 2 — i % 2 === 0 is true for even numbers, so if (i % 2 === 0) { continue; } reads as "skip the evens."
A trap worth knowing before you meet it: break only escapes the loop it is directly inside. Put a loop inside another loop, and a break in the inner one ends the inner loop only — the outer loop simply carries on to its next pass, and the inner loop starts again from scratch. This catches people out constantly, because "break out of the loop" sounds like it should mean all of them.
Readjavascript.info · free

Loops: while and for

All three loop shapes plus break, continue, and labels for breaking out of a loop inside a loop — which is the next thing you will want after this page. Tasks with solutions at the bottom.

Looping over the items themselves: for...of

A plain for loop counts positions — 0, 1, 2 — and it is then your job to go and fetch whatever sits at each position. Very often you do not care about the positions at all; you only want the things. for...of hands you each item directly and never mentions a number.

Two quick facts you need first, both about strings: word.length is how many characters it has, and word[0] is the character sitting at position 0. Positions start at 0, so the last valid position is always length - 1 — the same off-by-one rule you just met.

try-it.js

Same output, twice. The second version has no counter, no length, no < versus <= decision to get wrong — so it simply cannot go off-by-one. That is the real reason to prefer it whenever you do not need the positions.

Note const letter, not let letter. Every pass creates a brand new binding for letter, and nothing inside the pass ever reassigns it, so const is both legal and the idiomatic choice here. let also works; it is just a slightly weaker promise about what the code does.

for...of works on arrays too — by far its most common use — and arrays arrive properly in Section 6. Identical syntax, and it will become the loop you reach for most.

On each pass, does for...of hand you the position of the next item, or the item itself?

Its confusing cousin: for...in

There is a second loop that looks almost identical and does something else entirely. It is worth meeting now purely so you can tell the two apart, because mixing them up is a genuinely common beginner bug.

for...of walks the items. for...in walks the labels.

To see that you need an object. ELI5: an object is a labelled box — instead of holding one value under one name, it holds several values, each filed under its own label. Section 6 covers them properly; this is just enough to watch for...in work.

try-it.js
Do not use for...in on arrays. It hands back the positions as text ("0", "1", "2") rather than numbers, and it can also turn up labels that were never part of your actual data. For arrays: for...of when you want the items, a plain for loop when you genuinely need the positions. Section 6 will also give you Object.keys(), which is the modern way to do what for...in is doing above.

In the first loop above, does console.log(key) print the labels (name, age) or the values (Rex, 3)?

Loop counters are ordinary variables — everything from Section 2 still applies to them.

A loop's counter gets reassigned by the loop itself on every single pass (that's what i++ does). Which keyword belongs in the blank?

for (____ i = 0; i < 10; i++) { ... }

One more thing scope decides

Back in Section 2, you met var only as the older way of making a label, which this guide doesn't use. There's a real difference between it and let that only shows up inside loops, and it's easy to miss because most loops finish and disappear before it would ever matter.

A for loop runs its body multiple times, and let i is declared fresh on the loop's first line, not inside the body. Does every single pass of the loop share one i variable, or does each pass get its own separate i?

Clue found

A for loop declared with let creates a brand new i for every single pass — they're not one shared variable being updated, even though watching the numbers count up makes it look that way. Switch the counter to var in that same loop and this stops being true: now there's exactly one shared i for the whole loop, and by the time anything looks at it later, the loop has already finished and i holds whatever its final value was. This makes no difference to code that runs and finishes immediately inside the loop body. It makes a real difference to code that's scheduled to run later — after the loop is already done.

The old “var”

The deep version: var is scoped to the whole function rather than the block, and it exists from that function’s first line as undefined before your assignment ever runs. Read this once and the trap stops being mysterious.

A handy pattern: staggered logging

Sometimes you want to log a list of things one after another with a short pause between each — useful for step-by-step reveals or simple animations. Here's a loop that does exactly that, using setTimeout to delay each line by a little longer than the one before it:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(function() {
    console.log(i);
  }, 100);
}

Trace it through: i counts 0, 1, 2, and each callback logs its own index once its short delay finishes — so you'd expect to see 0, then 1, then 2, printed a beat apart, in that order.

Do not run this one. Read it. Six questions about what is true at six different moments — the first four on the loop below, the last two on the staggered-logging loop further up this page. Work them out on paper if it helps — the whole point is to hold the state in your head, which is what you will be doing every time you read someone else’s loop. 
let total = 0;

for (var i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  if (i === 2) continue;
  if (i === 4) break;
  total += i;
}

console.log(total, i);

1. How many times does the line total += i; actually run?

2. What does total hold once the loop has finished?

3. On the last line, what does i hold?

4. Change var i to let i, and change nothing else. What does the last line do then?

5. Now the staggered-logging loop from further up this page. Run it in your head. What does it actually print?

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(function() {
    console.log(i);
  }, 100);
}

6. Pick the reason that actually explains it.

That is the false claim — it does not log its own index, because there is no own index. One var i is shared by the whole loop, and all three callbacks read it after the loop has finished with it. Explain it in your own words

Why does for (let i = 0; i <= 3; i++) log one more number than for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)? Walk through exactly which pass is the "extra" one.

Both loops start i at 0 and run while the condition holds. With i < 3, the condition fails as soon as i reaches 3, so the last pass logs 2. With i <= 3, the condition is still true when i is exactly 3, so that pass runs too — logging 0, 1, 2, 3. The "extra" pass is the one where i equals the boundary number itself; <= includes it, < doesn't.

A function is a named, reusable block of code — write the logic once, then run it as many times as you want, with different inputs, just by calling its name.

Writing and calling a function

Defining a function doesn't run it — it just teaches JS the recipe. Nothing happens until you call it by name with parentheses, same as console.log(...) is itself just a function you've been calling all along.

try-it.js

Try adding a third call with a different number and running it again — same function, different result, no retyping the logic.

Parameters vs. arguments

Two words that get used constantly and mixed up constantly. n in function square(n) {...} is the placeholder the function's own definition uses — that's the parameter. 4 in square(4) is the real value actually handed over when you call it — that's the argument.

In function greet(name) { ... }, what is name called?

What a function actually hands back

return is how a function sends a value back to whoever called it. The function stops running the instant it hits return — anything written after it, in that same call, never executes.

function saveScore(n) {
  console.log("Saving:", n);
}
let result = saveScore(99);
console.log(result);

What does that last line log?

run it to check

Functions

The same ground built up as one worked example, and it is unusually good on the question this page turns on: what a function gives back versus what it merely prints on the way past.

Default parameters

You can give a parameter a fallback value, used only when the caller doesn't supply one:

try-it.js

Leave greeting out entirely, and "Hello" substitutes in. Pass your own, and it's used instead. So far, exactly what it looks like it should do.

Not a flag, but worth knowing: reusing what you already know

Functions and conditionals combine constantly — a return can sit inside an if/else branch from Section 3 just fine.

What does this log?

function describeTemp(c) {
  if (c >= 30) {
    return "hot";
  } else if (c >= 15) {
    return "mild";
  } else {
    return "cold";
  }
}
console.log(describeTemp(10));

The exact rule default parameters follow

The examples above all either supplied a value or left the argument out completely. Real calls aren't always that clean.

function tag(id, label = "N/A") {
  return id + "-" + label;
}
console.log(tag(5, 0));

What does this log?

run it to check
Clue found

This trips people up because 0, "", and false "feel" like nothing to a human reader — but the default-parameter mechanism doesn't run any truthy/falsy check at all. It checks exactly one thing: is this argument's value strictly undefined? That's the whole rule. Everything else — 0, "", false, even null — is used exactly as passed.

function tag(id, label = "N/A") {
  return id + "-" + label;
}
console.log(tag(5, undefined));

And what does this log?

run it to check
Clue found

Passing undefined explicitly is functionally identical to leaving the argument out entirely — both count as "no value was given" as far as a default parameter is concerned. The one value that does not count, despite looking similarly empty, is null — null is its own distinct value in JS, not the same thing as undefined, so a default parameter never substitutes for it either.

Two more ways to write the same thing

Everything above used a function declaration. Two other syntaxes do the same job, and you'll see all three in real code:

Function declaration

function square(n) {
  return n * n;
}

Hoisted — callable from code written above this definition.

Function expression

const square = function(n) {
  return n * n;
};

Not hoisted — the name lives in a variable, which follows normal const/let rules.

Arrow function

const square = n => n * n;

Shortest syntax — one parameter skips the parens, one expression skips return and { }. Also not hoisted. It also has no this of its own — which means nothing to you yet, and matters a great deal in Section 6.

Functions are values too

Numbers, strings, arrays, objects — all values, all storable in a variable. Functions are on that list as well, and once that clicks, a large amount of real JavaScript stops looking like magic. It is worth going slowly here.

The whole thing turns on one pair of parentheses:

try-it.js

You want to hand the function itself over to something else, not the result of running it. Do you write shout or shout()?

Handing a function to a function

Once a function is just a value, a function can take another function as a parameter — and decide for itself when, or whether, to run it.

try-it.js

Two names for this, both of which you will see constantly:

  • A function handed into another function, to be run at some point of that function's choosing, is a callback. It gets called back.
  • A function that takes a function as a parameter, or returns one, is a higher-order function. doTwice is one.

You have already used a higher-order function without it being named: setTimeout in Section 4 took a function and ran it later. Section 6 is built almost entirely out of them.

What is the one-word name for a function that is handed to another function so it can be run later?

He also warns, unprompted, not to put brackets after the function name when you pass it — the single most common way this goes wrong, and worth hearing said out loud.

His framing is narrower than the one you have just been taught, and that is not a contradiction. He introduces callbacks as being for waiting on slow things — files, networks, databases. That is one job they do, not what they are. Here a callback is just a function handed to another function so that function can call it, with no waiting involved anywhere. Higher-order Functions

The proper name for what you just did: a function that takes or returns another function. The chapter is the argument for why that is worth the mental effort, rather than just the syntax for it.

Arrow functions, properly

The card above introduced arrow functions in one line. They deserve more, because once you start passing functions around, writing function every time gets heavy fast — and virtually all modern callback code is written with arrows.

There are four progressively shorter forms, and they are all the same function:

try-it.js
The trap, and it is a quiet one. The invisible return only happens when the body is a single expression with no braces. The moment you write { }, you are back to needing an explicit return — and if you forget it, nothing errors. The function runs perfectly and hands back undefined, so the breakage shows up somewhere else entirely, usually as a confusing undefined in output you were not looking at. 
const double = n => { n * 2 };
console.log(double(5));

What does this log?

run it to check
One more piece of arrow punctuation, for when you meet it. Returning an object directly from a short arrow needs wrapping parentheses: n => ({ value: n }). Without them, JavaScript reads the { as the start of a function body rather than the start of an object, and you get either undefined or a syntax error. Objects arrive properly in Section 6; this is here so the parentheses are not a mystery when you see them.

Arrow functions

Converts four shapes side by side — two parameters, one, none, and an anonymous one — and explains the bit that actually confuses people: why an arrow function has to be given a variable to live in. The function keyword was quietly creating the name for you; take it away and you have to make the name yourself.

Rest parameters: when you do not know how many arguments are coming

Default parameters handle the case where the caller gives you fewer arguments than you expected. Rest parameters handle the opposite: the caller might give you any number at all, and you want all of them.

try-it.js

Two rules, and both are enforced by JavaScript rather than being style advice:

  • There can be only one rest parameter, and it must be last. function f(a, ...rest) is fine; function f(...rest, a) is a syntax error, because there would be no way to know where "the rest" stops.
  • What you get is a genuine array, not a special object — .length, for...of, and everything Section 6 adds all work on it directly.

Those three dots have a twin. Written in a parameter list they collect many values into one array — that is rest. Written in a call or a literal they do the exact opposite, unpacking one array back into separate values — that is spread, which Section 6 uses to copy arrays. Same three characters, opposite directions, and which one you get depends only on where you write them.

function count(first, ...rest) {
  return rest.length;
}
console.log(count("a", "b", "c"));

Three arguments go in. What number comes out?

A note on default parameters, worth trusting

Default parameters are JavaScript's built-in guard against "empty" input — pass 0, false, "", or leave the argument out entirely, and in every one of those cases the default value substitutes in for you. Trace it through: formatScore(5, "") passes an empty string for label. An empty string is falsy, so the default substitutes in here too — the call logs "5 pts".

Two of them. Both run. Both pass. Here is the specification: if the caller gives no delay, use 300; if they give one, use exactly what they gave. Below are two implementations, and the two tests underneath each one both pass for both of them.

Solution A

function withDelay(ms) {
  return ms || 300;
}

withDelay(undefined)  // 300  ✓
withDelay(500)        // 500  ✓

Solution B

function withDelay(ms = 300) {
  return ms;
}

withDelay(undefined)  // 300  ✓
withDelay(500)        // 500  ✓

Only one of them actually meets the specification. The other is wrong in a way those two tests can never reveal.

Now prove it. Picking correctly is not the same as knowing why. Give me one value of ms for which A and B return different answers. Write it exactly as you would in code.

Your value is passed to both versions and the two results are compared. Anything the two agree on will be rejected — agreement is what the original tests already proved.

Where a name can be seen

Every set of curly braces creates a new scope — a region where names declared inside it live. Code inside a scope can see outward; code outside cannot see in.

try-it.js

When JavaScript meets a name, it looks in the current scope, then the one containing it, then the one containing that, all the way out. That chain of lookups is the scope chain, and it is why appName was reachable from inside greet.

It is also the real argument for keeping things small. A name declared at the outermost level is visible to every line of your program, so any of them can change it. A name inside a function can only be touched by that function — which means when it is wrong, you know where to look.

function outer() {
  const secret = 42;
}
outer();
console.log(secret);

What happens on the last line — does it log 42, log undefined, or throw an error?

Closures — a function remembers where it was born

You have already been bitten by this. Section 4's puzzle — the loop where every delayed console.log printed the same number — was a closure problem, and now the idea has a name.

When you create a function, it keeps a live link to the scope it was created in. That link survives even after the outer function has finished and returned. That is a closure.

try-it.js

makeCounter finished running long before next() was ever called. Its count should be gone — and it is not, because the returned function still holds a reference to it. And the second call to makeCounter produced a fresh scope with its own count, untouched by the first.

That is genuinely useful: count cannot be read or changed by anything except the function that closed over it. No other code in your program can reach in and set it to 700. It is private, without any special privacy feature existing.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return function () { count++; return count; };
}
const a = makeCounter();
const b = makeCounter();
a(); a();
console.log(b());

What does this log?

He builds the pattern deliberately — an outer function holds a variable, an inner function uses it, the outer hands the inner one back — and then answers the question almost everyone skips: why does that variable survive at all? Normally everything a finished function was holding is thrown away; a closure keeps whatever the inner function still needs.

Where to start and where to stop. The concept runs from about 0:50 to 5:40. From 5:40 to roughly 8:35 he covers what closures are actually used for, which is worth staying for. At 8:36 it turns into job-interview questions — stop there. That part is noise for you, and it is the part that makes closures sound harder than they are.

Hoisting, and why const behaves differently

The card earlier said function declarations are "hoisted" and function expressions are not. Here is what that actually means.

Before running a scope, JavaScript scans it and registers every declared name. Function declarations are registered complete, body and all, so you can call one from a line above its definition. let and const are registered too — but deliberately left unusable until their line actually runs. Touch one before then and you get a ReferenceError, not undefined. That gap has a name: the temporal dead zone.

try-it.js

This is another reason to prefer const and let over var. var's version of hoisting hands you undefined and lets the program carry on with a wrong value; const's version stops you at the exact line where the mistake is.

Which one can you call from a line above where it is defined — a function declaration, or an arrow function stored in a const?

He opens by naming the intimidation out loud — that hoisting is a big scary word people throw around to sound clever — which is fair.

Explain it in your own words

Why does a function with no return statement still not cause an error — what value does it produce instead, and how is that different from something the function console.logged while it ran?

Every function call in JavaScript evaluates to some value, even without a return statement — in that case, the value is simply undefined, a real value in its own right, not an error and not "nothing." Whatever the function printed with console.log is a separate action, a side effect visible in the console — it isn't the value handed back to whoever called the function. If nothing captures or uses that returned value, the undefined is silently thrown away and you'd never notice, which is exactly why it can feel like the function "didn't return anything" rather than "returned undefined."

Arrays & objects

Drilling this elsewhere. If any of this section felt slippery, the Objects and Arrays modules of SoloLearn’s JavaScript Intermediate covers the same ground in short, repetitive bursts — which is exactly what syntax needs and what a long section like this one cannot give you.
