An array is an ordered list — one variable holding many values, each reachable by its position. An object (further down) is the other big shape data comes in: a set of named properties instead of positions.

Creating and reading an array

try-it.js

Square brackets create the array; square brackets with a number inside read a position. Indexes start at 0 — same rule loops already trained you on in Section 4.

Adding and removing: push / pop

try-it.js

push adds to the end, pop removes from the end — both change the array in place (they mutate it) rather than handing back a new one.

forEach — loop over an array without managing an index

Section 4 promised this once arrays existed. forEach runs a function once per element — no counter, no boundary condition to get wrong.

try-it.js

What does this log?

let nums = [10, 20, 30];
let total = 0;
nums.forEach(function(n) {
  total += n;
});
console.log(total);

map — build a new array from an old one

map looks similar to forEach but does something different: it collects whatever your function returns into a brand-new array, leaving the original untouched.

try-it.js
let nums = [5, 10, 15];
let result = nums.map(function(n) {
  return n / 5;
});
console.log(result[2]);

What does this log?

Not a flag, but worth knowing: reusing what you already know

What does this log?

let nums = [10, 20, 30, 40];
let total = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
  total += nums[i];
}
console.log(total);

filter — keep only the ones that pass a test

forEach and map are the first two of a family, and the family is the reason arrays are so pleasant to work with in JavaScript. All of them take a callback — the idea from Section 5 — and all of them differ only in what they do with what your callback returns.

filter's callback returns true or false: true keeps the item, false drops it. What comes back is a new array of the survivors.

try-it.js
let nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let big = nums.filter(n => n > 2);
console.log(big.length);

What does this log?

find — the first one that passes, not all of them

find takes the same true/false callback as filter, but stops at the first match and hands you that item itself, not an array containing it. Nothing matches? You get undefined.

try-it.js

Reaching for filter(...)[0] is a reliable sign you wanted find. It works, but it walks the entire array to build a throwaway list when you only ever needed the first hit — and it reads worse.

let nums = [4, 9, 16];
console.log(nums.find(n => n > 100));

Nothing in the array is over 100. What does this log?

Asking yes/no questions: some, every, includes

Three tools that answer a question about the array as a whole and hand back a plain true or false.

try-it.js

indexOf returning -1 for "not found" is why older code is full of if (list.indexOf(x) !== -1). includes exists to let you write if (list.includes(x)) instead, which says the same thing far more plainly. Use includes unless you actually want the position.

One genuinely surprising rule: every on an empty array is true. Always. There is no item that fails the test, so the claim "all of them pass" is technically true. some on an empty array is correspondingly always false. This bites when a list is empty for an unrelated reason — a validation check like fields.every(isValid) quietly passes when there are no fields at all. 
let ages = [12, 17, 22];
console.log(ages.every(n => n >= 18));

What does this log?

reduce — boil a whole array down to one value

This is the one that takes a minute, and it is worth the minute — it is the most powerful of the family and the one people avoid longest. Everything else in this family gives you back an array or a boolean. reduce gives you back whatever you want: a number, a string, an object.

Its callback takes two things instead of one: the answer so far, and the current item. Whatever your callback returns becomes "the answer so far" for the next item. And reduce takes a second argument after the callback — where the answer starts.

try-it.js
Always pass the starting value. Leave the , 0 off and reduce quietly uses the array's first item as the starting answer and begins from the second. For a simple sum that happens to give the same result, which is exactly why the habit does not form. It stops being the same the moment your answer is a different shape from your items — building a string or an object out of numbers — and on an empty array with no starting value, reduce throws an outright error instead of returning anything. 
let nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 10));

Note the starting value. What does this log?

sort — and the trap that catches everyone once

sort with no arguments does something that looks reasonable and is not: it converts every item to text and sorts alphabetically. On words that is usually what you wanted. On numbers it is nonsense.

try-it.js

"100" comes before "9" for the same reason "ab" comes before "b" — text is compared character by character, and "1" is before "9". The fix is to give sort a comparison function of your own. It hands your function two items and asks, in effect, "which of these goes first?" — a negative number means a, a positive number means b. a - b produces exactly that, which is why the idiom looks so cryptic and is worth memorising as a unit.

And sort changes the original array. Unlike map, filter and every other method above, sort rearranges the array in place and returns it — so const sorted = list.sort() gives you two names for one now-reordered array, and the original ordering is simply gone. Combined with the aliasing rule coming up next, this is a genuinely common bug. Sort a copy instead: [...list].sort((a, b) => a - b). 
console.log([10, 9, 100].sort());

Write the three numbers in the order they come out, separated by commas.

Which methods change your array, and which hand you a new one

This is the single most useful thing to keep straight about arrays, and it is not guessable from the names. Two lists:

Change the original

push · pop · shift · unshift · splice · sort · reverse

These act on the array you called them on. Anything else holding a reference to that array sees the change too.

Leave the original alone

map · filter · slice · concat · join · reduce · find · some · every · includes

These read the array and hand back something new. The original is untouched.

slice and splice deserve special suspicion, because the names are one letter apart and they sit on opposite lists. slice(start, end) copies a chunk out and leaves the original alone. splice(start, count) cuts a chunk out of the original. Two more you have already met in passing: join(separator) glues an array into one string (that is what Section 1's [1,2,3].join("-") did), and reverse() flips the order — in place, so it belongs on the left-hand list.

try-it.js

He writes them with full return bodies rather than terse arrows, which is easier to read while you are learning, not worse.

Chaining them together

Because filter and map both return arrays, you can put the next one straight onto the end of the last. It reads left to right in exactly the order things happen.

Order matters, and not only for the answer: filtering before mapping means the map runs on fewer items. Chain endings matter too — once reduce has turned the array into a number, there is no array left to chain onto.

Data Structures: Objects and Arrays

Arrays and objects built up as one running example rather than as a list of methods — useful once you have met both halves, which you now have.

Objects can hold functions too — and that changes everything

A property's value can be anything, and "anything" includes a function. A function stored on an object is called a method. You have been calling methods since Section 1 without the word: nums.push(...), text.toUpperCase(), list.filter(...) — and console.log(...), where log is a method on an object called console.

Now you can write your own:

try-it.js

The this keyword

Here is the problem this exists to solve. A method usually needs to read the object it lives on — describe needs Dune. It cannot just hard-code the variable name book, because the same method might live on a thousand different objects, or on one that gets renamed, copied or built inside a loop. So JavaScript hands the method a reference to the object it was called on, and that reference is called this.

ELI5: this means "whoever I was called on". And the rule for working out who that is turns out to be almost embarrassingly literal:

That second sentence is the part that catches people, so it is worth stating on its own: this is not fixed when you write the function. It is worked out again every single time the function is called. Which means you can break it simply by calling the same function a different way.

try-it.js

Nothing was changed about the function. It was simply called with nothing to the left of a dot, so there was no object to be this, and this.title came back undefined. This exact detachment is what happens when you hand a method to something else to call later — an event listener, a setTimeout, an array method — which is why this has a reputation for being slippery. It is not slippery; it just answers a question about the call, not about the code.

Worth knowing before you experiment, because it will confuse you otherwise. When a function is called with nothing to the left of a dot, this is not simply empty — in a browser it becomes the page-wide window object. Usually that means this.something is undefined and you get the clean result above. But window already has a handful of built-in properties of its own, and name is one of them — it holds an empty string. So a detached method reading this.name hands back "" rather than undefined, which looks like an entirely different bug. That is exactly why the examples here use title and not name. (In strict mode and inside modules, this really is undefined in that situation and reading a property off it throws outright — arguably the better behaviour, since at least it is loud.) 
const book = { title: "Dune", describe: function() { return this.title; } };
const d = book.describe;
console.log(d());

What does this log?

Complete the rule: inside an ordinary method, this is whatever sits immediately to the left of the ____ at the moment of the call.

The this keyword

Gives the same working rule you have just been given — if the function is a method on an object, this is that object — and then shows constructor functions called with new, which is where you will meet this next.

One claim to file with an asterisk. He says that in a plain function — one not attached to an object — this is the window object. That is true only in JavaScript’s older, looser mode. In strict mode, and inside modules, which Section 16 introduces, this is undefined there instead and reading a property off it throws. You will meet both behaviours in this same guide. The half that matters now is unchanged: method on an object → the object; plain function → not the object. Do not memorise “always window”.

Object methods, “this”

Says outright what the video leaves out: in strict mode a plain function’s this is undefined, and the window answer is old behaviour that strict mode fixed.

When two good sources explain this differently, neither is wrong. MDN gives the short rule — in a method, this is the object it was called on. javascript.info builds a whole model of how JavaScript tracks variables first, and warns you on the way in. The second is the deeper version of the first, not a contradiction. Expect that pattern generally: a simple rule you can use today, and a fuller account that explains why the rule holds. Learning the simple one first is not learning it wrong.

Why arrow functions are the wrong choice for a method — and the right one inside it

Back in Section 5 the arrow-function card said it "has no this of its own". This is what that means, and it cuts both ways.

An arrow function does not get handed a this when it is called. Instead it reaches outward to whatever this already meant in the code surrounding where it was written. So as an object method it is simply broken:

try-it.js

The object literal is not a function, so it creates no this for the arrow to borrow — the arrow reaches past it to the surrounding code, where this is not your song. Rule of thumb: never use an arrow function as an object method.

And now the flip side, which is the entire reason arrows were designed this way. Inside a proper method, a nested callback written with function gets its own this — and loses your object. Written as an arrow, it borrows the method's this and keeps working:

try-it.js

obj.method()

this is obj — whatever is left of the dot. The normal, useful case.

standalone()

No dot, no object. this is not yours — undefined, or the page-wide global object in older non-strict code.

arrow function

No this of its own, ever. Borrows from wherever it was written. Wrong for methods, right for callbacks inside them.

This is not academic, and it arrives sooner than you think. Section 18 introduces Phaser, a game framework where every single thing you do inside a scene goes through this — this.add, this.physics, this.input. Without this section that code would be pure copying. With it, you can read it. 
const song = { title: "Blue", play: () => this.title };
console.log(song.play());

Bracket notation, and why it is not just a longer dot

Earlier you saw user["age"] does the same as user.age. That makes it look like pointless extra typing. The difference only shows up when the property name is not known when you write the code:

A dot always means "the property literally spelled like this". Brackets mean "work out this expression, then use the answer as the key". That is also exactly why for...in back in Section 4 had to use dog[key] — key was a variable holding the name, not the name itself.

const user = { name: "Sam", age: 28 };

Nesting: the shape real data actually comes in

Arrays hold anything, and objects hold anything, which means arrays hold objects and objects hold arrays. One shape in particular — an array of objects — is what almost every real list of things looks like, including the mood tracker you build in Section 8:

Nothing new is needed to work with this. Every array method from earlier in this section takes a callback, and inside that callback each item is simply an object you read with a dot. That is the whole trick.

const entries = [

Reaching for something that is not there

Nesting brings one specific crash with it, and it is worth meeting deliberately rather than at 11pm:

try-it.js

Asking for a property that does not exist gives you undefined, which is harmless. Asking for a property of that undefined is a genuine error that stops your whole script — undefined is not an object and has nothing to look inside. Optional chaining (?.) is the guard: "if the thing on my left is null or undefined, stop here and give back undefined; otherwise carry on." It works for calls (obj.maybeMethod?.()) and positions (list?.[0]) too.

Do not sprinkle it everywhere. ?. silences a crash, and a crash is information. If a value is supposed to always exist, a loud error at the moment it does not is far better than an undefined quietly flowing three screens away and breaking something unrelated. Use ?. where a value is genuinely optional; fix the cause where it is not. 
const user = { name: "Sam" };
console.log(user.pet?.name);

There is no pet. What does this log?

Turning an object into an array: Object.keys, values and entries

Objects have no filter, no map, no reduce. Three built-in functions bridge the gap by handing you the object's contents as an array — at which point the whole toolbox from earlier in this section applies to object data too.

try-it.js

Note Object with a capital O — these are not methods on your object, they are functions you pass your object to. And this is the modern replacement for for...in from Section 4: Object.keys(obj).forEach(...) does the same job with none of for...in's awkwardness.

Which of the three gives you an array of [key, value] pairs, rather than just the keys or just the values?

Assigning an array doesn't copy it

Numbers and strings copy when you assign them to a new variable. Arrays and objects don't — this is where a lot of real bugs come from.

let listA = ["a", "b"];
let listB = listA;
listB.push("c");
console.log(listA.length);

What does this log?

run it to check
Clue found

This isn't specific to variable assignment either — it's exactly the same rule when an array is passed into a function. The parameter name is just another alias for the same array the caller passed in, not a fresh copy, so a function that pushes to its parameter is mutating the caller's original array too.

Making a real, independent copy

let original = [1, 2, 3];
let copyA = original;
let copyB = [...original];
copyA.push(4);
copyB.push(5);
console.log(original.length);

What does this log?

run it to check
Clue found

Three common ways to make a real, independent shallow copy: spread syntax ([...original]), original.slice(), or Array.from(original). All three build a brand-new array and copy each element's value across. One catch worth knowing: if the array holds other arrays or objects inside it, those inner ones are still shared between the copy and the original — a "shallow" copy only makes the outer array itself independent.

Destructuring — unpacking in one line

Pulling several values out of an array or object is so common that JavaScript has dedicated syntax for it. It looks alarming for about ten minutes and then becomes the way you write everything.

From an array, by position:

try-it.js

From an object, by name:

try-it.js
The one difference to hold onto: arrays destructure by position, so the names you pick are entirely up to you. Objects destructure by name, so the names inside the braces must match the property names exactly — const { nmae } = user gives you undefined and no warning whatsoever.

Where this really pays off is in parameters. A function taking an object can unpack it right in its own parameter list, which is why almost all modern JavaScript — and all of the React Native code in Section 19 — is written this way:

try-it.js
const [, second] = ["a", "b", "c"];
console.log(second);

Note the gap before the comma. What does this log?

Array destructuring matches by position. Object destructuring matches by what?

Spread works on objects too

The [...original] trick above has an object twin, and it is how you make a changed copy of an object without touching the original — the pattern almost every modern app is built on.

try-it.js
The same shallow-copy catch as arrays. { ...user } copies the top layer only. If a property holds another object or an array, the copy and the original still point at that same inner thing — change it through either name and both see it. For flat objects this never matters; for nested ones it is the aliasing bug from earlier in this section, one level down and much harder to spot. 
const user = { name: "Sam", age: 28 };
console.log({ age: 99, ...user }.age);

Read the order carefully. What does this log?

Two more containers: Set and Map

Arrays and objects cover most of what you need. Two other containers exist because each solves one problem those two do badly.

A Set holds only unique values. Adding something twice does nothing the second time. Which makes de-duplicating a list a one-liner:

try-it.js

.has() is the other reason to reach for one. On a long array, includes() has to walk the whole thing; a Set answers immediately no matter how big it is. With ten items nobody would notice. With fifty thousand, it is the difference between instant and frozen.

A Map is an object whose keys can be anything. Object keys are always strings — write obj[1] and the 1 is silently converted to "1". A Map keeps the real key, of any type, and remembers insertion order:

try-it.js
When to reach for which. Plain object for a fixed set of named properties describing one thing — that is your mood entry. Array for an ordered list. Set when the only question is "have I seen this before". Map when the keys are dynamic, or not strings, or when you genuinely care about the order they were added. Most of the time, an object or an array is right; knowing the other two exist is what stops you writing forty lines to avoid a duplicate. 
const s = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]);
console.log(s.size);

A backup utility, worth trusting

Put the last two ideas together and you get a genuinely useful little helper — hand it any list, get back a safe copy to experiment with:

backupList(...) hands you back a safe, independent copy of whatever array you pass in — push to the result all you like, the array you originally passed in stays untouched. Trace it through: saved.push("file3.txt") only touches saved, so console.log(original) still logs just the original two files.

function backupList(list) {
  const backup = list;
  return backup;
}

let original = ["file1.txt", "file2.txt"];
let saved = backupList(original);
saved.push("file3.txt");

console.log(original);

Explain it in your own words

const scores = [1, 2, 3]; scores.push(4); runs with no error, but const scores = [1, 2, 3]; scores = [5, 6]; throws one. What exactly does const protect, and what does it leave completely alone?

const protects exactly one thing: the binding between the variable name and the value it currently points to. scores = [5, 6] tries to point the name scores at a completely different array, which is exactly the reassignment const blocks. scores.push(4) never touches the variable itself — it reaches into the array scores already points to and changes what's inside it. const has no opinion at all about that; mutation of the array's contents (push, pop, splice, sort, or changing an object's properties) is entirely unrestricted.

Selecting elements

document.querySelector(selector) hands back the first real element matching a CSS-style selector — the same kind of selector you'd use in a stylesheet. document.querySelectorAll(selector) hands back every match at once.

The Document Object Model

What the page actually is, underneath the selecting: a tree of objects the browser built out of your HTML and hands to JavaScript. Worth reading if “the DOM” still feels like a word rather than a thing.

Creating, changing, and removing elements

document.createElement(tag) makes a new, detached element — it does nothing to the page until you attach it somewhere with .appendChild(...). Once you've got a real element, .textContent sets its visible text safely; .innerHTML instead parses whatever string you give it as actual HTML, tags and all.

let box = document.createElement('div');
box.textContent = "Hello world";
document.body.appendChild(box);

Does the word "world" show up bold on the page?

element.addEventListener('click', function(){...}) wires up code to run when something happens. You'll also see element.onclick = function(){...} in older code and tutorials — it works, but only one function can ever be assigned that way per element per event.

btn.onclick = function() { console.log("first"); };
btn.onclick = function() { console.log("second"); };
btn.click();

Changing how something looks: classList

You can set styles straight from JavaScript — box.style.backgroundColor = "red" — and you almost never should. Appearance belongs in your stylesheet. JavaScript's job is to say what state an element is in; CSS decides what that state looks like. Classes are how you say it, and classList is how you change them.

try-it.js
I am a real element on this page. Run the code above and watch me.

toggle is the one you will use most: it flips the class on or off depending on what is already there, which is exactly what a "selected", "expanded" or "dark mode" button needs. It also takes a second argument to force a direction — toggle("on", true) means "make sure it is on", regardless of the current state.

This guide runs on it. The sidebar you are looking at uses classList for every single state — locked, active, and the done class that puts a ✓ next to a finished section. When Section 6 ticked itself off, that was one classList.add('done') call. Open DevTools, find a nav button in the Elements panel, and watch its class list change as you move around.

The exception, so the rule does not become dogma: .style is right for values that are genuinely computed at runtime — a position in pixels, a progress bar's width taken from real data. A class cannot express "37.4% wide". Section 9's game sets positions this way. But for anything that is a state — active, selected, hidden, error — use a class.

Which classList method adds the class if it is missing and removes it if it is already there?

The event object — the argument you did not know you were being handed

Every event handler is called with one argument, automatically, whether you ask for it or not. Name it and you get a whole object describing what just happened. Convention is e or event.

try-it.js

The three you will actually use:

  • e.target — the deepest element the event really started on. Click an icon inside a button, and e.target is the icon.
  • e.currentTarget — the element your listener is attached to. Usually the same as target. When they differ, something interesting is happening — see bubbling, below.
  • e.key — on keyboard events only, the key as text: "a", "Enter", "ArrowLeft", " " for the space bar.

Which property of the event object tells you the element the event actually started on — the deepest one, not the one you attached the listener to?

There are far more events than click

"click" is one string among dozens. The name is the only thing that changes; addEventListener works identically for all of them.

input

Fires on every keystroke, live, as the user types. Character counters, live search, instant validation.

change

Fires once, when the user finishes and leaves the field — or immediately for checkboxes and dropdowns.

keydown / keyup

A key going down, and coming back up. e.key says which. keydown is what games listen for — Section 9's paddle included.

submit

Fires on the <form>, not on the button. Listening on the button misses the Enter key entirely.

Also worth knowing they exist: mouseenter/mouseleave, focus/blur, scroll, resize, and dblclick — which is what reveals the hidden puzzle panels in this guide.

try-it.js
nothing yet

Run it, then type — the text on the right updates on every keystroke. Then click somewhere else and check the console: change fires only at that moment. That difference is the whole reason both exist.

You want a character counter that updates as the user types, not when they finish. Which event — input or change?

Stopping the browser doing its own thing: preventDefault

Some elements already do something when acted on, with no JavaScript involved at all. A link navigates. A checkbox ticks. And — the one that will cost you an evening if nobody warns you — a form submits, which reloads the page.

Your handler runs first. Then the default happens anyway. So the classic first form goes: click submit, your code runs perfectly, the page reloads, everything you just did is wiped, and the console is cleared before you can read it. It looks exactly like your code never ran.

form.addEventListener("submit", function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();     // stop the reload -- FIRST line, always
  // now your own code, which will actually survive
  const value = input.value;
  console.log("submitted:", value);
});

Put it first, before anything that could throw. If an error happens above the preventDefault line, the default still goes ahead and the page reloads anyway — taking your error message with it.

Why bother with a form at all? You could put a click handler on a plain button and skip all this. A real <form> gets you the Enter key for free, proper keyboard and screen-reader behaviour, and browser-native required-field validation. It is the right tool — it just comes with one default you have to switch off.

Your submit handler runs, and then the page reloads and wipes everything. What single call inside the handler stops that?

Events travel upward — and that turns out to be useful

Click a button that sits inside a list item that sits inside a list. The click does not fire only on the button. It fires on the button, then on the list item, then on the list, then on the body, then on the document — each in turn, outward. This is called bubbling, and it is not a quirk; it is the design.

The immediate consequence: a listener on a container hears clicks on everything inside it. The useful consequence has a name — event delegation.

Say you render fifty list items, each with a Delete button. You could attach fifty listeners. But then you re-render the list, every element is thrown away and rebuilt, and all fifty listeners are gone — so you attach fifty more, every single time. Instead, attach one listener to the container, which never gets rebuilt, and let e.target tell you what was clicked:

try-it.js

Two new pieces in there, and both earn their place:

  • data-name="Ash" in the HTML becomes el.dataset.name in JavaScript. Any attribute starting data- works this way, and it is the standard place to hang an id on an element so a click can be traced back to a record. The value is always a string, even when it looks like a number.
  • e.target.closest("li") walks up from whatever was actually clicked until it finds the nearest matching ancestor. You need it because e.target might be a <span> or an icon inside the thing you care about. Nothing matched? It returns null, which is what the if (!li) return; guard is for.
e.stopPropagation() stops the bubbling. It exists, it works, and it should be your last resort — it silently prevents every listener further out from ever hearing the event, including ones written by someone else, including "close this menu when the user clicks anywhere". Bugs caused by a stray stopPropagation are miserable to track down precisely because nothing errors and nothing logs. Prefer checking e.target and returning early.

Rather than attaching a listener to each of fifty list items, you attach one to the list itself and use e.target to work out which item was clicked. What is that technique called?

One consequence of bubbling catches everybody exactly once, and it is worth meeting before it costs you an afternoon.

<button id="save"><span>Save</span></button>

document.getElementById("save").addEventListener("click", function (event) {
  console.log(event.target.tagName);
});

You click directly on the word “Save”. What does this log — BUTTON or SPAN?

Clue found

event.target is where the click started. event.currentTarget is the element whose handler is currently running — which is what this also refers to in a normal function handler. Put an icon or a span inside a button and target stops being the button. This is the bug behind half the “my click handler gets the wrong element” questions ever asked.

The clearest treatment of the distinction that trips everyone: event.target is what was actually clicked; event.currentTarget is the element whose handler is running. They are different elements most of the time, and confusing them is a real bug rather than a technicality.

Event delegation

The written version of the video. It reaches for closest() where the video uses matches() — both are fine and neither corrects the other. matches() asks “is this the thing I want?”; closest() asks “is this, or anything above it, the thing I want?”, which is what you need when the clickable thing has something nested inside it.

Never build HTML out of what a user typed

Earlier you established that textContent treats its input as plain text and innerHTML parses it as real HTML. That difference stops being a curiosity the moment the string came from a person:

// the note came from a text box the user typed into
list.innerHTML = "<li>" + note + "</li>";

Type <b>hello</b> into that box and it renders bold — mildly annoying. Type something with an onerror handler on a broken image tag and the browser runs it, with the same access to the page and to localStorage as your own code. On a page only you use, that is a curiosity. On anything other people load, it is the single most common web vulnerability there is, and it has a name: cross-site scripting.

Three ways out, in order of preference:

  • createElement plus textContent — build the element, set its text. Always safe, because text is never parsed as markup. This is what Section 8's render function does.
  • Escape the string first — convert <, > and & into their harmless entity forms before inserting. This guide has its own escapeHtml function doing exactly that, for exactly this reason.
  • insertAdjacentText — for dropping plain text at a position without touching the surrounding markup.

The rule is short enough to memorise: anything a person typed goes in through textContent, never innerHTML.

You are putting text a user typed onto the page. Which property do you set on the element so the text can never be parsed as HTML?

Why getElementById sometimes returns null

This one will happen to you in your first hour of writing a real page, and it looks like your JavaScript is simply broken. Nothing runs. No visible error unless the console is open. And the element is definitely there in the HTML — you can see it.

The cause is timing. The browser reads an HTML file strictly top to bottom, and runs each <script> the moment it reaches it. A script in the <head> therefore runs before the body exists. document.getElementById("thing") returns null, and the next line — null.addEventListener(...) — throws.

Script at the end of body

Put <script src="app.js"></script> just before </body>. Everything above it already exists. Simplest fix, and what your own project will do.

defer

<script defer src="app.js"> in the head: downloads immediately, runs after the HTML is parsed. Note it only works with src — it is ignored on inline scripts.

DOMContentLoaded

Wrap your code in document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () { ... }). Works anywhere, and is what you will see in a lot of existing code.

Where should a plain <script> tag go so that the page's elements already exist by the time it runs — in the head, or at the end of the body?

    Making it stick: localStorage

    Everything above disappears the instant you refresh. localStorage.setItem(key, value) and localStorage.getItem(key) save real data in the browser itself — it survives refreshes and even closing the browser entirely. On a laptop it sits there until something clears it — but that is not the whole story on a phone, and the difference decides whether the app you are about to build keeps its data or quietly loses it. This is exactly the mechanism Sections 4-6's flag tracking already uses behind the scenes, and what the mood tracker in Section 8 is built on.

    How long “saved” actually lasts

    Almost every tutorial you will read treats localStorage as permanent. On a desktop browser that is close enough to true. On an iPhone it is not, and the exception is aimed squarely at the kind of app you are building.

    Safari runs something called Intelligent Tracking Prevention. Its job is to stop advertisers following you around the web by leaving data in your browser. It cannot tell the difference between an advertiser’s tracking data and your mood tracker’s entries, so it treats both the same way: after seven days with no interaction from you, it deletes all of it.

    “All of it” is broader than it sounds. The rule covers:

    • localStorage — everything the mood tracker saves
    • sessionStorage and IndexedDB — the other two browser storage tools
    • service worker registrations and their caches — which is the part that surprises people, because that is the thing that makes an app work offline. Section 19 builds one.

    “Interaction” means a tap, a click or typing. Scrolling does not count. So: you build the tracker, you deploy it, you log your mood every day for a fortnight, you get busy, and nine days later you open it to an empty list and a service worker that has forgotten how to work offline. Nothing errored. Your code is fine. You would have no reason on earth to suspect the browser.

    And here is the part worth remembering, because it is the fix. A site that has been added to the home screen is exempt. Its data is kept separate from Safari’s, and the seven-day rule does not apply to it at all.

    That single fact is the strongest argument for the first thing Section 19 teaches. Adding your app to the home screen sounds like a cosmetic touch — a nicer icon, no address bar. It is not. It is what makes your data durable. Everything else that section covers is about distributing your app to other people; this one is about your own app not losing your own entries.
    What this does not mean. It is not a reason to avoid localStorage — it is the right tool for this app and you should use it. It is a reason to know what “saved” is actually promising, to tell anyone using your app to install it properly, and — when the data genuinely matters — to give them a way to export it. A “download my entries” button is a good instinct to develop early.

    Your mood tracker is deployed and works perfectly. A friend uses it on their iPhone in Safari, then doesn’t open it for nine days. What have they lost, and what one thing could they have done to prevent it?

    let entry = { mood: "good", note: "walked outside" };
localStorage.setItem('demoEntry', entry);
console.log(localStorage.getItem('demoEntry'));

    What actually gets logged? (Run it for real if you're not sure — it's a genuinely common surprise.)

    run it to check
    Clue found

    This is the single most common real-world localStorage bug, and it fails silently — no error, just quietly wrong data sitting there. Open DevTools' Application panel (steps below) after running this and you'll see exactly this broken string saved under the key demoEntry, in your own browser, right now.

    let entry = { mood: "good", note: "walked outside" };
localStorage.setItem('demoEntry2', JSON.stringify(entry));
let raw = localStorage.getItem('demoEntry2');
let restored = JSON.parse(raw);
console.log(restored.mood);

    And what does this one log?

    Clue found

    The pattern to default to, always: JSON.stringify(...) going in, JSON.parse(...) coming back out, for any object or array you want localStorage to actually hold onto correctly. Plain strings and numbers don't need this — JSON.stringify on a string that's already a string just gives back an equivalent string, so it's harmless even when it's not strictly needed.

    Explain it in your own words

    Why does localStorage.setItem('x', {a: 1}) silently "work" — no error — while still being wrong? What's actually happening underneath, and what's the fix?

    setItem never checks what type of value it's given — it just calls JavaScript's default string conversion on whatever's passed in and saves that. An object converts to the string "[object Object]" without throwing, so nothing about the call looks wrong: no error, no warning, just a value quietly saved that has already lost everything except the fact that it used to be an object. JSON.stringify before saving, JSON.parse after reading, is the fix — it's a genuine conversion that actually preserves the object's structure, rather than JS's default one-line summary of it.

    Project: your first app — mood tracker

    Everything from here on is one real, working thing, not isolated exercises — a small daily mood/symptom tracker, built from pieces you already know: an array of objects (Section 6), real DOM + events (Section 7), and localStorage (Section 7). It's smaller and more tractable than the game coming after it — deliberately, per the plan in the decisions log — and its optional stretch feature previews exactly the coordinate math the Canvas game needs next.

    The data model: one array, real objects, real ids

    Every entry is a plain object: { id, mood, note }. The id is the one new piece — a real, unique value that survives no matter where the entry ends up in the array later. This guide's own progress-notes page already does exactly this (Date.now() + '-' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2,7)) — reuse that same idiom here.

    Write a function called createEntry(mood, note) that returns a new entry object: { id: a real unique value, mood: mood, note: note }. Each call needs a genuinely different id — Date.now() + '-' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2,7) is the guide's own pattern, reused.
    your-code.js

    Render-from-state: one function draws the whole list, every time

    Rather than hand-editing the list a little bit on every change, one function rebuilds the whole visible list from the current array, called fresh after every add or delete. It's more work up front and far fewer bugs later — the screen can never quietly drift out of sync with the real data if it's always redrawn from that data.

    Write a function called renderEntries(container, entries) that clears container, then appends one real <li> per entry, with text that includes the entry's mood and (if present) its note.

      entries = entries.filter(e => e.id !== targetId) is the clean way to drop an entry when you own the variable — when entries is yours to point somewhere new.       Now: wire up delete for real

      Render and delete, put together, should mean each Delete button removes exactly the entry sitting next to it — click any one, and only that entry disappears. See for yourself, live, right here — three real entries, three real Delete buttons:

        Click a Delete button above to see what actually gets deleted.

        First, the thing you just watched. Every Delete button reported the same result, and none of them deleted the entry beside it. That is not a delete bug. You have met it before, in Section 4, wearing different clothes — here is the shape of the loop that drew those buttons: 
        for (var i = 0; i < entries.length; i++) {
  var btn = makeDeleteButton();
  btn.onclick = function () {
    remove(entries[i]);  // which i?
  };
}

        var i gives the whole loop one i, not one per pass. The three buttons are created, the loop runs to completion, and i comes to rest at 3 — one past the last entry. Nobody clicks anything until after that. So all three handlers read the same finished variable and all three ask for entries[3], which does not exist. It is the staggered-logging loop from Section 4 exactly: code scheduled to run later reads the variable after the loop has already finished with it. There a delay moved the reading to later; here a click does.

        Two fixes, both one line: declare the counter with let so each pass gets its own, or capture the entry’s id on the button itself and read that instead of an index. Neither is what the puzzle below is about. Getting the right entry is half of a working delete; the other half is doing the right things to it, in the right order, and that half is where real apps break.

        No code to write. Get the sequence right. A working delete is a handful of operations that every real app does in one specific order. Some of the lines below do not belong in it at all — they are things that look like a delete and are not. Build only the ones that do, in the order that actually works. The lines that belong are each individually correct: the wrong order on its own is enough to break the app.

        The user has clicked Delete on the entry with id id. entries is the array your app holds in memory, and container is the element the list is drawn into.

        The order matters for a reason worth saying out loud: memory is the truth, storage is a copy of the truth, and the screen is a picture of the truth. Change them in any other order and you save or draw something that was already out of date.

        The missing letter: U

        Your tracker can Create an entry, Read the list back, and Delete an entry. That is three of the four operations every real app is built from — CRUD: create, read, update, delete. The one it cannot do is change an entry that already exists, and that is not a stretch feature. Anyone who logs a mood and then remembers what actually happened will want to fix the note.

        The instinct is to reach into the array and change the object in place. Do not. Everything in this app already works on the principle that a change produces a new array, which is then saved and re-rendered — the delete function above does exactly that with filter. Updating follows the same shape, using map:

        try-it.js

        Three things you already know, doing all the work. map walks the array and builds a new one. The ternary decides, per entry, whether this is the one being changed. Object spread makes a copy of that entry with the changed fields written over the top — { ...entry, ...changes }, changes last, so changes win. Everything else is passed straight through unmodified.

        Why not just entry.note = "long day"? It would work, today, in this app. It stops working the moment anything else holds a reference to that array or that entry — a rendered copy, an undo stack, a filtered view — because all of them are looking at the same object and none of them asked to be changed. That is the aliasing rule from Section 6, arriving in a real app. Producing a new array instead means the only way anything sees the change is by being handed the new array on purpose, which is exactly the discipline every UI framework you will ever meet is built on.

        Delete builds a new array with filter. Update builds a new array with which array method?

        Write updateEntry(entries, id, changes): it returns a new array in which the entry with the matching id has the properties in changes written over it, and every other entry is passed through untouched. An id that matches nothing changes nothing. The second test deliberately re-uses the same array as the first — so if your version modifies the original rather than building a new one, that test will fail and tell you.
        your-code.js

        Editing forces a new idea: state that is about the interface, not the data

        Changing the data is the easy half. The harder half is the screen. Delete needs no interface at all — click, gone. Edit does: the entry has to turn into something you can type in, and then turn back.

        Which means the app has to remember something that is not part of any entry: which entry is currently being edited. That is a new kind of state — it describes the interface, not the data. It never gets saved to localStorage, because it is meaningless tomorrow.

        let entries = loadEntries();
let editingId = null;      // interface state: nothing is being edited right now

function startEdit(id) {
  editingId = id;
  render();                // no data changed -- only the screen
}

function saveEdit(id, newNote) {
  entries = updateEntry(entries, id, { note: newNote });
  editingId = null;        // leave edit mode
  saveEntries(entries);    // the DATA changed, so persist it
  render();
}

function cancelEdit() {
  editingId = null;        // no save -- the entry is untouched
  render();
}

        Notice what startEdit does not do: it does not save. Nothing about the stored data has changed — the user has only announced an intention. Only saveEdit writes to storage. And cancelEdit is not an afterthought; without it there is no way out of edit mode except committing, which is a genuinely bad interface.

        Then the render function branches on that one value:

        function renderWithEdit(container, entries, editingId) {
  container.innerHTML = "";
  entries.forEach(function (entry) {
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    if (entry.id === editingId) {
      const input = document.createElement("input");
      input.value = entry.note;        // start from what is already there
      li.appendChild(input);
    } else {
      li.textContent = entry.mood + " — " + entry.note;
    }
    container.appendChild(li);
  });
}

        One list, one render function, one if. There is no separate "edit screen" and no second code path — the same function draws both states, and which one you get falls out of the value of editingId. Change the value, call render again, and the interface follows. That single idea is what every UI framework in existence automates for you; doing it by hand once is how it stops being magic.

        Setting input.value from the existing note matters more than it looks. An edit box that opens empty is not an edit box — it is a "retype the whole thing" box. Starting from the current value is the difference between fixing a typo and doing the work twice.
        Live, against the real page. Write renderWithEdit(container, entries, editingId) following the shape above: one <li> per entry, and for the entry whose id matches editingId, an <input> inside that li whose value is that entry's note. The checker renders three entries with the middle one in edit mode, then renders again with editingId set to null and checks the input has gone.
          your-code.js

          One bad value in storage should not brick the whole app

          JSON.parse does not return null when handed something that is not valid JSON. It throws — and an uncaught throw stops the script dead, at that line, with nothing after it running at all. Since loadEntries() runs on every single page load, one corrupt value in localStorage means your app never starts again. Not "shows an error" — never starts, until you clear storage by hand.

          It is not far-fetched, either: a half-finished write, a version of your code that stored a different shape, or you poking at localStorage in the console at midnight. This is exactly what try/catch is for.

          try-it.js

          The structure is: try { ... } holds the code that might fail, and catch (err) { ... } runs only if something inside the try threw. The moment anything in the try block throws, the rest of that block is abandoned and control jumps to the catch — so anything after the failing line inside try never runs. err.message is the human-readable description; there is also err.name for the error type.

          Notice the Array.isArray check as well. catch only saves you from throws. '{"a":1}' is perfectly valid JSON that parses without complaint into an object — and then entries.map(...) fails somewhere else entirely, with a far more confusing message. Catching the throw and validating the shape are two different jobs and you need both.

          Do not wrap everything in try/catch. A catch block that swallows an error and carries on silently turns a loud, findable crash into a quiet wrong answer three screens away — which is strictly worse to debug. Use it where failure is expected and recoverable: parsing data you did not write, a network call, reading storage. For your own logic being wrong, let it throw. The crash is the bug report.

          Which pair of keywords lets you attempt something that might throw, and carry on with a fallback instead of the script stopping dead?

          Write safeLoad(raw). It takes whatever came out of localStorage and always returns a real array: the parsed array if raw is valid JSON containing an array, and an empty array in every other case — invalid JSON, valid JSON that is not an array, or nothing saved at all. It must never throw.

          Where try / catch belongs in the bigger picture: which failures you should catch, which you should let crash loudly, and why catching everything is worse than catching nothing. Directly about the decision you just made.

            Optional stretch: a trend line, and a preview of the game

            Not required, and not gated — but this is exactly the piece the decisions log flagged as previewing the Canvas game coming up next: turning a list of numbers into real screen positions. Map each mood ("Low"/"Okay"/"Good" → 1/2/3, say) to an x,y pixel pair, spread evenly left to right, and draw an SVG <polyline> through them:

            x — spread evenly

            x = padding + i * (width - 2*padding) / (count - 1)

            y — flipped, since SVG grows downward

            y = padding + (max - value) / (max - min) * (height - 2*padding)

            Explain it in your own words

            Why does deleting by array index (entries.splice(2, 1), say) get riskier the more the list changes, while deleting by id doesn't have that problem at all?

            An index is only ever "whichever entry currently happens to sit at position 2" — true at the instant it was captured, and silently wrong the moment anything before position 2 gets added or removed, since everything after it shifts. An id has no such dependency: it was assigned to one specific entry when that entry was created and never means anything else, no matter how many times the array is re-sorted, filtered, or changed around it. Index-based delete isn't wrong today; it's a bug waiting for the array to change shape once.

            The canvas element and its coordinate system

            <canvas> is a blank drawing surface. canvas.getContext('2d') hands you the tool that actually draws on it — ctx.fillRect(x, y, width, height) for rectangles, ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, Math.PI*2) for circles. The one genuinely new thing, and the single biggest source of beginner confusion here: the origin (0,0) is the top-left corner, x grows to the right same as always, but y grows downward — the opposite of the graphs from school, where up is positive.

            Keeping it moving: the requestAnimationFrame loop

            Canvas is a static bitmap — nothing about it is "live." An animation is really just: draw a frame, wait a tiny bit, draw a slightly different frame, repeat, fast enough that it reads as motion. requestAnimationFrame(loop) is how you ask the browser to call your function again right before its next repaint — synced to the display, and automatically paused when the tab isn't visible, unlike an old-style setInterval loop that just keeps firing on a fixed timer regardless.

            x-ranges must overlap

            a.x < b.x + b.width && a.x + a.width > b.x

            AND y-ranges must overlap

            a.y < b.y + b.height && a.y + a.height > b.y

            Moving something with the keyboard

            A paddle that cannot be moved is not a game. Section 7 gave you keydown and e.key; this is the shape games actually use them in, and it is not the obvious one.

            The fix is to stop treating a key press as an action, and treat it as a state. Keydown records that a key is down. Keyup records that it is up. The game loop — which is already running sixty times a second — reads that record and moves accordingly.

            the pattern

            Two separate ifs, not else if — so holding left and right together is expressible, and so is holding left and up in a game that has both. That is diagonal movement, for free, from the same three lines.

            e.key versus e.code. e.key is the character produced — it changes with the keyboard layout, and it is "a" or "A" depending on Shift. e.code is the physical key, always "KeyA" regardless of layout or Shift. For arrow keys they behave the same. For WASD movement, e.code is the correct choice, or a French AZERTY keyboard cannot play your game.

            Everything on the last page was keyboard. That is the right place to start and it works perfectly on the machine you are writing it on.             There are two ways to read a finger, and the one nearly every tutorial shows you is the one you should not use.

            Pointer events — use theseTouch events
            Eventspointerdown, pointermove, pointerup, pointercanceltouchstart, touchmove, touchend, touchcancel

            Use pointer events. They have worked in every browser since July 2020, and the reason to prefer them is not modernity — it is that you can test them right now, on this laptop, with a mouse. A pointerdown handler you write today runs when you click it and runs again, unchanged, when you tap it on your phone in Section 19. With touch events you would write it twice and only ever be able to test half of it.

            The shape is exactly the click handler you already know:

            the pattern

            Two details in there are worth more than they look.

            The dragging flag. On a phone, pointermove only fires while a finger is actually touching the screen. On your laptop it fires whenever the mouse moves across the canvas, pressed or not — so without the flag the paddle follows your cursor around without you ever clicking, and the game behaves differently on the two devices you are trying to support with one code path. The flag makes “pressed” explicit, and both devices then agree.

            pointercancel. This is the one people leave out and then cannot explain. It fires when the browser or the operating system takes the gesture away from you mid-move — a call arrives, the finger slides off the edge of the screen, a notification drops down. There is no pointerup in that case, so without this line dragging stays true forever and your paddle keeps following a finger that stopped existing. Both events do the same job here, which is why they share one release function.

            Where the finger actually is, which is not where you think

            A pointer event gives you e.clientX — the distance from the left edge of the window. Your canvas needs the distance from the left edge of the canvas. Those are different numbers, and there is a second trap underneath the first one.

            A canvas has two widths. canvas.width is its drawing surface — the coordinate system you write code in. Its CSS width is how big it looks on screen. On your laptop they are usually the same and the bug stays hidden. On a phone, or the moment you make the canvas responsive, they are not — a 400-wide canvas displayed at 200px means every finger position is out by a factor of two, and your game becomes mysteriously unplayable on exactly the device you built it for.

            Write pointerToCanvasX(clientX, rectLeft, rectWidth, canvasWidth). It takes the pointer’s window x, the canvas’s left edge and displayed width (both from canvas.getBoundingClientRect()), and the canvas’s drawing width. Return the x in canvas coordinates. A canvas 400 wide but displayed at 200px is showing everything at half size.

            function canvasX(e) {
              const r = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
              return pointerToCanvasX(e.clientX, r.left, r.width, canvas.width);

            getBoundingClientRect() is where r.left and r.width come from — the canvas’s real position and displayed size, measured right now. canvas.width is the drawing surface. Two different widths, which is the whole point.

            Wire all that up, open it on a phone, and the paddle moves — while the whole page scrolls underneath it, and a quick double-tap zooms in on your game. The browser assumes a drag means scroll and a double-tap means zoom, because on almost every page it does.

            Why does this guide teach pointerdown rather than touchstart, even though most tutorials you will find use touchstart?

            Why your game runs at double speed on someone else's machine

            Everything so far moves things by a fixed amount per frame: y += 3. That quietly assumes every machine runs the same number of frames per second. It does not.

            requestAnimationFrame matches the display's refresh rate. On an ordinary 60Hz monitor that is 60 frames a second. On a 120Hz laptop or a gaming monitor it is 120 — so y += 3 moves the dot twice as fast, and your game is unplayable on better hardware than yours. On a slow machine under load it drops to 30 and everything crawls. Same code, three different games.

            The fix is to stop thinking in "pixels per frame" and start thinking in pixels per second. requestAnimationFrame hands your callback a timestamp; the gap between this one and the last is how much time actually passed.

            the pattern

            At 60fps delta is about 0.0167, so the dot moves 3px per frame. At 120fps it is about 0.0083 and it moves 1.5px per frame — twice as often, half as far, identical speed on screen. Expressing speeds in seconds also makes them readable: SPEED = 180 means "crosses a 360px canvas in two seconds", which you can reason about. y += 3 means nothing until you know the frame rate.

            The two extra lines are not optional, and here is what each one is for.

            if (!lastTime) lastTime = timestamp; handles the very first frame. lastTime starts at 0, so without this the first delta is the entire page-load time expressed in seconds and your dot teleports before you have done anything.

            delta = Math.min(delta, 0.05); handles every other gap. requestAnimationFrame stops being called while the page is hidden — a switched tab on a laptop, a locked screen or an incoming call on a phone. When it comes back, one single frame reports the whole gap. Lock your phone for five minutes and delta arrives as 300: at 180 pixels per second your dot moves 54,000 pixels in one frame, straight past the paddle, through every collision check you wrote, and off the world. Clamping to 50ms says “never believe a gap bigger than three frames”, which is exactly right — a real gap that large means the game was not running, not that everything should lurch.

            Copy the pattern with both lines in it. Every version of this you find online will have one, the other, or neither, and the bug only shows up on a device you are not testing on.
            Write a function called moveBy(pixelsPerSecond, deltaMs) that returns how far something should move this frame, given the milliseconds that have passed. A full second at 300 pixels per second is 300 pixels.

            A game is not always playing

            Right now your game starts the instant the page loads and never stops. A real one has moments: a title screen, play, a pause, an ending, and a way back to the start. All of that comes from one variable.

            This is the same idea as Section 8's editingId — one piece of state that is about the interface rather than the data, and everything else reads it:

            the pattern

            The loop keeps running the whole time — it never stops, it just does different things. That matters, because it means the paused screen can still animate, and the game-over screen can still listen for a key press.

            Restart is where this pays off, and where it goes wrong. Restarting is not "reload the page" — it is putting every piece of state back to its starting value. And it is very easy to reset the score, the positions and the lives, and forget the one you added last week. Anything you can change during play must be reset in startGame(): score, lives, positions, speeds, timers, spawn counters, difficulty. If a second playthrough starts unexpectedly hard, that is always the cause, and having a single function that owns the reset is what makes it findable.

            Pausing on purpose, when the player looks away

            Clamping delta stops your game exploding when the player comes back. It does not stop the game running while they are away — and for anything with a timer, a countdown or a score, that is its own problem. A player who takes a phone call should not lose a life to a dot they could not see.

            The browser will tell you. visibilitychange fires whenever the page is hidden or shown, and document.hidden says which just happened:

            the pattern

            Two things are happening there and both matter. Setting the state to paused is the game-design half — your update should already be checking gameState, so everything stops on its own. Setting lastTime = 0 is the plumbing half, and it works because of the guard you just wrote on the previous page: a lastTime of 0 means the next frame treats itself as the first one and starts the clock fresh.

            This is not the same as the clamp, and you want both. The clamp is a seatbelt — it limits the damage from any gap, including ones you never anticipated. Pausing is a decision — it is you saying what should happen when the player is not looking. Ship the clamp because things go wrong; ship the pause because it is the behaviour a player expects.

            Coloured rectangles will take you a long way, and at some point you will want a picture. Canvas draws images with drawImage — but an image file has to load first, and that is where the trap is.

            the pattern

            Setting src starts a download that takes time. Call drawImage before it finishes and nothing appears — no error, no warning, just an empty canvas. Which looks exactly like your coordinates being wrong, and is not.

            Attach onload before setting src, not after. A cached image can finish loading immediately, before your next line runs — so a handler attached afterwards is attached to something that has already fired, and never runs at all. This is your first meeting with waiting for something, and Section 14 is entirely about doing it properly.

            Also worth knowing: drawImage takes optional width and height to scale, and a longer nine-argument form that cuts one frame out of a larger image. That is how a spritesheet works — every frame of an animation in a single file, drawn one rectangle at a time. Section 18's Phaser handles all of this for you, which is most of the reason it exists.

            HTML & CSS

            Everything so far has run inside this guide's own page. That page already existed — you never had to make one. From the next section onward you leave the sandbox and build in real files, and the very first thing you will need is a file this guide has never shown you: index.html.

            This section is the other half of the job. HTML is the structure — what things are. CSS is the appearance — what they look like. JavaScript, everything you have learned so far, is the behaviour. Three files, three jobs, and keeping them separate is most of what "well-built" means.

            The skeleton every page has

            An HTML file is plain text with tags in it. Every real page starts with the same five things, and each one earns its place:

            • <!DOCTYPE html> — line one, always. It is not really a tag; it tells the browser "use modern standards". Leave it out and the browser switches to a legacy mode where some CSS behaves differently, silently.
            • <html lang="en"> — wraps everything. The lang matters: it is how a screen reader knows which language to pronounce your text in.
            • <meta charset="utf-8"> — says "this text is UTF-8". Skip it and apostrophes, accents and emoji can come out as mojibake.
            • <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> — without this exact line a phone pretends to be a 980px-wide desktop and renders your page zoomed out. Every responsive thing you do later depends on it.
            • <title> — the browser tab, the bookmark name, and the blue link in search results.
            Write a complete page skeleton in the editor. It needs all five: the doctype, an <html> with a lang, a head containing charset, viewport and a real title, and a body with something visible in it. Press Render to see it; press Check when you think it is right.
            index.html
            preview

            The preview is a genuine, separate page — its own document, its own styles. Nothing you write in there can affect this guide.

            A second voice on this section. Coding For Dummies covers this ground across “Building the Silent”, “Getting More Out of HTML”, “Getting Stylish with CSS” and “Next Steps with CSS”. Read those for selectors, the cascade and how tags nest — all of which are stable and none of which have changed.

            Two warnings, and they matter. That book is from 2016, so read it for the concepts and not for the layout advice: anything using floats to position things has been superseded by the flexbox and grid you are learning here. And skip the Twitter Bootstrap chapter entirely. Bootstrap is a framework that solves the problems this section teaches you to solve yourself, in a style that contradicts it, and a 2016 version of it will teach you habits you would then have to unlearn. You are not missing anything.

            Tags, attributes, and nesting

            Almost every tag comes in a pair: an opening tag, some content, a closing tag. <p>Hello</p>. A handful have no content and so no closing tag — <img>, <br>, <input>, <meta>.

            Attributes go inside the opening tag and configure it: <a href="https://example.com">. You have already met two of them constantly — id and class — from the other side, in getElementById and classList.

            Nesting must not cross over. <p><strong>hi</strong></p> is fine; <p><strong>hi</p></strong> is not. Browsers will silently guess what you meant and often guess wrong, which produces a page that looks broken with no error anywhere.

            The tags you will actually use, nearly all the time:

            Text

            <h1>–<h6> headings, <p> paragraphs, <strong> and <em> for emphasis that means something, <span> for a scrap of inline text you need to target.

            Lists and links

            <ul>/<ol> with <li> inside, and <a href="...">. A link goes somewhere; a <button> does something. Do not swap them.

            Boxes

            <div> is a meaningless block used purely for layout, and <span> is its inline twin. Reach for them only when no tag with actual meaning fits.

            Headings are an outline, not a font size. <h1> through <h6> describe the structure of your document, and screen-reader users navigate by jumping between them — many will pull up a list of every heading on the page to find their way around. Skipping from h1 straight to h4 because it "looks the right size" breaks that outline. Pick the heading level that is structurally correct, then change the size in CSS.

            Images, and the attribute you must never skip

            <img src="cat.jpg" alt="A ginger cat asleep on a keyboard">. src is the file. alt is the text that stands in for the image — read aloud by a screen reader, and shown on screen if the file fails to load.

            Two rules that cover every case:

            • If the image means something, describe what it shows. Not "photo", not "image of a cat" — a screen reader already announces that it is an image. Just say what is in it.
            • If the image is purely decorative — a swirl, a divider — use alt="", deliberately empty. That tells assistive technology to skip it. Leaving alt off entirely is the one thing that is always wrong: then the file name gets read out instead, and "IMG_20240113_final_v2.jpg" helps nobody.
            Add an <img> to the body below with a genuinely descriptive alt. The image file does not exist, which is deliberate — a broken image is exactly when alt earns its keep, and you will see your own text appear in its place.

            You are adding a purely decorative swirl that carries no information at all. What exactly should its alt be?

            Semantic HTML: tags that mean something

            You could build any page out of nothing but <div>. Plenty of real sites do, and it is called div soup. The page looks identical — and is much worse.

            HTML has tags that say what a region is: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <footer>. They style exactly like a <div> and cost nothing extra to type. What you get back:

            • Screen-reader users can jump. These are called landmarks, and assistive software offers them as a menu — "skip to main content" works because <main> exists. With div soup there is nothing to skip to and the whole page has to be read linearly.
            • Search engines read them. Content inside <main> is weighted differently from a footer.
            • Your own code gets simpler. document.querySelector('main') beats hunting for .content-wrapper-inner.
            The rule of thumb: reach for a <div> only when no meaningful tag fits and you genuinely just need a box to hang layout on. That happens, and it is fine. It just should not be the default.
            Rewrite the div soup below using real landmarks. You need a <header>, a <nav> containing a <ul> of at least two links, a <main>, a <footer>, and exactly one <h1> on the page.

            Forms, and the label that must be wired up

            Section 7 taught you to listen for submit and call preventDefault. This is the other half — the markup that makes a form worth using.

            The piece that matters most, and the piece almost everyone gets wrong at first, is the label. A label has to be connected to its field, by matching for to the field's id:

            <label for="mood">How are you feeling?</label>
<input type="text" id="mood" name="mood">

            Do that and three things start working at once: clicking the label focuses the field, a screen reader announces the label when the field is focused, and the tap target on a phone gets much bigger. Skip it and the field is announced as just "edit text, blank" — completely unusable without sight.

            A placeholder is not a label. It is grey, it disappears the instant you start typing, it usually fails contrast requirements, and screen readers treat it inconsistently. Placeholder text is for an example of the format — placeholder="e.g. 07:30" — never for the name of the field.

            Input types worth knowing: text, email, number, date, checkbox, radio, password. They are not cosmetic — type="email" gets you free validation and an @ key on a phone keyboard; type="number" gets a numeric keypad. For longer text use <textarea>; for a fixed set of options use <select> with <option>s.

            And on buttons: inside a form, <button> defaults to type="submit". If you want a button in a form that does not submit it — a Cancel, say — you must write type="button" explicitly, or it will submit the form and you will spend an hour wondering why.

            Build a small form: at least two fields, each with its own id and a matching <label for> with real text, plus a submit button. Use a sensible type on at least one field. Render it and click a label — if the field focuses, you wired it correctly.

            Three files, and how they find each other

            A real project is not one file. The smallest sensible shape, and the one your mood tracker should have:

            my-tracker/
  index.html
  styles.css
  app.js

            The HTML file is the one the browser opens; it pulls the other two in. CSS goes in the head. JavaScript goes wherever it can safely find your elements — which is the Section 7 timing problem again, now from the HTML side:

            <head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</head>

            defer is what makes that safe: the file downloads straight away, in parallel, but does not run until the whole page has been parsed. The alternative is putting <script src="app.js"></script> just before </body>, which works just as well and needs no explaining. Either is fine. A plain script in the head with no defer is the one that breaks.

            The href and src values are relative paths — relative to the HTML file itself. styles.css means "next to me". css/styles.css means "in the css folder next to me". ../styles.css means "one folder up". Get one wrong and nothing errors visibly; the page just renders unstyled, which is the second most common "why is my site broken" of all time. The first is the one from Section 13: capital letters.

            Write the head of a page that pulls in styles.css and app.js, with the JavaScript loaded in a way that guarantees your elements already exist when it runs. Keep the doctype and the rest of the skeleton.
