            A rule, a selector, and the cascade

            CSS is a list of rules. Each rule points at some elements and sets some properties on them:

            h1 {                 /* the selector: which elements */
  color: #1e293b;    /* a declaration: property: value; */
  font-size: 28px;
}

            Three selectors do most of the work, and you already know all three from JavaScript:

            • h1 — every element of that type.
            • .card — every element with class="card". This is the one you should reach for by default, because many elements can share a class.
            • #total — the one element with id="total". Ids are unique, so this styles exactly one thing.

            They combine the same way querySelector combines them: nav a is "any link inside a nav", .card h2 is "an h2 inside a card", button.primary is "a button that also has the primary class".

            When two rules disagree

            This is the part that makes people think CSS is broken. Two rules both apply to the same element and set the same property. Only one can win, and the rules for who wins are fixed:

            1. Specificity first. An #id beats any number of .classes, and a class beats any number of plain tag names. It is not "how many characters" — it is which kind.
            2. Then source order. If specificity ties, the one written later in the file wins.
            .btn { color: blue; }
.btn { color: green; }

            Both rules have exactly the same specificity. Which colour does the button end up?

            Clue found

            Now the version that actually catches people. Change the first rule to #save { color: blue; } and green stops winning no matter how far down the file it sits — because an id outranks a class outright, and order only breaks ties. Nine times out of ten, "my CSS isn't applying" is not a typo. It is another rule quietly outranking yours. Open DevTools, click the element, and look at the Styles panel: the losing rule is shown with a line struck through it.

            Do not fix that with !important. It works, which is exactly the problem — it wins by force, and the only way to beat an !important later is another !important. A few months of that and no rule in the file can be reasoned about. Fix the specificity instead, or stop using ids for styling and use classes for everything.

            Which selector would you write to style every element with class="card"?

            Every element is a box, made of four layers

            Once you see this, most mysterious CSS spacing stops being mysterious. Every element on a page is a rectangle built out of four nested layers:

            The two that get confused constantly: padding is inside the border and pushes your own content inwards; margin is outside it and pushes other elements away. Want breathing room inside a card? Padding. Want a gap between two cards? Margin — or better, gap on their flex container.

            .box {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 2px solid black;
}

            How many pixels wide is that box on screen, in total?

            Clue found

            That default has a name: box-sizing: content-box. It is a decision from the 1990s that almost nobody wants any more, and it is harmless right up until a width is expressed as a percentage. width: 100% means "100% of the space available" — and then padding and border get added on top of that 100%. The box is now wider than the space it was given, and it sticks out.

            Style the .card so it has at least 16px of padding, a visible border, a margin underneath it, and uses box-sizing: border-box.

            Flexbox — the one layout tool you actually need

            CSS has several layout systems. You can build almost anything with one of them, so learn this one properly and add the rest later if you ever need them.

            Set display: flex on a container and its direct children become flex items, laid out in a row. Everything else is adjusting that:

            .row {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;  /* along the row: where the spare space goes */
  align-items: center;             /* across the row: how items line up */
  gap: 12px;                       /* space between items, without margins */
  flex-wrap: wrap;                 /* let items drop onto a new line if cramped */
}

            The two that get mixed up: justify-content works along the direction of the row (left–right by default), align-items works across it (top–bottom by default). Switch to flex-direction: column and they swap meanings, which is confusing exactly once.

            Useful values for justify-content: flex-start (default), center, space-between (first and last pinned to the edges), space-around. For align-items: stretch (default — equal-height cards for free), center, flex-start.

            .row { display: flex; }
/* three divs inside, no widths set on any of them */

            Before flex was applied, those three divs each filled the full width. Once the parent becomes a flex container, do they still fill the width, or do they shrink to fit their own content?

            Clue found

            To make a flex item take up the leftover space instead, give it flex: 1. Two items both set to flex: 1 share the space equally. But watch what that means: the item’s width is now decided by the container, not by the item — so any width or percentage you set on it is fighting a number it cannot see. That is the second place boxes end up wider than the room they were given.

            Make .row a flex container: items spread apart with space-between, centred vertically with align-items, and at least 8px of gap.

            When flexbox is the wrong shape

            The last page called flexbox the one layout tool you actually need, and for most of what you will build that is true. Here is the exception, stated by the people who wrote the spec: flexbox was designed for layout in one dimension — a row or a column. Grid was designed for two — rows and columns at the same time.

            That sounds like a distinction without a difference until the first time it bites you, so here is the moment it does.

            The bug you will hit and not be able to name

            You have six cards. You use flexbox with flex-wrap: wrap so they flow onto a second line on a narrow screen. Four fit on the first row, two land on the second — and those two are wider than the ones above them, or centred, or spaced differently. Nothing lines up. You did not do anything wrong.

            the thing that does not do what you expect

            Why: when flex items wrap, each new row is an independent flex line. The browser shares out the leftover space within that line only. The second row has no idea the first row exists, so it has no reason to line its items up with anything. Flexbox is doing exactly what it was designed to do — you asked a one-dimensional tool a two-dimensional question.

            Grid answers the question you were actually asking:

            style.css

            Three new things, and they are most of what you will ever need:

            • display: grid on the container. The children become grid items; you do not touch them at all.
            • 1fr — a fraction of the space left over. 1fr 1fr 1fr is three equal columns. 2fr 1fr is a wide column and a narrow one, two-thirds and one-third. It is easier than percentages because it already accounts for the gap.
            • repeat(3, 1fr) — shorthand for writing 1fr three times. repeat(12, 1fr) is a lot less typing.

            Every item now sits in a real column, and row two lines up with row one because they are the same columns.

            The one line worth memorising

            Fixing the column count at three means three columns on a phone as well, which is unreadable. You could write a media query. You do not have to:

            style.css

            Read it right to left: every column is at least 220px and at most one equal share (minmax(220px, 1fr)), and the browser fits in as many as will go (auto-fill). Three columns on a laptop, two on a tablet, one on a phone, and you wrote no breakpoints at all. It reflows at every width in between, including the awkward ones you would never have thought to test.

            This does not replace flexbox and you should not go back and rewrite anything. A row of buttons, a label beside an input, a header with a logo at one end and a menu at the other — all one-dimensional, all flexbox, all still correct. The rule of thumb is genuinely as blunt as it sounds: one direction, flexbox. Two directions, grid. And they nest happily — a grid of cards where each card is a flex column is an ordinary, sensible thing to write.

            You lay out six cards with display: flex and flex-wrap: wrap. Four fit on the first row and two wrap to a second, but the two on the bottom row do not line up under the ones above. Why not?

            Write the one grid-template-columns value that gives you as many columns as will fit, each at least 200px wide, with no media queries.

            CSS variables — write the value once

            By the third screen you will have typed the same brand colour into eleven rules, and changing it means finding all eleven. CSS has real variables — it calls them custom properties — and they work like const did in Section 2.

            :root {
  --brand: #3b5bdb;
  --ink: #1e293b;
  --radius: 10px;
}

.btn    { background: var(--brand); border-radius: var(--radius); }
.badge  { border: 2px solid var(--brand); }

            :root means the whole document, so anything declared there is available everywhere. The name must start with two dashes, and you read it back with var(--name). Change the value in one place and everything that referenced it follows — which is also, in about four lines, how a dark mode gets built.

            A typo in a variable name fails completely silently. var(--brnd) does not error and does not warn; the property is simply dropped as if you never wrote it, and your element renders with no background at all. If a colour has vanished for no visible reason, check the spelling of the variable before you check anything else. You can also supply a fallback: var(--brand, #333).

            Making it work on a phone

            Most of responsive design is not media queries. It is not fighting the browser in the first place:

            • Use max-width rather than width. max-width: 600px means "up to 600, but narrower if you must" — which is exactly what a phone must.
            • Let text wrap. Fixed heights on things containing text are how you get overlapping words on a smaller screen.
            • flex-wrap: wrap costs nothing and stops a row overflowing.
            • Have the viewport meta tag. Without the line from page one, none of this applies at all.

            When you genuinely need different rules at different sizes, that is a media query:

            @media (max-width: 600px) {
  .row { flex-direction: column; }
}

            Read it as "when the screen is 600px or narrower, also apply these rules". Everything outside the query still applies; the query only adds or overrides. Working small-screen-first — plain rules for narrow, a min-width query to add complexity for wide — usually produces simpler CSS, because the phone layout is nearly always the simpler one.

            Two things at once. Declare a custom property on :root and use it in at least two rules (one of them the card’s background), and add a media query that stacks .row into a column below 600px.

            Reacting to the pointer, and to the keyboard

            A pseudo-class styles an element only in a particular state. You attach it to a selector with a colon:

            .btn:hover  { background: #364fc7; }   /* pointer is over it */
.btn:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #f59e0b; outline-offset: 2px; }
.btn:active { transform: translateY(1px); }  /* being pressed */
.btn:disabled { opacity: .5; cursor: not-allowed; }

            Add transition: background .15s; to the base rule and the change animates instead of snapping. That single line is most of what makes an interface feel considered rather than cheap.

            :hover alone is only half the job, and it is the half that does not matter on a phone. Plenty of people never touch a mouse — they move through a page with the Tab key. The browser draws a focus ring so they can see where they are. Somewhere very early, almost everyone discovers outline: none makes that ring go away and thinks they have tidied something up. What they have actually done is make the page impossible to navigate without sight of a cursor. If you remove the default outline you must draw a visible replacement. :focus-visible is the modern version — it shows the ring for keyboard users and stays out of the way for mouse clicks.

            The accessibility floor

            Accessibility is a large field. Five things get you most of the way, and you have already met four of them in this section:

            1. Real labels on every field. Done, on the forms page.
            2. Meaningful alt on every image. Done.
            3. Landmarks and one h1. Done — that is what the semantic tags bought you.
            4. A visible focus state. Just covered.
            5. Enough colour contrast. Grey text on a white background is the single most common failure. The standard asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text — DevTools shows you the ratio when you click a colour swatch in the Styles panel, and tells you whether it passes.

            One more that costs nothing: use the right element. A <div onclick> is not a button. It cannot be reached by Tab, does not respond to the Enter or Space keys, and is announced as nothing in particular. A real <button> gets all of that for free. Most accessibility work is not extra work — it is not undoing work the browser already did for you.

            Give .btn a :hover state and a genuinely visible :focus (or :focus-visible) state. Render it, then click into the preview and press Tab — you should be able to see where you are.

            Quick recall check

            The question every tutorial skips

            Section 9 taught you to draw an image onto a canvas with playerImg.src = "player.png". This section taught you <img src="photo.jpg">. Neither said where those files come from, and no tutorial you find will either — they hand you a zip and move on.

            You are going to need real files: a character and a background for the game, an image or two for the app, an icon for the phone. Where you get them is not a detail, and getting it wrong is one of the few mistakes in this guide that can cost you money rather than time. An image you found on Google Images is somebody's work. Putting it in something you publish — and Section 13 publishes to a real public URL — is copyright infringement whether or not you knew.

            The good news is that the free, properly-licensed material is genuinely excellent, and one source in particular removes the problem entirely.

            Four licences, and what each one asks of you

            LicenceWhat you must doSafe to just use?
            CC0 / public domainNothing at all. Use it, change it, sell it.Yes
            CC-BYCredit it: title, creator, a link, the licence, and say if you changed it.Yes, if you actually write the credit
            CC-BY-SAAll of the above, and anything you build on it must carry the same licence.Care needed
            “Free for personal use”Ask the creator before anything public. This is not a licence, it is a restriction.No

            CC0 is the one to look for. It is a formal release into the public domain: no credit, no conditions, commercial use fine. It is not a favour someone might withdraw — it is a legal instrument, and it is what makes it possible to ship something without a lawyer.

            Where to actually look

            • Kenney (kenney.nl) — game art, UI, and sound, by one prolific creator. Everything is CC0. Their own words: “You’re free to use them, even in commercial projects… attribution is not required.” The one thing you may not use is their logo. Start here for the game. One consistent art style across thousands of pieces solves a problem you do not know you have yet, which is that assets from five different artists look like a ransom note.
            • OpenGameArt (opengameart.org) — far larger, and mixed licences. Every single item has its own, and they include CC-BY, CC-BY-SA, OGA-BY and GPL as well as CC0. You must read the licence on each asset, not on the site.
            • Freesound (freesound.org) — sound effects. Mixed licences again, filterable, and it is where a real jump or coin noise comes from.
            • Unsplash and Pexels — photographs for a website. Free and no credit required, though crediting is good manners.
            • Google Fonts (fonts.google.com) — free to use and to embed, including commercially.
            Write the credits file on the day you download the asset, not at the end. Make a CREDITS.md in your project the first time you save a non-CC0 file, and add a line: what it is, who made it, the link, the licence. Trying to reconstruct that three months later, from forty files with names like tile_04.png, is genuinely impossible, and the only honest options left are to remove them or to guess. Ten seconds now.
            You have a list of assets, each { name, licence }. Write needsCredit(assets) that returns an array of the names that have to appear in your credits file — that is, everything not released as 'CC0'. Keep the original order. This is filter and map from Section 6, doing a real job.

            Making an icon, with no design software at all

            Section 19 will require an app icon at exactly 192×192 and 512×512 pixels, and it is emphatic that missing one of them is the single most common reason an app refuses to install. You do not own Photoshop and you are not going to buy it for two squares.

            You do not need to. You already know how to draw on a canvas and you already know how to make a browser hand you a file. Put a canvas in an HTML file, draw on it, and export it:

            make-icon.html — a throwaway file, run it once

            Change SIZE to 192, run it again, and you have both files. Change the colour and the letter and you have your own. canvas.toDataURL('image/png') turns whatever is on the canvas into an actual PNG, and an <a> with a download attribute makes the browser save it.

            Those two measureText lines are not padding, and they are worth understanding. The obvious way to centre text on a canvas is ctx.textBaseline = 'middle', and it is wrong here. That centres the line box — the invisible band that leaves room for the descenders on letters like g and y. A capital M has no descender, so it gets pushed about 20 pixels above the true centre on a 512px icon. On body text nobody would notice. On an icon, where a centred letter in a square is the entire design, it looks subtly wrong and you will not be able to say why.

            measureText hands you the real ink: actualBoundingBoxAscent is how far the glyph rises above the baseline, actualBoundingBoxDescent how far it drops below. Half their difference is exactly how far to nudge it. This is a good habit for any text you draw on a canvas — a score, a “Game Over”, a label.
            Notice what just happened. The canvas API from Section 9 — which you learned in order to make a game — solved a problem in Section 19 that has nothing to do with games. That is what general-purpose tools are, and it is the reason this guide taught you the browser rather than a framework. Nobody had to build you an icon generator; you had one already.

            One more, and it is the one people break

            A designer tells you the blue ring Chrome draws around a focused button is ugly, so you add button:focus { outline: none; } and it goes away. Someone navigating your page with the Tab key instead of a mouse now sees exactly what?

            Clue found

            The focus ring is not decoration - it is the only position indicator a keyboard user has. outline: none on its own is one of the most common accessibility failures on the web. If the default ring does not suit the design, replace it: style :focus-visible, which shows a ring for keyboard focus and stays out of the way for mouse clicks.

            Your first unguided build

            Everything up to here has handed you a starting point. This does not. There is no starter code, no checker, and no worked example — a written brief, and you build it.

            That change is deliberate and it is the whole point of the rest of this guide. Being shown a solution and then completing a partial one is exactly right while a skill is new, and it stops being right the moment the skill is not new any more — at that stage the scaffolding is just something extra to read. Building unaided from a specification is the only rung that proves the skill transferred rather than being remembered. Everything from here on has one of these.

            The brief: a profile card page. One folder, two files, built in VS Code and opened in your browser. Small on purpose — the difficulty is that nobody is holding your hand, not that the thing is hard.
            1. A folder containing index.html and styles.css, with the stylesheet linked in.
            2. A complete page skeleton: doctype, lang, charset, viewport, a real title.
            3. Landmarks: a <header> with exactly one <h1>, a <nav> with a list of at least three links, a <main>, a <footer>.
            4. Inside main: a card with an image (any image, real alt), a short paragraph about you, and a button.
            5. Styled with a custom property for your accent colour, used in at least two places.
            6. The card uses box-sizing: border-box, real padding, and a border or shadow.
            7. The nav links sit in a flex row with a gap.
            8. The button has a hover state and a visible focus state.
            9. Below 600px the nav stacks into a column.

            7. Click your card in the Elements panel and look at the box-model diagram DevTools draws in the sidebar. Is the padding where you think it is?
            8. Read your HTML aloud, ignoring the CSS. Does the order still make sense? That is roughly what a screen reader gets.

            The rule that makes the terminal readable: no news is good news

            Before any of the commands below, one idea — and it is the single most useful thing anyone can tell you about a terminal. Most commands say nothing at all when they work. They were written by people who thought a program should only speak when it has something to tell you, and “I did what you asked” is not something worth telling you. So a command that makes a folder, moves a file or changes where you are prints nothing, hands you a fresh prompt, and that blank line is the success message.

            This trips up almost everyone once, and it trips them up in the worst possible way: you run something important, see nothing happen, assume it failed, and run it again — or give up on a step that actually worked. So do not ask “did something appear?”. Ask “did an error appear?” If there is no error and you have your prompt back, it worked.

            Version control with git & GitHub

            Right now your project folder is just files on disk — no history, no backup, nothing stopping a bad edit from being permanent. This section fixes that: a real, running record of every change you've ever made, and a free copy of it living outside your own machine.

            Same honest limit as Section 11: the concept checks below are graded exactly as rigorously as ever, but whether you actually create a GitHub account and push real code happens entirely outside this page — the capstone is a self-report checkbox, not a live check.

            git and GitHub are two different things

            git is the actual version-control tool — free, runs entirely on your own computer, tracks every change you make to a project over time so you can always go back. GitHub is a separate company's website that hosts a copy of a git project online, plus adds extras (issues, pull requests, a place other people can find your code). You install git once; you only need a GitHub account once you want a project backed up online or shared with someone else.

            Fill in the blank — yes or no: could you install git, create a project folder, and use git init/add/commit to build a real, working history of every change — without ever creating a GitHub account?

            Clue found

            Millions of real projects use git with no GitHub involved at all — GitHub is popular because it's free, well-built, and where most open-source code already lives, not because git needs it.

            The local workflow: init, add, commit

            Three commands, and each one does exactly one thing:

            git init

            Turns the current folder into a git project. One-time, right at the start.

            git status

            Shows what's changed since your last commit. Safe, read-only — run it constantly.

            git add <file>

            Marks a file's current state to be included in the next commit. Doesn't save anything yet.

            git commit -m "message"

            Actually creates a saved snapshot, using whatever's currently staged.

            You edit index.html (already tracked by git) and save it in VS Code, but haven't run git add yet. What would git status most likely report about that file?

            Put the three commands in order — turning a brand-new folder into a tracked project with its first real commit:

            How git works, explained in 4 minutes

            Four minutes, and it gives you the picture these commands only make sense inside. Most people think code lives in two places, your machine and GitHub. It lives in four: the working directory where you edit, the staging area, the local repository, and the remote one. Every command on this page is a move between two of those. Animated, and it is the clearest four minutes on git anywhere.

            Two of them talk and one is completely silent, and the silent one is the one people re-run three times because they think it did not work.

Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/you/mood-tracker/.git/

[main (root-commit) 3f9a2c1] Initial commit

root-commit means it is the first one.
If instead you get "Please tell me who you

email. It prints the two commands to fix it.

            The pattern is worth naming, because it holds for every git command you will meet: the ones that change what git is about to do tend to be silent, and the ones that change history print what they did. git add only moves things into position, so it says nothing. git commit makes something permanent, so it hands you a receipt.

            Branches, briefly

            Everything so far has happened on one line of history: main. That's fine solo, but it doesn't scale to "try something risky" or "two people editing at once" — which is exactly what branches solve.

            Working on main

            Every commit changes your one real, working version directly. A half-finished experiment sits there, broken, until you fix it.

            Working on a branch

            git checkout -b experiment makes a separate line of history. Commit freely there — main stays untouched until you deliberately merge the branch back into it.

            You want to try a risky rewrite without touching your main, working code — try it separately, merge it back only if it actually works. What's the git concept built exactly for this?

If branching and merging feel abstract, half an hour here will fix that faster than any amount of reading.

            Undoing a mistake: git log + revert

            git log shows your project's full history \u2014 every commit, with a unique hash, newest first. That hash is how you point at a specific past commit. To undo one safely \u2014 including after you've already pushed it, where quietly rewriting history can cause real problems for anyone else using the repo \u2014 git revert <hash> creates a brand-new commit that reverses those exact changes. History stays honest (both the mistake and the fix are visible), which is why revert, not reset, is the safe default once something's been pushed.

            .gitignore — the files that must never go in

            Not everything in your folder belongs in the repository. A file called .gitignore, sitting next to your .git folder, lists what git should pretend it cannot see. The leading dot means hidden — ls -a in the terminal to see it.

            # dependencies — thousands of files, reinstallable from package.json
node_modules/

# macOS clutter
.DS_Store

# build output — generated, not written
dist/

# anything with a secret in it
.env

            The two that matter most, for opposite reasons. node_modules/ is enormous — tens of thousands of files that anyone can recreate in seconds with one command, so committing it makes your repository huge and your diffs unreadable for no benefit at all. And .env is where API keys live: anything committed to a public repository should be treated as permanently public, even if you delete it in the very next commit, because git keeps the whole history and the internet keeps copies. Real keys get scraped from GitHub within minutes by bots that do nothing else.

            .gitignore only works on files git is not already tracking. Add a file to .gitignore after you have already committed it and git carries on tracking it, quite happily, forever. You have to remove it from tracking as well: git rm --cached .env, then commit. This trips up nearly everyone the first time, because the ignore file looks right and does nothing.

            README.md — the file GitHub shows first

            Put a README.md at the root of your repository and GitHub renders it on the front page, automatically. It is written in Markdown — # for a heading, - for a bullet, backticks for code — the same format as the notes you can export from this guide.

            Four things, and it can genuinely be this short:

            • What it is, in one sentence.
            • A live link, once Section 13 has given you one.
            • How to run it — for a static page, "open index.html" is a complete answer.
            • What you learned or found hard. Optional, and the part that is actually worth reading in a learning project.

            Write it for yourself in six months, not for a stranger. Six-months-from-now you will have forgotten why any of it works, and that is the person the README is really for.

            What file name does GitHub automatically display on a repository's front page?

            Merge conflicts — the scary-looking thing that is not scary

            Sooner or later git will stop mid-merge and tell you there is a conflict. It looks alarming and it is not: it means two changes touched the same lines and git is refusing to guess which one you meant. That is git being careful, not git breaking.

            It marks the spot directly in your file:

            <<<<<<< HEAD
<h1>My Mood Tracker</h1>
=======
<h1>Mood Log</h1>
>>>>>>> feature-rename

            Above the ======= is what you already had. Below it is what is coming in. Fixing it is exactly three steps, and none of them are magic:

            1. Open the file and decide what the lines should actually say. You may keep one side, the other, or write something new.
            2. Delete all three marker lines — the <<<<<<<, the ======= and the >>>>>>>. Leaving one in is the classic follow-up mistake, and it will be sitting in your live site announcing itself.
            3. git add the file and git commit. That commit is the resolution.

            Working alone you will mostly meet this after editing the same file both on your machine and directly on GitHub.com. That is a good reason to pick one place and stick to it — and if you are ever truly lost mid-merge, git merge --abort puts everything back exactly as it was.

            After choosing which version of the lines you want, what must you also remember to delete before committing?

            what a conflict looks like when it starts, and when you back out
            $ git merge feature-rename
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
Nothing is broken and nothing is lost. git
has stopped and is waiting for you to choose.

            A friend says: "I don't get why I need GitHub at all — can't I just email someone my HTML file?" What's the real difference between that and a deployed URL?

            An emailed HTML file only works if the person opens it locally, on their own machine, with file:// — the exact limitation Section 11 spent a whole section explaining.             The four lines

            index.html — inside <head>
            • <title> — the tab, the bookmark, the browser history, and the blue headline in a search result. It is the single highest-value line in your <head> and the one most likely to still say Document.

            • apple-touch-icon — what iOS uses when somebody adds your site to their home screen. MDN names 180×180. This is the same job as the icons Section 19 asks for, made the same way.

            Everything you have built so far, you built with this page next to you. This one is different, and deliberately so. Below is a specification — what the finished thing has to do — and no code at all. Not a single line. How you get there is yours to work out.

            Why there is no code here, stated plainly. Following a worked example teaches you to follow worked examples. The evidence on this is unusually clear: learners who study examples and are then handed the same problem without the example produce markedly better work than learners who keep the example, and the gap is largest on exactly the thing you care about — being able to do it again later, alone, on a problem nobody has written a tutorial for. That is the whole point of Part Two. So the code is gone.

            What has not gone is help. There is a hint ladder further down, folded shut. Open a rung the moment you are genuinely stuck — not after an hour of grinding. Struggling productively and struggling pointlessly look identical from the inside, and the research on novice programmers is blunt about which one people actually end up doing when no help is available: the artefacts they produce score roughly half as well. Getting unstuck fast is not cheating. Opening a hint you did not need is the only mistake available here, and it is a cheap one.

            The single most common way a first solo build goes wrong is building all of it and then debugging all of it at once. Do this instead:

            One criterion, one commit, one sentence in the commit message saying what it does. When something breaks three criteria later, git log tells you exactly which change did it — which is the entire reason Section 12 existed.

            Acceptance criteria — how you know you are done

            These are stated as things a stranger could observe, not as steps to follow. That is on purpose: a criterion you can check by looking cannot be fudged, and working out the steps yourself is the exercise.

            Where to look things up — this is not the part you are supposed to struggle with. There is a real distinction here and it is worth internalising. Working out what the app should do and how the pieces fit is the thinking, and struggling with it is how it sticks. Remembering the exact incantation for staging a file or pointing GitHub Pages at a branch is not thinking, it is recall, and struggling with it teaches you nothing at all — the evidence backs this split cleanly: unaided problem-solving helps conceptual understanding and transfer, and does precisely nothing for procedural steps. So look the procedure up, every time, without guilt: Section 11 for the terminal, Section 12 for git, this section for deploying, and the reference card for all of it on one page. Professionals look these up daily.

            The hint ladder

            Four rungs, each folded shut. Open the lowest one that matches where you actually are. Going straight to rung four costs you the exercise; sitting stuck for two hours costs you more.

            Start from what is already working. You are not building a new app; you are adding to one that runs. Open v1, get it running locally, and confirm it still works before you touch anything.

            Then pick the criterion that looks smallest, not the one that looks most interesting. The first one you finish is worth more than the best one you start, because finishing one proves the loop works end to end — edit, refresh, see the change, commit.

            If every criterion still looks equally large, that is a sign the criterion is too big rather than that you are stuck. Split it. “Filter by mood” is really: put some buttons on the page; make clicking one store which mood is selected; make the render function ignore entries that do not match. Three tiny things, each independently checkable.

            You already have the pattern and it has a name: render from state. Section 8 built the whole tracker on it. It says there is one source of truth held in variables, and one function whose only job is to redraw the page from that truth. Nothing else is allowed to poke at the DOM.

            Everything on the list below is the same move: add a new piece of state, then teach the render function to respect it. A filter is a variable holding the selected mood. A search is a variable holding the typed text. A sort order is a variable holding "newest" or "oldest". In every case the flow is identical — something changes the variable, then calls render, and render works out what the page should look like from scratch.

            The trap to avoid: reaching into the page and hiding individual list items when a filter changes. It works for about ten minutes and then two features start fighting over the same elements. Change the state, re-render everything. Redrawing a short list is free.

            Open the console first. Every single time, before forming any theory. A red error with a file and a line number is the machine telling you where the problem is, and ignoring it to go and re-read your own code is the most expensive habit available to you.

            If the console is clean but the behaviour is wrong, the fault is in your logic rather than your syntax, and the question to ask is: which of my assumptions is false? Put a console.log immediately before the line that misbehaves and print the actual values going into it. Nine times out of ten one of them is undefined, or a string where you expected a number, and the bug is one step earlier than you were looking.

            Three specific ones that will probably happen to you, in roughly this order of likelihood:

            • Nothing happens when you click — the element did not exist yet when you attached the listener, or you attached it to a different element than you think.
            • The list renders once and never updates — you changed the data but did not call the render function afterwards.
            • Everything works until you refresh — you changed the data in memory but never saved it, or you saved it under a different key than you read it back from.

            If it works locally and breaks on the live URL, go straight to the case-sensitivity trap earlier in this section. It is the most likely cause and it catches everybody exactly once.

            Note that none of the above is code. That is deliberate — it is the shape of the answer, and turning a shape into working lines is the part you are here to practise.

            Waiting for things

            Every line of JavaScript you have written so far has finished instantly. Real programs constantly have to wait — for data from a server, for a timer, for an image to load, for a file to be read. This section is about what happens during the wait, and it is the biggest single idea left in the language.

            JavaScript does one thing at a time

            There is exactly one thread running your code. One. It picks up a piece of work, runs it to completion, and only then looks for the next. Which means that while your code is running, nothing else can happen — no clicks are handled, no animation frames fire, nothing is repainted.

            This is why a slow loop freezes the whole page. Not slows it — freezes it. The spinner stops spinning, buttons stop responding, and the browser eventually offers to kill the tab. It is not that the page is busy elsewhere; it is that the single thread is inside your loop and cannot leave until it finishes.

            So how does anything ever happen "later"? You hand the job to the browser and go home. The browser is not single-threaded — it has timers, a network stack, a rendering engine. You say "run this function when the timer is up", the browser holds onto it, and when your code has completely finished, it hands the function back to be run. That handover queue is the whole mechanism.

            try-it.js

            A zero-millisecond delay still runs last. setTimeout does not mean "in 0ms"; it means "put this in the queue, and take it out no sooner than 0ms from now" — and the queue is only ever checked once the currently running code has completely finished.

            console.log("A");
setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0);
console.log("C");

            In what order do the three letters appear? Write them with no spaces.

            Clue found

            Because the queue is only checked between pieces of work, a delay is a minimum, never a promise. Ask for 100ms while the thread is busy for 400ms and your callback runs at 400. This also means the value a delayed callback reads is whatever that value is when it finally runs — not what it was when the timer was set. That gap is where a whole family of bugs lives.

            try-it.js

            setTimeout runs once; setInterval runs forever. Both hand back an id, and that id is the only way to cancel them — clearTimeout(id) and clearInterval(id). Throw the id away and you have created something you cannot stop.

Start one every time a view opens without ever clearing it and you end up with twelve of them running at once, all doing the same work, and the page gets progressively slower for no visible reason. If you start a timer, know exactly where it gets stopped.

            A promise is a receipt for a value you do not have yet

            Callbacks work, and they stack badly. Three things in sequence gives you three levels of nesting; five gives you a shape people genuinely call callback hell, where the error handling is duplicated at every level and the order of the code no longer matches the order of events.

            A Promise is an object representing a value that is not ready yet. It is in exactly one of three states: pending (still waiting), fulfilled (worked, here is the value), or rejected (failed, here is the error). Once it settles it can never change again.

            try-it.js

            You will mostly consume promises rather than build them — nearly every modern browser API already hands you one. But building one, as above, is what shows you the shape: something eventually calls resolve with a value, or reject with an error, and whoever is holding the promise finds out.

            A promise has just rejected. Which of its two handlers runs — .then() or .catch()?

            Promise

            It opens on an analogy — a singer, and fans waiting for a song — and then says the analogy is not accurate and explains where it breaks down, which is exactly what this guide does with its own metaphors. Three tasks with worked solutions.

            There is no video here, and I want to be exact about why. It is not that I read a pile of them and judged them all poor — the searches for promises and async/await came back with nothing usable at all, so there was nothing to judge. That is a gap in the hunt rather than a verdict on what exists, and it is worth another look later. The reading above is genuinely good, and the event-loop video earlier in this section covers the machinery underneath. If something better turns up, this is where it will go.

            async and await — the same thing, written to be read

            Chained .then() calls are a real improvement on nested callbacks and still do not read like the thing they describe. async/await is syntax over exactly the same promises that lets you write waiting code in a straight line.

            try-it.js

            Three rules cover it:

            • await only works inside a function marked async. Use it anywhere else and it is a syntax error.
            • await pauses that function until the promise settles, and hands you the value. It does not block the page — the single thread goes off and does other work in the meantime, which is the entire point.
            • An async function always returns a promise, no matter what you write in the return statement. return "all done" gives the caller a promise that fulfils with "all done".

            And the payoff for errors: an await that rejects throws, which means the ordinary try/catch from Section 8 works on it. One error mechanism for both kinds of code.

            async function load() {
  try {
    const data = await getSomething();
    return data;
  } catch (err) {
    console.log("failed:", err.message);
    return null;
  }
}
            async function f() {
  return 42;
}
console.log(f());

            What gets logged — 42, or something else?

            Clue found

            Which has a consequence worth bracing for: a missing await does not error. Assign the result of an async call to a variable without awaiting it and that variable holds a Promise object, not your data. Then data.length is undefined, data.forEach is not a function, and the error appears somewhere else entirely. If a value is mysteriously a Promise, look for the await you did not write.

            Write waitThen(ms, value): it returns a promise that fulfils with value after ms milliseconds. The tests await it, and they will tell you if you handed back a plain value instead of a promise.

            Async/await

            The same chapter series, one step on: how await is the promise chain rewritten to be read top to bottom, and where try / catch fits once it is.

            fetch — getting data from somewhere else

            A note on this page. A page opened straight from your hard drive is not allowed to call real web addresses — a browser security rule you will meet properly in Section 11's local-server material. So this section gives you a simulated fetch. It takes real time, returns real promises, and fails in the real ways. Everything you write here works unchanged against the real thing once your page is served properly.

            fetch is a two-step wait, and the second step surprises everyone:

            try-it.js

            The first await gets you the response's headers — the status, whether it worked. The body may still be arriving, so reading it is a second wait: response.json() returns another promise. Two awaits, always.

            fetch does not reject on a 404. This catches everyone. A response that came back saying "not found" is, as far as fetch is concerned, a complete success — it asked, it got an answer. It only rejects when the request could not be made at all: no network, DNS failure, blocked by the browser. So try/catch alone is not enough. You must check response.ok yourself, or a 404 page sails on into your code as if it were data.
            try-it.js

            Three outcomes, three different code paths, and a real app needs all three: it worked, the server answered but said no, and we never reached the server. Which maps directly onto what the user should see — the data, a "not found" message, or a "check your connection" message. Silence is not one of the options.

            A fetch comes back with a 404. Does the await throw?

            Write an async function fetchTitle(id) that fetches "/api/posts/" + id and returns the post's title. If the response is not ok, return null. If the request throws, also return null. The simulated API knows posts 1, 2 and 3; anything else 404s, and the id "offline" fails outright.
            your-code.js
            Readjavascript.info · free

            Fetch

            response.json(), and the check people skip: fetch does not reject on a 404. A response that arrived is a success as far as the promise is concerned, so you have to look at response.ok yourself. Its task — fetch several GitHub users and handle the ones that fail — is a good one.

            It is thinner than this section on wrapping a failed request in try / catch. Take the response.ok check from it, and the error handling from here.

            Three awaits in a row is usually a mistake

            Once await reads like ordinary code, it is very easy to write this:

            const a = await fetch("/api/posts/1");
const b = await fetch("/api/posts/2");
const c = await fetch("/api/posts/3");

            Each line waits for the one before it to finish. Three requests that could all have been in flight at once instead run one after another, and the page takes three times as long for no reason. The same thing happens inside a loop, once per item, which is how a list of twenty things takes twenty times longer than it needs to.

            If the requests do not depend on each other, start them all and wait for the set:

            try-it.js

            Promise.all takes an array of promises and gives you one promise that fulfils with an array of all their results, in the same order. It rejects the moment any of them rejects — which is usually what you want, and when it is not, Promise.allSettled waits for all of them and reports each outcome separately.

            Sequential is right when each step needs the one before it. Fetch a user, then fetch that user's orders — the second genuinely cannot start until the first has answered. The mistake is only sequential-by-accident, where the steps were independent and you never noticed. The tell is a series of awaits where no line uses the result of the line above it.

            Which built-in takes an array of promises and waits for all of them at once?

            What the person looking at the screen sees

            Waiting is invisible unless you show it. Every piece of data you load has three states the interface has to handle, and the third one is the one people skip:

            1. Loading — say so. A blank space is indistinguishable from a broken page, and the wait is the moment people decide your app is slow.
            2. Loaded — the data. Including the case where the data is legitimately empty, which needs its own words rather than nothing.
            3. Failed — say what happened and offer a way to try again. This is the one that gets left out, and it is the one your user actually meets on a train.
            async function show() {
  status.textContent = "Loading…";
  try {
    const posts = await getPosts();
    status.textContent = posts.length ? "" : "Nothing here yet.";
    render(posts);
  } catch (err) {
    status.textContent = "Could not load. Check your connection and try again.";
  }
}
            Also: disable the button. If a click starts a request, that button must go disabled until it finishes — otherwise an impatient triple-click sends three requests, and the one that answers last wins, which may not be the one you wanted. This is the single most common bug in a first app that talks to a server.

            The one that catches everyone, and it is not in the code above

            Your server is up. It answers. It answers 404 Not Found, because the id you asked for does not exist. Your code is try { const r = await fetch(url); } catch (e) { ... }. Does that catch block run?

            Clue found

            fetch rejects only when the network failed. Not when the server said no. The promise fulfils for every reply that arrives, so an error status reaches you as an ordinary Response with response.ok set to false and response.status holding the number. You have to check it yourself, every time, before you touch the body. Nothing else in JavaScript works this way, which is exactly why it catches people who have understood everything else on this page.

            And one about asking for several things at once

            You run Promise.all([a, b, c]). Requests a and b succeed in 50ms. Request c rejects at 400ms. When you catch that rejection, what has happened to the two results that already came back?

            Clue found

            Promise.all throws away the winners. It is all-or-nothing by design, and that is usually right: three things you need together are worth nothing individually. But when the parts are independent, it is the wrong tool, and losing four good results because a fifth failed is a bug you will write once and remember. Promise.allSettled never rejects. It gives you an array of {status, value} or {status, reason}, one per promise, and you decide what a partial success means.

            One more time, on the error path

            Everything above assumed the happy case. It is worth being precise about the unhappy one, because the shape of the code depends on it: if the server sends back a 404 or a 503 the fetch promise rejects, which is what makes the try/catch you already know the right tool for the job - one handler, and every kind of failure ends up in it.

            That sentence is false, and it is the most expensive false thing in this section. A 404 does not reject. Nothing above is going to tell you what does happen instead - you are going to trace it, one step at a time, and watch where the error handling you wrote fails to fire.

            Here is the code, exactly as most people first write it. Four questions, each about the state of things at one specific moment. Answer them in order.

            // the id 9999 does not exist
status.textContent = "Loading…";
try {
  const res = await fetch(URL);
  const data = await res.json();
  render(data);
  status.textContent = "";
} catch (err) {
  status.textContent =
    "Could not load. " +
    "Check your connection.";
}

            1. The server has answered 503. The line const res = await fetch(URL) has just finished. State of play?

            2. Same moment. Does your catch block run?

            3. The next line runs: const data = await res.json(). The server sent back an HTML error page. What happens?

            4. Put it together. You wrote status.textContent = "Loading…" at the top, a try/catch, and no res.ok check. The server 503s and its body happens to be valid JSON. What does the person looking at the screen see?

            All four. That is the bug traced end to end. The fix is one line, and it is the line the section has been building towards: if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Server said " + res.status); immediately after the first await. That converts a status you cannot see into a throw you already know how to handle, and your existing catch does the rest. Write it every single time - the day you leave it out is the day you spend an afternoon looking for a network problem that was never there.

            Level 2: build it yourself, from the description alone

            This one is different from everything before it, on purpose. There is no function name, no signature, no starter code and no shape suggested. You get a description of how the thing should behave and an empty box. Deciding what to write is the part being tested - it is the gap between finishing a guide and being able to build something without one.

            It is marked one skill at a time. Four separate groups of checks run against your code, and each awards its own badge. Get the data onto the page but muddle the filtering and you earn the page badge and not the collection one. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and anything you earn stays earned.

            Your code is run with three things already defined. Everything else is yours.

            • fetch - behaves exactly like the real one, including on the error path.
            • listEl - a real, empty <ul> element.
            • statusEl - an element whose textContent you can set.

            What it has to do:

            1. Show a message containing the word Loading before any data arrives.
            2. Ask fetch for "/api/posts". Each post looks like { title, published, date }, where date is an ISO string like "2026-07-04".
            3. On success, put only the published posts, newest first, into listEl - one <li> each, holding the post's title. Then clear the status.
            4. If there are no published posts, leave the list empty and say something containing Nothing.
            5. If the server answers but the response is not ok, leave the list empty and show a message containing the status number.
            6. If the request never reaches the server, leave the list empty and show a message containing the word connection.

            Your code may use await at the top level - it is run as an async function. It is also run twice against the same elements at one point, which is worth thinking about.

            Debugging & getting unstuck

            Every section so far had someone standing behind you. When an exercise failed, a message explained exactly what was wrong. Nothing outside this guide does that.

            This is the section that replaces me. Not more JavaScript — the ability to look at something broken, with no explanation attached, and work out why. It is the single skill that separates people who can code from people who can code when it works.

            An error message is not an insult. It is a report.

            Beginners skim errors and go back to staring at the code. That is exactly backwards — the error already contains most of the answer, in four parts:

            TypeError: Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading 'name')
↑ type     ↑ what went wrong

    at showUser (app.js:14:22)
               ↑ file, line, column

            The type narrows it to a category. The message usually names the exact value or property involved. The location tells you where to look. Read all three before you look at a single line of your own code.

            There are four you will meet over and over, and knowing what each one means saves you most of the work:

            SyntaxError

            Your code is not valid JavaScript, so nothing ran at all. Almost always a missing bracket, brace or quote — and usually a line or two above where it is reported, because that is where the parser first got confused.

            ReferenceError: x is not defined

            You used a name that does not exist. A typo, a missing declaration, or a variable from a scope that has ended. Section 5's scope chain is the thing to check.

            TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined

            The commonest of all. You reached through something that was not there. The message names the property, so look for what should have produced the value on its left.

            TypeError: x is not a function

            You called something that is not callable. A typo in a method name, a missing await, or a variable holding the wrong kind of thing entirely.

            The most valuable habit in this entire guide: copy the error message and paste it into a search engine. Not "my code doesn't work" — the literal text of the message, minus your own variable names. Every one of these errors has been hit by hundreds of thousands of people, and the first result is very often exactly your situation. Skipping this step is the difference between being stuck for two minutes and being stuck for two hours.

            You have const user = users.find(u => u.id === 7); followed by console.log(user.name);, and no user has id 7. Which error type do you get?

            Clue found

            Note where that error is reported: on the console.log line. But the bug is on the line above, where a lookup quietly failed and returned undefined instead of complaining. This gap is the single most important idea in debugging — the line that throws is usually not the line that is wrong. The throw is where the bad value finally got used; the bug is wherever it was created.

            Now produce one deliberately. Write a line or two that genuinely throws a ReferenceError. You are allowed to look back at the card above.
            your-code.js
            And one more: make it throw a TypeError. There are several ways; any real one counts.
            your-code.js

            The stack trace tells you how you got there

            Under the message is a list of function calls, innermost first. Read it top-down: the first line is where it broke, the next is what called that, and so on back to the original event.

            TypeError: Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading 'title')

  at renderEntry (app.js:41:18)
     ← it broke HERE
  at renderList (app.js:55:5)
     ← which called that
  at handleSubmit (app.js:70:3)
     ← which called that
  at HTMLFormElement.<anonymous>
     ← which was your form submit

            Two things make it far more useful than it looks. First, it tells you the path — so if renderEntry looks fine, you can go up a level and ask what renderList handed it. Second, ignore frames that are not your files. When a stack is twenty lines of library internals, scroll until you find the first one with your own file name on it. That is where your involvement starts, and it is nearly always the useful frame.

            In a stack trace, is the function where the error actually occurred listed at the top or the bottom?

            Elsewhere on this. Coding For Dummies has “Coding and Debugging Your First Web Application”, which walks the same loop from a different angle, and “Researching Your First Web Application”, which is the closest thing either of your outside resources has to the “turn a vague idea into a plan” problem. SoloLearn does not cover debugging at all.

            And a word about the rest of this guide. From here on — modules, Phaser, service workers, getting an app onto a phone — you will not find the material in a beginner book or a beginner app, and that is not a gap in your learning. It is what the second half of this guide is for. The real reading at this level is the official documentation for the thing you are using, which is why the last page of this section is about reading docs rather than about finding a better book.

            Pausing your program mid-run

            console.log is how everyone starts, and it has a ceiling: you only ever see what you thought to print, and finding the right spot means editing, saving and re-running over and over. A breakpoint stops the program at a line and hands you the whole world at that moment.

            Do this on your own project, now, rather than reading about it:

            1
            DevTools → Sources.Find your app.js in the file tree on the left.
            2
            Click a line number.It turns blue. That is a breakpoint — the program will freeze there.
            3
            Use the page until that line runs.Everything stops. The line is highlighted, and it has not executed yet.
            4
            Hover over any variable.Its real value, right now, appears. No logging, no guessing. The Scope panel on the right lists everything in reach.
            5
            Step through it.Step over runs the current line and stops on the next. Step into goes inside a function call. Resume carries on until the next breakpoint.

            There is also debugger; — a real JavaScript statement. Put it in your code and, if DevTools is open, the program stops there exactly as if you had clicked the line. Useful for a spot that only happens under conditions you cannot easily click your way to. Never commit one; it will freeze your live site for anyone with DevTools open.

            Two features worth knowing early. Right-click a breakpoint and choose conditional breakpoint to type an expression — it only stops when that is true, which is how you catch "it breaks on the 400th item" without pressing Resume four hundred times. And the Watch panel lets you pin an expression so its value updates as you step.

            You need to inspect several variables at one moment in the middle of a function. What is the tool for that, rather than adding six console.log lines?

A breakpoint pauses execution with every variable in scope already on screen, without you having to know where the problem is first.

            The console does more than log

            try-it.js

            console.table on an array of objects is transformative for exactly the data shape your app uses. console.count answers "is this running more often than I think", which is the cause of a surprising number of bugs. console.warn and console.error are colour-coded and filterable, so your own messages do not get lost among everyone else's.

            Log the object, not a string of it. console.log("user: " + user) gives you the famously useless [object Object]. console.log("user:", user) gives you something you can expand and click through. And one genuine trap: an object logged to the console is a live reference — expand it later and you may be looking at values it acquired after the log ran. If you need the state at that exact moment, log a copy: console.log({ ...user }).

            Everything above assumes a screen you can open DevTools on

            Every technique on the last three pages — reading the error, walking the stack trace, setting a breakpoint, poking at the console — assumes you are sitting in front of a browser with developer tools. Sections 18 and 19 take your work somewhere that has neither: your own phone.

            And that is precisely where the interesting bugs live. Section 19 will tell you that iOS behaves differently in several specific ways — an install prompt that does not exist, storage that is deleted on a schedule, a service worker with its own rules. Those are not the surprises. The surprises are the ones nobody wrote down. Without a console you are reduced to guessing, changing one line, redeploying, and looking at the screen again. That loop is unbearably slow and you will stop enjoying this.

            You do not have to. The desktop tools attach to the phone over a cable, and everything you already know starts working again.

            iPhone and Mac: Safari Web Inspector

            1. On the iPhone: Settings → Safari → scroll down to Advanced → turn on Web Inspector.
            2. On the Mac: Safari → Settings… (or ⌘,) → the Advanced pane → tick Show features for web developers. A Develop menu appears in the menu bar.
            3. Plug the phone into the Mac with a cable and unlock it.
            4. Open your site in Safari on the phone.
            5. On the Mac: Develop menu → your iPhone’s name → the page. A full Web Inspector window opens, attached to the page running on the phone.

            You now have the console, the elements tree, the network tab and breakpoints — for a page that is running six inches away on a different device. console.log from the phone appears on your Mac. You can select an element and watch it highlight on the phone screen.

            The part that matters most for Section 19. This also works on WKWebView — which is exactly what a Capacitor app is. So when you wrap your game or your tracker into a real installed app and something misbehaves inside it, that app is not a black box. Same Develop menu, same inspector, same console. Without this, debugging a Capacitor build is genuinely miserable; with it, it is an ordinary Tuesday.
            Android, for completeness. Enable Developer options on the phone, turn on USB debugging, plug it in, then open chrome://inspect#devices in Chrome on the computer and click inspect next to the tab. Same idea, same payoff. You will not need this for your own phone, but you will the first time someone reports a bug you cannot reproduce.
            Do this once now, before you need it. Turn on both toggles and attach the inspector to any page at all — this guide will do. Fifteen minutes on a calm afternoon, versus working it out for the first time while something is broken and you are already frustrated. Setting up your tools is not procrastination when the tool is the thing that ends the guessing.

            Narrowing it down, instead of staring at it

            When there is no error at all and the code just does the wrong thing, the instinct is to reread it hoping to spot the mistake. That mostly fails, because you will read what you meant rather than what you wrote. Do this instead:

            1. Say precisely what is wrong. Not "it's broken" — "when I click Save with an empty note, the entry is added twice." A vague symptom cannot be hunted.
            2. Find the smallest thing that still fails. Cut the input down. Comment out half the code — is it still wrong? Then it is in the half that is left. Halve again. Five rounds narrows a 300-line file to ten lines, and this beats reading every single time.
            3. Check your assumptions, one at a time. Every bug lives inside something you were certain about. Is that variable really what you think? Is that function really being called? Is it called once? Print it. Do not reason about it — look.
            4. Change one thing at a time. Change three and something works, you have no idea which, and you have probably introduced a fourth problem.
            5. Explain it out loud, to nothing. This sounds ridiculous and genuinely works — it is called rubber-duck debugging. Being forced to say each step in order exposes the step you had been skipping. You will frequently stop mid-sentence.
            And when nothing works: stop. Go away for twenty minutes. Every developer has the experience of finding the bug in four seconds the next morning after two hours the night before. Fatigue makes you read what you meant, over and over. This is a real technique and not a consolation prize.
            Debug something for real. The function below is supposed to say whether a piece of text reads the same backwards. It is wrong, and nobody is going to tell you how — run the tests and read the failures.
            your-code.js

            Two of the five fail. The pattern of which two is the entire clue — that is what reading test output is for.

            Looking things up without drowning

            Nobody remembers all of this. Professionals look things up constantly; the skill is not recall, it is knowing where to look and whether to trust what you find.

            • MDN is the reference. Search mdn plus the thing — mdn array filter. It is written by the people who write browsers, it is current, and every page has the parameters, the return value, examples, and a browser-support table. When an AI answer and MDN disagree, MDN is right.
            • Paste the error, not a description. Strip your own variable names out and search the literal message.
            • Check the date. A Stack Overflow answer from 2013 may describe a genuinely obsolete approach. Look for a more recent answer below the accepted one — it is often better, because the accepted one was accepted in 2013.
            • Never paste code you cannot explain. This is the important one. If you cannot say what each line does, you have not fixed the bug — you have moved it somewhere you will not recognise later. Ask for an explanation, or work through it until it makes sense, before you keep it.
            On asking an AI, since you are talking to one. It is genuinely fast and it is confidently wrong often enough to matter — especially on anything recent, and on library-specific details. Treat an answer as a hypothesis, not a fact: run it, check it against MDN, and make sure you can explain it. The failure mode is not getting a wrong answer. It is getting a plausible one you did not verify, and building on it.

            You have an error you do not understand. What is the single highest-value first move?

            Checking your own work

            Up to now, something has always told you whether you were right. From here, that is your job, and it is a skill you can practise rather than a feeling you either have or do not.

            Before you call anything finished, go through this. Every item is a thing that has bitten a real person:

            1. Is the console clean? Open it. Any red at all, deal with it now — errors do not get better on their own.
            2. The empty case. No entries, empty input, nothing saved yet, first ever visit. This is where most first apps fall over, because you always tested with data in it.
            3. The too-much case. A very long note, fifty entries, a huge number. Does the layout survive it?
            4. The wrong case. Submit the form empty. Put letters where a number goes. Click the button twice quickly. Press Enter instead of clicking.
            5. Refresh. Does the saved state come back correctly? Does it come back twice?
            6. Keyboard only. Put the mouse down and Tab through it. Can you reach and use everything, and always see where you are?
            7. Narrow window. Drag it to phone width. Anything overflowing or overlapping?
            8. Read it back tomorrow. If you cannot tell what a function does from its name and shape, rename it or split it — while you still remember.
            Write the checks down for your own project. A short list in your README that you actually run before you push is worth more than an intention to be careful. It also turns "I think it works" into "I checked these nine things", which is a different kind of claim.

            Which case does almost every first app break on — the one you never see while building, because you always had data in it?

            There is a general principle behind that list, and it is worth more than the list itself: you cannot test your own work while thinking like its author. As the author you know the intended path and you walk it every time. Testing means deliberately doing the unintended thing — the wrong order, the empty box, the double click, the impatient refresh. Every item above is just a different way of not being yourself for a minute.

            Reading one for real

            Traces get longer than the examples above, and the useful habit is knowing where to start. The first line under the message is the frame the error was thrown in, so that is the file and line to open first - everything below it is just the path the program took to get there, and you can safely ignore it while you work.

            Half of that is true, and the half that is false is the expensive half. The first line is indeed where it was thrown. Opening it first is the habit that keeps people stuck for an hour, and the frames below it are the opposite of ignorable - one of them is where the mistake actually is.

            No explanation of this one. It is a real trace from a shopping cart, and you are going to work out where to look using nothing but the names in front of you.

            TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toFixed')
    at formatPrice   (cart.js:31:24)
    at renderLine    (cart.js:58:16)
    at renderCart    (cart.js:72:7)
    at applyDiscount (cart.js:19:5)

            1. Five frames. Which one do you open first? Not which one broke - which one are you most likely to find the mistake in.

            That is the method, and it is worth more than the answer. Read the trace bottom-up as a story - a click, then a discount, then a render, then a format - and ask which step had a reason to change the value that eventually broke. The throw tells you where the damage surfaced. The frame that had a motive tells you where it was done. Then bisect between them rather than rereading either.

            Nobody is giving you the broken program. You get what a real developer gets - a description of what the thing should do, and a user complaining about what it does instead. You write it correctly from scratch, and the complaints are the cases you are being marked on.
