            The third place to get unstuck

            You have two channels so far and both are good ones. The documentation is authoritative and always current. An AI is fast, available at two in the morning, and confidently wrong often enough that you check it.

            There is a third, and for one specific kind of problem it beats both: a person who has hit this before. Docs tell you what something does. An AI tells you what usually works. A human tells you “ah, that’s the thing where Vite caches the old build — delete dist”, which is the answer you would never have found by reading, because nobody wrote it down.

            Learning alone at a few hours a week, this is the channel most likely to decide whether you finish. The failure mode is not asking a bad question. It is being stuck for a fortnight on something a stranger would have answered in ten minutes, and quietly losing interest. That is how most self-taught projects actually die — not a decision to stop, just a slow drift after one problem outlasted the enthusiasm.

            Why most questions get ignored

            “My code doesn’t work, can anyone help?” gets nothing, and not because people are unkind. It is because answering it means asking you five questions first, and nobody has the time. The thing you are competing for is a stranger’s attention, and the way you win it is by making your problem cheap to understand.

            There is a name for what to send, and three properties it needs:

            • Minimal. As little code as possible that still shows the problem. Not your whole file — the ten lines that break.
            • Complete. Everything needed to reproduce it is in the question itself. If your snippet calls renderList() and you did not include it, nobody can run anything.
            • Reproducible. Someone else, following your steps, sees the same thing you see.

            Then four things around it, and the third is the one people leave out:

            the shape of a question that gets answered
            The part nobody believes until it happens to them. Cutting your code down to the smallest version that still breaks solves the problem a genuinely large proportion of the time. Every line you delete is a line you have to justify keeping, and somewhere around the fourth deletion you go “hang on, why is that there”. This is the bisection method from earlier in this section, wearing a different hat.

            So write the question properly even on the days you never send it. It is not admin before the real work. It is the debugging.

            Where to actually ask

            • Stack Overflow — best for a specific, answerable, technical question. Search first; there is a real chance your question is eight years old and already answered. Check the date on any answer you find.
            • A project’s own community — Phaser, Vite and most tools have a Discord or forum. Far better than Stack Overflow for “is this normal?” and “am I holding this wrong?”, and much more forgiving of a beginner.
            • Reddit — r/learnjavascript and r/learnprogramming tolerate a vaguer question than Stack Overflow will, and are kinder about it.
            • GitHub issues — only when you genuinely think the tool is broken, never for “how do I…”. Search the closed issues first.
            Two courtesies that cost nothing. Say what you already tried — it stops three people suggesting it again. And when something works, go back and say so, and say which part fixed it. The next person with your problem finds your thread, and the answer they need is the one you did not bother to add.

            Cutting your code down to the smallest version that still breaks does something useful even before you post it. What?

            You post: “My localStorage code throws an error, here is my whole 300-line app.js, please help.” Name two things wrong with that as a question.

            Modules, npm & libraries

            Your app is one app.js. That is fine at 200 lines and unbearable at 800. This section is how real projects are organised — and it is a hard requirement for Section 18, because Phaser and its build tool are built entirely on it.

            Why one file stops working

            Load two plain <script> files on a page and they share one enormous global namespace. Every top-level const in both is visible to both. Which means:

            • Declare const state in each and the second one throws — or worse, with var, silently overwrites the first.
            • Nothing tells you what depends on what. Reorder your script tags and something breaks for no visible reason.
            • Nothing is private. Any function in any file can reach in and change anything.

            Modules fix all three. Each file gets its own scope, and nothing leaves it unless you say so explicitly.

            export and import

            // storage.js — one job, stated at the top of the file
export function saveEntries(entries) { /* ... */ }
export function loadEntries() { /* ... */ }

const KEY = "moodEntries";     // no export: private to this file, permanently
            // app.js
import { saveEntries, loadEntries } from "./storage.js";

const entries = loadEntries();

            Those are named exports — most files should use them. There is also a default export, one per file, for when a file is fundamentally about a single thing:

            // MoodEntry.js
export default class MoodEntry { /* ... */ }

// app.js
import MoodEntry from "./MoodEntry.js";     // no braces, and you pick the name

            Braces mean named, no braces means default. That is the whole distinction, and getting it wrong is the most common import error there is — undefined is not a constructor almost always means you forgot or added a pair of braces.

            In the browser, the path needs the .js and needs to start with ./. import x from "storage" works in Node and fails in a browser. Write "./storage.js" — relative, and with the extension. Build tools like Vite are more forgiving, which is its own trap: code that works in your project breaks the moment it runs without one.

            Modules

            Three chapters: what a module is, export and import in full, and loading one on demand rather than up front.

            Four things change the moment a file is a module

            To use modules in a plain page, the script tag needs type="module":

            <script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

            And that one attribute changes four things at once:

            1. It is deferred automatically. Module scripts always wait for the HTML to be parsed, so the Section 10 timing problem simply stops existing. No defer needed.
            2. It has its own scope. A top-level const is no longer global. Nothing else can see it, including your console — which surprises people the first time they try to poke at a variable from DevTools.
            3. Strict mode is on, permanently. A handful of sloppy old behaviours become errors, including accidentally creating a global by assigning to an undeclared name.
            4. It will not run from a file. Open it by double-clicking and you get a CORS error and a blank page.
            That last one catches everybody exactly once. Modules are fetched, and a browser refuses to fetch across the file:// origin for security reasons. So a module page opened by double-clicking is not slow or partly broken — it does not load at all, and the console says something about CORS that looks unrelated. The fix is the local server from Section 11, which is exactly why that section existed. From here on, always serve your project.

            Your module page works when served by a local server and shows a CORS error when you double-click the HTML file. Is something broken?

            Which is the first hint of something larger. Once a project has modules, it wants a server. Once it has a server, it wants that server to rebuild automatically when you save. Once it does that, it may as well also bundle everything for production and strip out what is unused. That whole stack has a name — a build tool — and it is the thing standing between you and Phaser.

            Node, and the package manager that comes with it

            Node is JavaScript running outside a browser — the same language, no document or window, but with access to your filesystem instead. You do not have to write any Node to need it installed, because every JavaScript tool in existence runs on it.

            Install it from nodejs.org and take the version labelled LTS, not "Current". LTS means long-term support: boring, stable, what everything else expects. (At the time of writing that is Node 24, but take whatever the site labels LTS rather than trusting this sentence's age.) Check it worked:

            node --version

            npm arrives with Node and is two things at once: a registry of over two million public packages, and the command-line tool that installs them.

            package.json — the file that describes your project

            cd my-project
npm init -y          # creates package.json with sensible defaults
npm install phaser   # adds a real dependency

            That leaves you with three new things, and it is worth knowing which of them matters:

            package.json

            Small, human, committed to git. It lists what your project depends on and the commands it can run. This is the file that matters.

            package-lock.json

            Records the exact version of every package, including packages your packages depend on. Also committed — it is what makes an install reproducible on another machine.

            node_modules/

            The actual downloaded code. Enormous, thousands of files, never committed — that is what the .gitignore line from Section 12 was for. Deleting it and running npm install rebuilds it exactly.

            Inside package.json, dependencies come in two lists. dependencies is code your app needs in order to run — Phaser goes here. devDependencies (installed with npm install --save-dev) is code only you need while working: build tools, test runners, formatters. Your users never download those.

            Versions look like "phaser": "^4.2.1", and the three numbers are a promise called semantic versioning:

            • 4 — major. Changed when something breaks on purpose. Upgrading may require work.
            • 2 — minor. New features, nothing broken.
            • 1 — patch. Bug fixes only.

            The ^ means "this or any later minor or patch, but never a new major" — so you get fixes automatically and never a surprise rewrite. That is also exactly why the lock file exists: ^4.2.1 is a range, and the lock file pins which point in that range you actually got.

            Every package you add is code you are responsible for

            Installing is one command, which makes it feel free. It is not. Anything you install runs with the same access as your own code, gets shipped to your users, and becomes yours to maintain when it breaks or is abandoned.

            Before adding one, ask:

            • Could I write this in twenty lines? If yes, write it. A package for something trivial is a dependency, a supply chain and a maintenance burden in exchange for saving you a few minutes once.
            • Is it maintained? On its npm page: when was it last published? Open issues piling up with no replies? A package untouched for four years is a decision, not a neutral fact.
            • How much does it drag in? Look at its own dependency list. A package with sixty transitive dependencies is sixty things you now depend on.
            • Is the name right? Typo-squatting is a real attack — packages named one character away from popular ones, containing something nasty. Copy the install command from the official docs rather than typing it from memory.
            The honest counterweight: do not write your own game engine, date library or crypto. Anything genuinely hard, widely used, and heavily tested is exactly what libraries are for — Phaser is a decade of work you get for one command. The judgement is not "libraries good" or "libraries bad", it is whether this particular one saves you more than it costs.

            The command nobody teaches you, and every CI server uses

            You clone a project, run npm install, and it works. A colleague clones the same commit a fortnight later, runs the same command, and gets a version of one library that you have never run. Both of you have the same package-lock.json. What did npm install do that it should not have been allowed to?

            Clue found

            npm install may rewrite the lock file. npm ci obeys it. Use install when you are deliberately adding or changing a dependency, and ci every other time - on a fresh clone, on another machine, and on any build server. ci deletes node_modules first, installs precisely what the lock file pins, and errors out if package.json and the lock have drifted apart, which is exactly the failure you want to hear about rather than have silently resolved for you.

            One number where the rules quietly change

            You depend on "^1.2.3" and you know what that allows: any 1.x from 1.2.3 up, never 2.0.0. Now you depend on "^0.2.3" instead. Does that allow 0.3.0?

            Clue found

            Under 1.0.0, the minor number is the breaking one. ^1.2.3 allows anything below 2.0.0; ^0.2.3 allows anything below 0.3.0. A pre-1.0 library is telling you it reserves the right to change its mind, and the caret respects that by tightening automatically. This matters more than it sounds: a great many small packages never leave 0.x, so the version of the rule you will actually meet most often is the one nobody explains.

            Below are two implementations of does this version satisfy the range ^0.2.3. They are both real, both plausible, and they agree on almost every input you would think to try. One of them is correct.

            implementation-a.js
            var satisfies = function(v){
  var p = v.split('.').map(Number);
  var r = [0,2,3];
  if(p[0] !== r[0])
    return false;
  if(r[0] === 0 && p[1] !== r[1])
    return false;
  if(p[1] < r[1])
    return false;
  if(p[1] === r[1] && p[2] < r[2])
    return false;
  return true;
};
            implementation-b.js
            var satisfies = function(v){
  var p = v.split('.').map(Number);
  var r = [0,2,3];
  if(p[0] !== r[0])
    return false;
  if(p[1] < r[1])
    return false;
  if(p[1] === r[1] && p[2] < r[2])
    return false;
  return true;
};

            Level 2: a toolkit, and a test that is worth having

            Two things to write, and the second one is the real exercise. Anyone can write three small functions. Writing a test that would actually catch someone breaking them is the skill this section is about, and it is the one nobody practises - because up to now every test in this guide was written for you.

            So your test is itself tested. It gets run against your code, which it must pass, and then against four deliberately broken versions, which it must fail. A test that waves broken code through is not a test.

            No starter code. By the time your code finishes, two things must exist:

            1. toolkit - an object with three methods:

            • slugify(s) - lower case, runs of anything that is not a letter or digit become a single -, no leading or trailing -. "Hello, World!" becomes "hello-world"; "A--B" becomes "a-b"; "" becomes "".
            • chunk(arr, n) - splits into arrays of n, last one short if it has to be. [1,2,3,4,5] by 2 gives [[1,2],[3,4],[5]]. An empty array, or n below 1, gives [].
            • pluck(arr, key) - the value of key from each object, skipping objects that do not have it. [{a:1},{b:2},{a:3}] plucked by "a" gives [1,3].

            2. check(t) - a function taking a toolkit-shaped object and returning true if it passes every test you think matters, false if it does not. It must test the object it is handed, not toolkit directly - that is what lets it be pointed at a broken one.

            The four broken versions each get one thing wrong, and the wrong things are ordinary: not lower-casing, losing the short final chunk, keeping missing keys as undefined, leaving a double dash in. If your check misses one, you will be told which.

            A class is a template for making objects

            Section 6 gave you objects with methods, and this meaning "whoever I was called on". A class is a factory that stamps out objects of that shape, so you do not have to write the same one out fifty times.

            try-it.js

            Three words carry all of it. class declares the template. constructor is the function that runs when a new one is made, and its job is to set up this. new is what actually makes one — it creates an empty object, points this at it, runs the constructor, and hands it back.

            Forgetting new is the classic first mistake. const p = Player("Sam", 100); throws — in a class, that is an outright error rather than a silent oddity, which is one of the genuine advantages of the syntax.             extends — starting from somebody else's class

            This is the piece Phaser is built on, and the reason this section exists at all.

            extends says "start from that class and add to it". Boss gets every method Player has, for free. Two rules go with it:

            • super(...) must be called first in a subclass constructor, before you touch this. It runs the parent's constructor, and until it has, this does not exist yet. Using this above it is an error.
            • A method with the same name replaces the parent's — that is called overriding. super.describe() lets you call the original from inside your replacement, which is how you add to behaviour rather than discarding it.
            Now read this, which is the whole of the next section: 
            class GameScene extends Phaser.Scene {
  constructor() {
    super("game");          // hand the scene's name up to Phaser
  }
  preload() { /* Phaser calls this for you */ }
  create()  { /* and this, once, when the scene starts */ }
  update()  { /* and this, every single frame */ }
}

            You are extending a class Phaser wrote, calling its constructor with super, and overriding three methods that Phaser calls at the right moments. Every this.add and this.physics inside them is a property the parent class gave you. None of that is Phaser-specific — it is this page.

That inversion is the entire idea behind the word "framework": a library is something you call, a framework is something that calls you.

            Classes

            Seven chapters, and the two that matter here are “Class inheritance” and “Private and protected properties and methods” — the # fields this section uses, with the reasoning for why they exist.

            When a class is the wrong tool

            Classes are not a more advanced way of writing everything. They earn their place when you need many things of the same shape, each with their own data and behaviour — players, enemies, scenes, connections. That is genuinely common in games, which is why game frameworks are built this way.

            They are the wrong tool when:

            • There is only ever one of it. A single config object is a plain object. new Config() called once is ceremony.
            • It has no data of its own. A class whose methods never touch this is a set of loose functions wearing a costume. Export the functions.
            • It is just data. Your mood entries are right as plain objects. Adding a MoodEntry class would buy nothing and make them harder to save as JSON.
            The mood tracker is deliberately class-free, and that was correct. Plain objects, plain functions, plain arrays. Everything you know about this going wrong applies inside classes too, and every class is one more place it can. Use one when you have many of a thing; otherwise a function is simpler, and simpler wins.

            You have a class whose methods never once refer to this. What should it be instead?

            There is a general version of that test, and it is worth carrying: reach for the simplest structure that holds the data you actually have. A value wants a variable. Several related values want an object. Many of the same shape want an array. Many of the same shape that each carry behaviour want a class. Moving up that ladder before you need to is the most common way a beginner project becomes hard to read — and every rung you skip is a rung you never have to debug.

            Write a class called Counter. new Counter(5) starts at 5; new Counter() starts at 0. It needs an increment() method that adds one and returns the new value, a reset() that sets it back to the starting number and returns it, and a value() method returning the current count.

            One more reason people reach for a class

            There is a practical argument for classes that is worth stating plainly, because you will hear it often: a class keeps data and the code that works on it in one place, so the methods and their data travel together. Which means that once something is a class, you can hand its methods around freely - pass counter.tick to setInterval, or straight into an event listener, and it behaves exactly as if you had called counter.tick() yourself.

            The last sentence is false, and it is the most common way a working program starts failing after a refactor. Rather than being told what goes wrong, you are going to do it deliberately - which is much harder to forget than reading about it.

            Below is a counter that works. It works when you call it normally, and it keeps working when you pull a method off it and call that on its own:

            const c = makeCounter(0);
const f = c.tick;
f();   // 1  - still fine
f();   // 2  - still fine

            Break it. Rewrite makeCounter so that it still behaves perfectly in ordinary use - c.tick() gives 1, 2, 3 and c.value() gives 3, and two counters keep separate totals - but const f = c.tick; f() no longer works.

            The rules, and they are the point. Returning nothing, counting wrong, or throwing on the first line are not answers - those are bugs anyone would catch immediately. You are introducing the kind that passes review, passes your own testing, and fails months later when somebody writes setInterval(c.tick, 1000).

            Level 2: a small world that moves and remembers

            A behaviour spec and an empty box. No class names, no method bodies, no starter code - whether to use classes here at all is one of the things you are deciding.

            Marked one skill at a time, four groups, four separate badges. And each of them needs a second, unrelated build later before it counts - one build is a good day, not a competence.

            When your code finishes, a value called world must exist, with five methods:

            • world.spawn(x, y, vx, vy) - adds a mover and returns a unique id.
            • world.step(dt) - advances every mover by its velocity times dt, where dt is in seconds. Any mover that ends up outside 0 to 100 on either axis is removed.
            • world.positions() - an array of { id, x, y }, x and y rounded to 2 decimal places as numbers.
            • world.save() - a string you could put in localStorage.
            • world.load(str) - restores from that string. Loading rubbish should throw, not fail silently.

            Two things are checked that are easy to miss. A world restored from save() must carry on identically when stepped again - so whatever step needs has to survive the round trip, not just what positions() shows. And two separate worlds must not share anything.

            Leveling up with Phaser

            Section 9 had you build a game by hand: a loop, a clock, keys held down, rectangles redrawn sixty times a second, collision worked out with arithmetic. It worked, and building it that way was the point — you now know what a game is.

            This section hands almost all of that to somebody else. Not because your version was wrong, but because you cannot see what a framework saves you until you have done the job without one.

            A library is something you call. A framework is something that calls you.

            That sentence turned up as a hidden clue at the end of Section 17, and it is the single most useful idea in this section, so here it is properly.

            Every tool you have used so far has been a library. You are in charge, and you call into it when you want something: JSON.parse(...), document.querySelector(...), fetch(...). Your code drives.

            Phaser is a framework. You hand it a class, and it decides when to call the methods on it. Phaser drives, and your code is what it calls. That reversal has a name — inversion of control — and it is why the setup looks so strange the first time.

            You do not have to take that on trust. Here is a framework — a real one, in about fifteen lines. Run it.

            mini-framework.js

            Notice what you did not write: nothing calls preload, create or update. You wrote the methods; MiniEngine decided when they run and what to pass them. Swap MiniEngine for Phaser and MyScene for a class that extends Phaser.Scene, and that is the entire architecture of this section.

            Look at the last argument. update(time, delta) — Phaser hands you delta, the milliseconds since the previous frame. That is the exact number Section 9 made you calculate by hand, and for the exact reason Section 9 gave: without it, your game runs at different speeds on different machines. You did the work; now you get it for free, and you know what it is for.

            What you built by hand, and what Phaser gives back

            Section 9, by handPhaser
            a requestAnimationFrame loop you started yourselfupdate(time, delta) — called for you, with the delta handed in
            an object tracking which keys are held downthis.cursors = this.input.keyboard.createCursorKeys()
            clearing the canvas and redrawing everything each framethe renderer does it
            overlap maths to work out whether two boxes touchthis.physics.add.collider(a, b)
            clamping x and y so things stay on screensetCollideWorldBounds(true)
            loading an image and waiting for onloadpreload() — the loader waits, then starts the scene
            This is a trade, not a free upgrade. You are giving up control of the loop, and in exchange you stop writing the same four hundred lines every game needs. The cost is real: when something goes wrong inside a framework, the stack trace is full of somebody else’s code, and you cannot debug it by reading your own file top to bottom. That is precisely why Section 15 came before this one.

            In one word: with a library, who decides when your code runs?

            Phaser calls your update method and passes it two numbers. The second is the milliseconds since the last frame. What is that number called?

            Clue found

            Here is the general shape, and you will meet it constantly from now on. Every framework you ever use works by defining the shape of a thing and calling you at fixed moments. React calls a function it names a component. Express calls a function it names a handler. Phaser calls methods it names preload, create and update. Learning a framework is mostly learning two things: what shape does it want, and when does it call me. Answer those two and the API reference stops being frightening and becomes a lookup table.

            Scaffolding the project with Vite

            Section 16 ended with a package.json containing three scripts — dev, build and preview — and a note that they all ran something called vite. This is that.

            Vite is a build tool. It does three jobs, and all three are ones you have already felt the need for:

            • It runs a local dev server, so your modules load instead of dying on the file:// CORS error Section 16 warned you about.
            • It reloads the page the instant you save, so you stop alt-tabbing to hit refresh.
            • It bundles for production — one command turns your many source files into a small folder you can deploy with what Section 13 taught you.

            Four commands. Run them in a terminal, in whatever folder you keep projects in:

            terminal
            npm create vite@latest my-game -- --template vanilla
cd my-game
npm install
npm install phaser

            Then npm run dev, and open the address it prints. You should get Vite’s starter page.

            The -- in the middle is not a typo. It separates the arguments meant for npm from the arguments meant for the tool npm is about to run. Leave it out and npm swallows --template vanilla itself, then asks you the questions interactively anyway. Harmless, but confusing the first time.

            Here is what you now have, and what each part is for:

            my-game/
            my-game/
├── index.html          the real entry point — Vite starts here, not at a JS file
├── package.json        your dependencies and your dev/build/preview scripts
├── package-lock.json   the exact versions, committed, from Section 16
├── node_modules/       the downloaded code — never committed
├── public/             files copied as-is, kept at the same name  ← assets go here
└── src/
    └── main.js         your code starts here
            The surprising one is index.html. With Vite, the HTML file is the entry point, not an afterthought — it is the thing Vite reads first, and it finds your JavaScript through the <script type="module" src="/src/main.js"></script> tag inside it. That type="module" is the same attribute from Section 16, doing the same four things.

            Which file does Vite treat as the entry point of your project?

            There is an official Phaser scaffolder, and you are deliberately not using it yet. npm create @phaserjs/game@latest will generate a Phaser project with Vite already wired up. It is genuinely good, and it is what you would sensibly reach for next time. It is skipped here because it generates exactly the wiring Section 16 just taught you to do by hand, and a generated file you cannot read is a file you cannot fix. Do it the long way once. Then use the shortcut forever.
            WatchFireship · 2:28

            Vite in 100 seconds

            Two and a half minutes on what you just ran. Vite does two jobs: serves your code while you work, and bundles it for production. The reason it starts instantly where older tools crawl is that in development it leans on the browser’s own module support — the import and export from Section 16 — instead of gluing every file together first.

            The config object, and one scene

            Delete everything in src/main.js and write this:

            src/main.js
            import Phaser from "phaser";
import GameScene from "./scenes/GameScene.js";

const config = {
  type: Phaser.AUTO,      // WebGL if the browser can, Canvas if it cannot
  width: 800,
  height: 600,
  backgroundColor: "#1e293b",
  scene: [GameScene]      // an array — a real game has several
};

new Phaser.Game(config);

            And in src/scenes/GameScene.js:

            src/scenes/GameScene.js
            import Phaser from "phaser";

export default class GameScene extends Phaser.Scene {
  constructor() {
    super("game");                       // the scene’s key — its name
  }

  create() {
    this.add.text(400, 300, "It works", {
      fontSize: "32px",
      color: "#ffffff"
    }).setOrigin(0.5);
  }
}

            Save. The page reloads itself and there is your text. Four things in there are worth naming:

            • import Phaser from "phaser" — a default import, no braces, exactly as Section 16 described. And no .js, no ./, because this one is a package in node_modules rather than a file of yours.
            • Phaser.AUTO — try WebGL, fall back to Canvas. Almost always what you want.
            • scene: [GameScene] — you hand Phaser the class itself, not an instance of it. Phaser constructs it when it is ready. Writing new GameScene() here is a common and confusing mistake.
            • super("game") — the key. It is how you refer to this scene from anywhere else: this.scene.start("gameover"). Section 17 told you super runs the parent constructor first; this is what the parent does with what you pass it.
            setOrigin(0.5) is doing real work. By default Phaser positions things by their top-left corner, so this.add.text(400, 300, ...) puts the text’s corner at the centre of the screen, not the text. setOrigin(0.5) means “treat the middle of this object as its position”. Leave it off and everything looks very slightly wrong in a way that is maddening to diagnose.

            In scene: [GameScene], are you giving Phaser the class, or an object made from the class?

            Four methods, called in a fixed order

            A scene is a class with up to four methods Phaser knows to look for. You write the ones you need and leave the rest out.

            • init(data) — runs first, before anything is loaded. Used for passing values in when one scene starts another. You can ignore it for a long time.
            • preload() — you queue files here. Nothing is loaded yet when the method finishes; Phaser then downloads everything you asked for and only moves on when it is all in. This is the async waiting of Section 14, handled for you.
            • create() — runs once, after loading finishes. This is where the world gets built. It is the only method a scene genuinely needs.
            • update(time, delta) — runs every frame, forever. Movement, input, win conditions.
            The number one beginner error in Phaser lives right here. Trying to use an image in create() that you never queued in preload() gives you a green box with a white cross in it, not an error message. That box is Phaser telling you “this texture key does not exist”. When you see it, the bug is nearly always a typo in the key string, or a file you forgot to load — not the thing you were actually working on.

            Which lifecycle method runs over and over, rather than once?

            Phaser scenes are just classes that call super with a key. Prove you can write that shape without Phaser in the room. Write a class BaseScene whose constructor takes a key and stores it as this.key, with a describe() method returning "scene: " followed by the key. Then write MenuScene which extends BaseScene, takes no constructor arguments, calls super("menu"), and overrides describe() to return the parent’s answer with " (menu)" added on the end.
            your-code.js

            Loading images

            src/scenes/GameScene.js
            preload() {
  this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png");
  this.load.image("ground", "assets/platform.png");
  this.load.spritesheet("dude", "assets/dude.png", {
    frameWidth: 32,
    frameHeight: 48
  });
}

create() {
  this.add.image(400, 300, "sky");     // "sky" — the key, not the filename
}

            The first argument is a key you invent. Everything afterwards refers to the image by that key, never by its filename. A spritesheet is one image file holding many frames in a grid; you tell Phaser the size of one cell and it does the slicing.

            Why those files must live in public/

            This is the one thing in this section that will genuinely bite you, and it fails in the worst possible way: it works perfectly while you are developing, and breaks only once you deploy.

            Vite works by following import statements. It starts at index.html, follows every import, and builds a map of everything your project uses. Anything on that map gets bundled, renamed with a content hash, and copied into the output folder.

            Now look again at that line: this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png"). There is no import. It is a string, read at runtime, long after Vite has finished. Vite never sees it, so sky.png is not on the map, so it is never copied. In dev the file happens to be sitting there and everything looks fine. Run npm run build, deploy, and every image 404s.

            The public/ folder is Vite’s escape hatch for exactly this. Files in it are not bundled, not renamed, and not analysed — they are copied into the output folder untouched, keeping their names. Which is precisely what a runtime string needs.

            where the files go
            my-game/
└── public/
    └── assets/
        ├── sky.png        →  this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png")
        ├── platform.png
        └── dude.png
            Vite’s own documentation tells you to do the opposite, and for Phaser it is wrong. The docs say “prefer importing assets unless you specifically need the guarantees provided by the public directory” — and that is good advice for a normal web app, where every image is referenced from HTML or CSS that Vite can read. Phaser is the specific case that needs the guarantees, because Phaser loads by string at runtime. Whenever a tool’s advice and your situation disagree, work out which assumption the advice was making. Here it is “your imports describe your files”, and for a game they do not.

            Your game shows every image perfectly with npm run dev, but after npm run build and deploying, they all 404. Which folder did the files need to be in?

            Clue found

            The generalisation is worth more than the rule. Any tool that works by reading your code can only manage what your code says out loud. A bundler follows imports; if you assemble a filename at runtime, it is invisible. The same blindness explains why a bundler cannot shrink code you reach by window["someName"], why a type checker gives up at the edge of a JSON file, and why search-and-replace across a project misses the one place a name was built by joining two strings. When a tool “mysteriously misses” something, ask first whether you told it in a form it can read.

            In this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png"), which of the two strings do you use afterwards when adding the image to the screen?

            Arcade physics

            Phaser ships several physics engines. Arcade is the simple, fast one: everything is a rectangle, there is no rotation or slopes, and it is what almost every 2D platformer or top-down game actually wants. Turn it on in the config:

            src/main.js
            const config = {
  type: Phaser.AUTO,
  width: 800,
  height: 600,
  physics: {
    default: "arcade",
    arcade: {
      gravity: { y: 300 },
      debug: false          // set true to see every hitbox drawn
    }
  },
  scene: [GameScene]
};
            debug: true is the single most useful line in this section. It draws every physics body as a coloured outline, so “why does he land in mid-air” stops being a mystery — you can see that the hitbox is taller than the sprite. Turn it on whenever anything collides wrongly, and turn it off before you deploy.

            Then, in create():

            src/scenes/GameScene.js
            create() {
  this.add.image(400, 300, "sky");

  this.platforms = this.physics.add.staticGroup();
  this.platforms.create(400, 568, "ground").setScale(2).refreshBody();
  this.platforms.create(600, 400, "ground");

  this.player = this.physics.add.sprite(100, 450, "dude");
  this.player.setBounce(0.2);
  this.player.setCollideWorldBounds(true);

  this.physics.add.collider(this.player, this.platforms);

  this.cursors = this.input.keyboard.createCursorKeys();
}
            • this.add vs this.physics.add — the first makes something that is only drawn; the second makes something that is drawn and has a body that gravity and collisions act on. Using the wrong one gives you a sprite that hangs motionless in the air, which is a surprisingly common half-hour.
            • static group — bodies that never move. Platforms, walls, floors. Cheaper, and they do not get shoved when something hits them.
            • .setScale(2).refreshBody() — scaling changes how a thing looks; refreshBody() is what tells the physics engine the invisible box changed too. Skip it and the graphics and the collisions disagree.
            • collider — one line replaces every overlap calculation from Section 9, and it works for a whole group at once.
            Everything is on this, and that is not decoration. Section 9 kept the player in a module-level variable because there was only ever one of everything. A scene is a class you may have several of, and Phaser may create and destroy them. Store state on this and each scene owns its own; store it in a module variable and every scene shares one, which is a bug that only appears once you add a second scene and is then very hard to see.

            Here is that bug, in plain JavaScript, so you can watch it happen:

            shared-state.js

            Scene A never touched its score, and it changed anyway. this.score inside a class would have given each scene its own.

            You want a floor that gravity does not drag downwards. Which kind of physics group do you make it in?

            Input and animation, in update

            src/scenes/GameScene.js
            update(time, delta) {
  if (this.cursors.left.isDown) {
    this.player.setVelocityX(-160);
    this.player.anims.play("left", true);
  } else if (this.cursors.right.isDown) {
    this.player.setVelocityX(160);
    this.player.anims.play("right", true);
  } else {
    this.player.setVelocityX(0);
    this.player.anims.play("turn");
  }

  if (this.cursors.up.isDown && this.player.body.touching.down) {
    this.player.setVelocityY(-330);
  }
}

            Two things there are worth stopping on.

            • setVelocityX, not x = x + 5. You set a speed and the engine moves it, taking delta into account for you. Section 9 made you multiply by delta by hand; here that is the engine’s job, which is exactly why the numbers look large — 160 is pixels per second, not per frame.
            • body.touching.down is what stops infinite jumping. It is only true on a frame where the player is standing on something. Take that check out and you can jump in mid-air forever — which, incidentally, is how you would implement a double jump on purpose.

            Animations are defined once in create(), then played by name:

            src/scenes/GameScene.js
            this.anims.create({
  key: "left",
  frames: this.anims.generateFrameNumbers("dude", { start: 0, end: 3 }),
  frameRate: 10,
  repeat: -1            // -1 means loop forever
});

            The true in anims.play("left", true) means “ignore this if that animation is already running”. Without it you restart the animation on frame zero sixty times a second, and the character appears frozen mid-stride while clearly moving.

            Why does the jump check this.player.body.touching.down before applying upward velocity?

            A scene keeps its own state on this, and its update receives (time, delta). Write a class ScoreScene that behaves that way, without Phaser. new ScoreScene() starts with a score of 0 and an elapsed total of 0. create() sets the score to 0 and returns it. addPoints(n) adds n to the score and returns the new score. update(time, delta) adds delta to the elapsed total and returns the new elapsed total.
            your-code.js

            The Scale Manager

            Your config says 800 by 600. A phone is not 800 by 600, and the next section is about phones, so deal with it here.

            src/main.js
            const config = {
  type: Phaser.AUTO,
  width: 800,
  height: 600,
  scale: {
    mode: Phaser.Scale.FIT,
    autoCenter: Phaser.Scale.CENTER_BOTH
  },
  scene: [GameScene]
};

            Those two lines are the difference between a game that is the wrong size on a phone and one that fits it properly. They do not make it playable — a game with no touch controls fits the screen beautifully and still responds to nothing. That is the next page. The four scale modes:

            • FIT — scales up or down to fit inside the available space, keeping the shape. You get letterbox bars. Almost always the right choice.
            • ENVELOP — covers the whole space, keeping the shape, cropping whatever overflows. No bars, but you lose edges.
            • RESIZE — the canvas becomes whatever size the space is, shape and all. Powerful, but now your code owns the layout, because the game area is a different shape on every device.
            • NONE — no scaling. The default, and the reason an untouched game is a postage stamp on a laptop and off the edge on a phone.
            The thinking behind FIT. Your game keeps pretending it is 800 by 600 forever. Every coordinate you write stays true; Phaser just draws that rectangle bigger or smaller. You never have to think about screen sizes again, at the price of some empty space at the edges. RESIZE removes the bars but hands you the whole responsive problem — and you have exactly enough experience to know that is not a small gift.

            Which scale mode keeps your game’s shape and fits it inside whatever space is available?

            Fitting the screen is half of it

            The Scale Manager sorted out size. Your game now fills a phone properly and every coordinate you wrote still means what it meant. And it is still driven entirely by this.cursors — the arrow keys — which a phone does not have.

            This is the single most common way a browser game arrives on a phone broken, and it is invisible from your laptop, because your laptop has a keyboard.

            What Phaser gives you back, again

            Section 9 had you convert window coordinates into canvas coordinates by hand, worry about the canvas being displayed at a different size from its drawing surface, and remember pointercancel. Phaser does all of that for you, and it is one of the clearest examples in this section of what a framework is actually for:

            src/main.js — inside create()

            pointer.worldX is the number you spent a page calculating in Section 9. Phaser has already taken the raw event, subtracted the canvas position, divided by the scale factor the Scale Manager is applying, and handed you the coordinate in the 800×600 space your code thinks in. Change the phone, change the orientation, change the scale mode — worldX stays correct.

            And because Phaser’s pointer is the same abstraction the browser’s is, a click and a tap arrive through the same handler. You test it with a mouse. It ships working on a finger.

            Two control schemes, and which to pick

            • Follow the finger. Whatever the player touches, the thing moves toward. Best for a paddle, a ship, anything that slides. Almost no code, and it is what the block above does.
            • On-screen buttons. Two sprites at the bottom of the screen with setInteractive(), each setting a flag your update reads. Necessary when the game needs discrete actions — jump, fire, left, right — rather than a position.

            The trap in the second one is that a button which sets velocity on pointerdown and never clears it on pointerup gives you a character that runs off the screen forever. Every action needs both halves, and pointerupoutside as well — the player’s thumb slides off the button far more often than it lifts cleanly.

            Do not ship keyboard-only and plan to add touch later. Which control scheme you choose changes how the game is designed — a jump button and a follow-the-finger paddle are different games. Decide before you build the level, not after. If your game only works with a keyboard, the whole of Section 19 gets you a beautifully packaged app nobody can play.
            Keep the keyboard too. Nothing about adding pointer input removes this.cursors. Read both, every frame, and the same build works on a laptop and a phone — which is the actual goal, not swapping one for the other.

            In Section 9 you wrote a function to convert a pointer’s window x into canvas coordinates. Which Phaser property replaces it, and why does it stay correct when the Scale Manager resizes everything?

            Your game uses Scale.FIT and CENTER_BOTH, and fills your iPhone screen perfectly. You have written no pointer handlers. What happens when you play it?

            Most Phaser code online looks nothing like yours

            You are about to search for help and find something that does not match this section at all. It will look like this:

            what you will find online
            var config = {
  type: Phaser.AUTO,
  width: 800, height: 600,
  scene: { preload: preload, create: create, update: update }
};
var game = new Phaser.Game(config);

var player;
var platforms;

function preload() { this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png"); }
function create()  { platforms = this.physics.add.staticGroup(); }
function update()  { player.setVelocityX(-160); }

            This is not out of date and it is not wrong — it is the other supported way of writing a scene, and Phaser’s own beginner tutorial uses it. It is fine for one small scene. It falls apart at two, because everything lives in shared variables.

            Translating it is mechanical. Four moves, and one very important thing that does not change:

            Function formClass form
            var player; at the top of the filethis.player, set in create()
            function create() { ... }create() { ... } as a method
            scene: { preload, create, update }scene: [GameScene]
            no constructor, no keyconstructor() { super("game"); }
            this.load, this.add, this.physicsidentical — no change at all
            That last row is the one that matters. In both styles, this is the Scene. Phaser calls those plain functions with this bound to the scene object, which is why this.load.image(...) works inside a bare function create(). So every line inside the three methods copies across untouched. The only thing you ever have to change is the wrapper and the shared variables — and the fix for those is to put this. in front of them.

            And most of it will be Phaser 3

            Phaser 4 arrived in 2026. The overwhelming majority of tutorials, forum answers and Stack Overflow posts are Phaser 3, and even parts of Phaser’s own documentation site still show Phaser 3 examples.

            Mostly this does not matter to you. Phaser’s own migration guidance says that if you use standard objects — sprites, images, text, groups, arcade physics, input, scenes, audio, tweens — your code is likely unchanged. Everything in this section is in that set. The rewrite in Phaser 4 was of the renderer underneath, which you are not touching.

            The changes that could catch you are all one level up from where you are working:

            • Phaser.Geom.Point was removed — use Vector2.
            • setTintFill(0xff0000) became setTint(0xff0000).setTintMode(Phaser.TintModes.FILL).
            • BitmapMask was replaced by a mask filter.
            • Phaser.Math.TAU changed meaning — it was half of pi, and is now two pi. This is the nasty one, because nothing errors; the maths just quietly comes out wrong.
            The rule for old tutorials, and it generalises well beyond Phaser. Try it. If it works, it works — code does not go stale on a schedule. If it breaks, check the version the tutorial was written for before you assume you made a mistake. Most beginner time lost to old material is spent debugging your own typing when the actual problem was a version gap that the error message never mentioned.

            You copy the body of a function create() from an old tutorial into your create() method. What is the one kind of line you will nearly always have to change?

            A Phaser 3 tutorial uses Phaser.Math.TAU. Why is that more dangerous than the other version differences listed above?

            From npm run dev to a link you can send

            Everything you need for this is already in your hands. Section 12 put the project on GitHub; Section 13 deployed a site. The only new step is the build.

            terminal
            npm run build      # produces dist/ — the whole site, minified
npm run preview    # serves dist/ locally, so you test what you deploy

            npm run preview is not an optional nicety. It is the only place the public/ mistake shows up before your users find it. Build, preview, click around, then deploy. Every time.

            Two things that will go wrong on your first deploy, and both have boring fixes. First, dist/ should be in .gitignore alongside node_modules/ — it is generated, so committing it means merge conflicts in minified code. Second, if you deploy to a GitHub Pages project site the URL has a subfolder in it (yourname.github.io/my-game/), and Vite assumes it is at the root. Everything 404s. The fix is one line in vite.config.js: base: "/my-game/". If your deploy shows a blank page and the console is full of 404s for files that definitely exist, that is what it is.

            Which command lets you test the built version locally before deploying it?

            ReadVite docs · free

            Deploying a static site

            Vite’s own page on this, and it settles the base question outright: base of / for a site at username.github.io, and base of /repo-name/ for a project repository. Getting that wrong is the blank page with 404s in the console you were just warned about.

            The queue nobody mentions until it bites

            In preload() you write this.load.image("sky", "assets/sky.png") and on the next line you try to use that texture. It fails, and the error says the key does not exist. The file is there and the path is right. What has this.load.image actually done at the moment that next line runs?

            Clue found

            preload queues. create consumes. The lifecycle is not four methods that happen to run in an order - it is a contract about what has finished by the time each one starts. Nothing is loaded during preload; the whole point of create existing as a separate method is that Phaser can wait in between. The general version outlives Phaser: whenever a framework gives you two hooks rather than one, the gap between them is where the waiting goes, and putting work in the wrong one fails in a way that looks like the file is missing.

            The second argument, and why it is not optional

            You write update() { this.player.x += 4; } and your game feels right on your laptop. Your friend plays it on a 120Hz screen. Without changing a line, what happens to your game on their machine?

            Clue found

            Per frame is not per second, and only one of them is a speed. Anything you add inside update without multiplying by delta is tied to the refresh rate of whatever screen it happens to be running on. It is the single hardest class of bug to notice, because it is invisible on the machine you built it on and obvious on everybody else\u2019s. setVelocityX avoids it for you - Arcade physics is already working in units per second - which is why physics-driven movement is safer than nudging x by hand.

            One habit to take from Vite's own documentation

            Vite is opinionated about assets, and its advice is good: keep files near the code that uses them, inside src/, so the bundler can hash and optimise them. That advice holds for a Phaser project too, so put your sprites in src/assets/ and load them from there.

            That is the folder that catches everyone, and the advice is wrong here specifically. No explanation this time - a real project, a real symptom, and you work out which of four plausible causes is the one actually happening.

            The game runs perfectly with npm run dev. After npm run build and npm run preview, the sky never appears and the console shows a 404 for the image. Nothing else changed.

            my-game/
  index.html
  package.json
  src/
    main.js
    assets/
      sky.png
      dude.png
  public/
    favicon.ico
            preload() {
  this.load.image(
    "sky",
    "src/assets/sky.png"
  );
}

            1. Three of these would produce a 404 in production. Only one of them explains why it worked perfectly in npm run dev and stopped working in npm run build. Which?

            2. The fix. Vite's own documentation tells you to import your assets so they get hashed and optimised. What do you actually do here?

            Both, and this generalises well past Phaser. Any tool that works by reading your code can only act on what your code says out loud. An import is a statement the bundler can read; a string assembled or passed at runtime is opaque to it. Whenever a tool has to know about a file, either import it so the tool can see it, or put it somewhere the tool copies without looking. The dangerous middle is a file the tool cannot see but the dev server happens to serve anyway - which is why npm run preview exists, and why it is the only place this shows up before your players find it.

            Level 2: one frame of a game, from the description alone

            Phaser cannot run in this page, and that turns out not to matter. Everything Phaser does for you in update - gravity, input, collecting things, deciding when the game is over - is ordinary JavaScript underneath, and that is what is being tested. If you can write one frame by hand you can read anybody's update method.

            Five groups, five separate badges, and each still needs a second build elsewhere before it counts.

            When your code finishes there must be a function called step(state, input, dt) that returns the next state. dt is in seconds.

            state = {
  player: { x, y, vy },
  coins: [ { x, y, taken } ],
  score,
  over
}
input = { left, right, jump }

            The rules:

            • Gravity pulls vy down every frame. Down is negative y, and the ground is y = 0 - nothing goes below it, and landing stops the fall.
            • left and right move the player horizontally. Both at once cancel out.
            • jump only works when the player is on the ground.
            • A coin within 10 units on both axes is collected: mark it taken and add 10 to the score. Coins are never removed from the array, and a taken coin cannot be taken again.
            • If over is true, the step changes nothing at all.
            • Everything scales with dt, so the game runs at the same speed on any screen.
            And the one that is really being tested. step must not modify anything it was given - not the state, not the coins inside it, not the input. It returns a new state and leaves the old one exactly as it was. Copying the outer object but not the array inside it is the version of this bug that hides longest.

            Bridging to mobile

            You have a mood tracker and a game, both deployed, both working in a browser. “Get it on my phone” sounds like one job. It is three, they cost wildly different amounts, and the cheapest one is free and takes an afternoon.

            Almost every tutorial you will find teaches the expensive one and never mentions the other two. That is how people end up believing a mobile app is out of reach.

            Three rungs, and you can stop at any of them

            The thing nobody says out loud. You do not need to pay anyone to have your own app on your own phone. The $99 and the $25 buy distribution — the right to hand it to strangers. Until you have something worth handing to strangers, you are not missing anything by not paying.

            What do the Apple and Google fees actually buy you — the ability to build an app, or the ability to give it to other people?

            Progressive web apps in 100 seconds

            The argument for the first rung, quickly: one codebase that runs on iOS, Android and the web; no app-store review and no thirty percent cut; installable straight from the browser. Fireship moves fast on purpose — this is the why, and the two further down this section are the how.

            The manifest — a file that says “I am an app”

            A progressive web app, or PWA, is your ordinary website plus two files. Add them and phones start treating it as an app: it installs to the home screen, opens without browser chrome, and keeps working with no signal.

            The first file is manifest.json, sitting next to your index.html:

            public/manifest.json
            {
  "name": "Mood Tracker",
  "short_name": "Mood",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#f8fafc",
  "theme_color": "#6366f1",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icons/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icons/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
  ]
}

            And one line in your HTML pointing at it:

            index.html
            <link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">

            Browsers will not offer to install your app unless the manifest passes a specific checklist. It is short, and worth knowing rather than guessing at:

            • name or short_name — either will do.
            • icons must include a 192×192 and a 512×512. Both. This is the one people miss.
            • start_url — what opens when the icon is tapped.
            • display (or display_override) — "standalone" is what removes the browser bars.
            • prefer_related_applications must be absent or false — setting it true means “install my store app instead”.

            And one requirement that is not in the file at all: the site must be served over HTTPS.

            You already have that. GitHub Pages serves every site over HTTPS, so the deploy you did in Section 13 already satisfies the hardest-sounding requirement on the list. You have been PWA-ready since then without knowing it.

            Your manifest has a 192×192 icon and everything else correct, but no install option appears. What is missing?

            Write isInstallable(manifest), returning true or false against the checklist above. It needs a name or a short_name; a start_url; a display or display_override; prefer_related_applications must not be true; and manifest.icons (an array of objects with a sizes property) must contain both "192x192" and "512x512".
            your-code.js
            ReadMDN · free

            Making PWAs installable

            The requirements list, stated plainly: a manifest linked from your HTML, a name, icons at 192 and 512 pixels, a start URL, a display mode — and the site served over https, or localhost while you are building. It is also honest about iOS, which is a page of this section on its own.

            The second file, and the first code you have written that outlives its page

            The manifest makes your app installable. A service worker is what makes it work with no signal, and it is the genuinely new idea in this section.

            Everything you have written so far has been code that runs while a page is open and dies when it closes. A service worker is different. It is a script the browser keeps aside, and it sits between your page and the network. Every single request your page makes goes through it first, and the worker decides what to answer with.

            Install, activate, fetch

            A service worker has three moments, and they happen in a fixed order. Rather than describe them, here they are running — the same trick as the mini game engine in Section 18, a fake small enough to read in full:

            mini-service-worker.js
            • install — runs once. This is where you copy the files your app needs into the cache, so they are on the phone before anybody loses signal.
            • activate — runs once, right after. This is where you delete caches from your previous version, which is how you avoid shipping an update that nobody ever sees.
            • fetch — runs for every request the page makes, forever. Cache first, network second, and the app opens with no signal at all.
            The trap is the opposite of what you expect. A service worker is so good at serving from the cache that it will happily serve your old app forever. You deploy a fix, refresh, and nothing changes — because the worker answered from the cupboard instead of going to the shop. That is what activate is for, and why real service workers name their cache "v1", "v2" and delete the old one on activate. If a change of yours will not appear, this is the first thing to suspect.

            Which of the three moments runs again and again, rather than once?

            Everything you have written until now stopped running the moment its page closed. What is different about a service worker?

            Clue found

            Notice what that unlocks, and it is more than offline. Once code can run without a page, it can be woken by things that have nothing to do with you looking at the app — a push notification arriving, a network connection returning, a background sync finishing. Every “how does an app do that when I am not even in it” question has the same answer: something is running that is not the page. You have just met the web’s version of it.

            Write the decision a real fetch handler makes. respond(url, cache, online): if cache has that url as a key, return its value. Otherwise, if online is true, return the string "network:" joined to the url. Otherwise return "offline".
            your-code.js
            Look at the last test case. Offline, and it still returns the page. That single line is the whole point of a service worker: your app opens on the Underground.

            On iPhone, nobody will prompt you

            On Android, Chrome shows an install banner by itself. On iOS it does not, and no code you write can make it. The event every tutorial uses to build a custom “Install app” button — beforeinstallprompt — does not exist on iPhone. Ship that button and it silently does nothing on the device you actually own.

            The real route on iOS is done by hand, and you should tell your users it exists because they will not guess:

            1. Open the site in Safari.
            2. Tap the Share button — the square with the arrow.
            3. Scroll down. Tap Add to Home Screen.
            4. Name it, tap Add. The icon appears with your other apps.

            From iOS 16.4 onwards that works from the Share menu in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Orion too. On 16.3 and earlier it is Safari only.

            This step is not cosmetic, and Section 7 explained why. Safari deletes all script-writable storage — localStorage, IndexedDB, and your service worker’s cache along with it — after seven days with no tap or keystroke on the site. A site added to the home screen is exempt from that rule entirely.

            So this is the step that makes your mood tracker’s entries durable and keeps your offline app actually working offline. Everything later in this section is about giving your app to other people. This one is about your own app not quietly emptying itself while you are busy.
            This is worth doing today, with the app you already deployed. Open your GitHub Pages URL on your phone, add it to the home screen, and look at it. You built that. It has an icon. It opens without a browser in the way. That is a real thing to have done, and it cost nothing.

            Fifty-one seconds showing exactly what this page just told you: iOS gives you no prompt. You open the site in the browser, press Share, scroll down, and choose Add to Home Screen. Worth watching once so you know what you are looking for — it is easy to assume it has not worked.

            Capacitor wraps what you already built

            A home screen icon is a real win, but it is still a web page. Capacitor turns the same files into an actual native app — one that can go in the App Store, use the camera, and appear in the app switcher like anything else.

            It works by running your web app inside the phone’s own browser engine, wrapped in a native shell. Which has one consequence that matters enormously to you: your game comes too. A web view runs canvas and WebGL, so the Phaser game from Section 18 works inside it without a single line changed.

            terminal — in your existing project
            npm i @capacitor/core
npm i -D @capacitor/cli
npx cap init

npm i @capacitor/android @capacitor/ios
npx cap add ios
npx cap sync

            npx cap init asks for an app name and an app id, and creates capacitor.config.json. One setting in it does all the work:

            capacitor.config.json
            {
  "appId": "com.yourname.moodtracker",
  "appName": "Mood Tracker",
  "webDir": "dist"
}
            "webDir": "dist" is the entire bridge, and you built it last section. Capacitor does not care how your site was made. It wants a folder of finished web files, and npm run build produces exactly that. Run npm run build, then npx cap sync to copy the result into the native project. Those two commands, in that order, every time you change something.

            What you need installed, and it is worth knowing before you start rather than halfway through:

            • Node 22 or higher. You have Node 24 from Section 16.
            • For iOS: a Mac, and Xcode 26 or newer. There is no way around the Mac — Apple does not allow iOS builds anywhere else. Xcode is a very large download; start it before you need it.
            • For Android: Android Studio 2025.2.1 or newer, plus Android SDK Platforms for API 24 or above. It installs the Java toolchain for you.

            Which folder does Capacitor take your app from — the one with your source code in it, or the one npm run build produces?

            Getting it onto your own iPhone, for nothing

            This is the part that surprises people. You do not need to pay Apple to run your own app on your own phone.

            With a free Apple account, Xcode gives you what Apple calls a Personal Team. Plug your iPhone into your Mac, open the project with npx cap open ios, pick your phone as the target, press play. It installs. It is on your home screen. It is yours.

            The limits, stated honestly:

            • It expires after 7 days. Then it will not open until you plug in and install it again.
            • Up to 10 app IDs, and 3 test devices per platform.
            Seven days is not a problem for what you are doing. You are not distributing anything; you are proving to yourself that the thing you built runs on your phone. Re-installing takes thirty seconds. When you have something you want other people to keep, that is the moment to pay — not before.

            True or false: you must pay Apple $99 before you can run an app you wrote on your own iPhone.

            Apple App StoreGoogle Play
            Cost$99 per year, ongoing$25 once, ever
            Stop paying andyour app comes downnothing happens
            You must owna Macany computer

            Apple waives the fee for nonprofits, schools and government bodies. Google’s $25 is a one-off registration and cannot be paid with a prepaid card.

            If you are going to publish one thing, publish on Google Play first. Twenty-five pounds-ish, paid once, no Mac required, and a faster route to being live.             Clue found

            This pattern has followed you through the entire guide, and it is worth carrying out of it. Hosting looked like it cost money — GitHub Pages was free. A game engine looked like it cost money — Phaser was free. A code editor, version control, a build tool, a database: all free, all professional-grade, all used by people being paid a great deal to use them. The paid tier in software is usually about scale, support or distribution — almost never about capability. When something looks priced out of reach, the first question is not “can I afford it” but “what is the free rung, and is it actually enough for what I am doing”. It very often is.

            Why this section is not about React Native

            You will hear about React Native constantly. It is what a lot of well-known apps are built with, and if you ask the internet “how do I make a mobile app with JavaScript” it is the answer you will get. So it is worth being clear about why you have not just used it.

            React Native does not use the web. There is no document, no querySelector, no CSS file, no <canvas>. It writes JavaScript that drives genuinely native components. Which means, concretely:

            PWA / CapacitorReact Native
            Your mood trackercomes as it isrewrite the whole interface
            Your Phaser gamecomes as it isdoes not come at all
            Sections 7, 8, 10 (DOM & CSS)still truemostly does not apply
            What it isa bridgea rewrite

            So React Native is not a harder version of what this section does. It is a different thing, for a different situation — an app that has to feel unmistakably native, lean hard on device hardware, or perform like a native app. If you build something later that genuinely needs that, it is the right tool and you now know enough to learn it.

            Wrapping a web app is not the amateur option. A very large number of apps on your phone right now are a web view in a native shell, including some you would never guess. The professional decision is not “always native”; it is choosing the cheapest thing that meets the requirement. For two things you have already built and want on a phone, that is a wrapper.

            In one word: for the two things you have already built, is React Native a bridge or a rewrite?

            The end of the guide is not the end of the work

            You started this not knowing what a variable was. You can now write JavaScript, build and deploy a real app, build a real game on a real framework, use the same tools professionals use, and put the result on a phone.

            Everything from here is the same loop, repeated: decide what to build, find out what you do not know, build it badly, fix it. That loop does not change, and nobody outgrows it. The difference between you now and a working developer is not method — it is how many times round the loop they have been.

            The single most useful thing you can do next is build something nobody asked for. Not a tutorial project. Something small and slightly annoying to you personally — a tracker for a thing you keep forgetting, a tool for a hobby, a game about a private joke. Tutorial projects teach you to follow. The first thing you build with no instructions is where the learning actually consolidates, because there is nobody to tell you which bit you have forgotten.

            Two habits worth taking with you, both of which this guide has been quietly drilling:

            • Read the error message. Actually read it. Section 15 exists because that one habit separates people who get unstuck from people who stay stuck.
            • Make the smallest version that runs, then grow it. Every section here started with something that worked and added to it. Never write two hundred lines and then find out.

            The update that never arrives

            Your app is installed on your phone and works offline. You fix a bug, redeploy, and open the app. You get the old version. You force-refresh and still get the old version. Nothing is broken, and your service worker is doing exactly what you told it to. What did you tell it to do?

            Clue found

            A cache with no version in its name is a bug with a delay on it. The first release works beautifully, and every release after it is invisible to anyone who already has the app. The pattern is two halves and you need both: const CACHE = "app-v3", so new code writes somewhere new; and, in the activate event, walk caches.keys() and delete every name that is not the current one. Miss the first half and updates never land. Miss the second and you keep every version you have ever shipped on the user\u2019s phone, forever.

            Shipping an update, once a service worker exists

            One consequence of all this is worth stating before you build anything real. Because the service worker sits between the page and the network and is installed once, shipping a fix is simply a matter of deploying the new files - the worker picks them up on the next visit the same way an ordinary web page does.

            It is not, and this is the single most reported problem with PWAs. A worker that was told to serve from the cache does exactly that, including for the file you just fixed. You are going to write the half that is missing - and you get a specification and an empty box, not code to correct.

            Write a function called stale(names, current).

            • names is an array of cache names, exactly as caches.keys() would give them to you.
            • current is the one your new worker is about to use.
            • It returns an array of the names that should be deleted, in the order they appeared.

            Two things it must get right, and they are the reason this is a puzzle and not a one-liner. The current cache is never deleted. And a phone may hold caches that have nothing to do with your app - anything not starting "app-" is somebody else's and must be left alone.

            sw.js
            Where it goes, once it works. Inside the activate event - the moment a new worker takes over and the only safe point to remove what the old one was serving:
            caches.keys().then(ns => Promise.all(stale(ns, CACHE).map(n => caches.delete(n))))

            Level 2: the last one, and it works with no signal

            The final build in the guide. It puts together the four things this section exists for: talking to the network, keeping what came back, versioning what you ship, and putting it on the page.

            Four groups, four badges, and for several competences this is the second context - which means passing here is what finally earns them.

            Your code runs with five things already defined:

            • caches - behaves like the real Cache Storage: keys(), open(name), delete(name). An opened cache has match(url) and put(url, response).
            • fetch - the real thing, including failing when offline.
            • listEl - an empty <ul>.
            • CACHE_VERSION - a string like "v2".
            • URLS - the addresses to show.

            What it has to do:

            1. Work in a cache whose name contains CACHE_VERSION, and delete every other app- cache before you start.
            2. For each URL, look in the cache first. Only go to the network on a miss.
            3. Anything you fetch successfully goes into the cache, so the next run works offline.
            4. Put one <li> per URL into listEl, holding the body text.
            5. If a URL is in neither the cache nor reachable, say so on the page for that URL and carry on with the rest. Nothing may throw.

            You may use await at the top level. Reading a response's body is await res.text(), and it is a separate step from getting the response - the same two-step wait as Section 14.
